### Pattern 146 — Vitest `coverage.watermarks`: calibrating the red/yellow/green thresholds in HTML reports  [official]

Vitest's HTML coverage reporter colors files green, yellow, or red based on configurable watermark ranges. The defaults — low 50%, high 80% — are inherited from Istanbul and rarely match real project expectations. When a new project starts with 30% coverage, every file appears red, causing developers to dismiss the report as noise. When a mature project reaches 90%, files with 82% appear green even though they fall below the team's 85% target. Calibrating `coverage.watermarks` to match actual project thresholds makes the visual report meaningful and actionable.

The `watermarks` object accepts four sub-keys (`statements`, `branches`, `functions`, `lines`), each a two-element array `[low, high]`. Values below `low` are red, between `low` and `high` are yellow, and above `high` are green. Aligning `high` with your `thresholds` percentage means green always implies the gate will pass.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — calibrated watermarks matching project threshold gates
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Thresholds: gate CI at 85% lines/statements/functions, 75% branches
      thresholds: {
        lines: 85,
        statements: 85,
        functions: 85,
        branches: 75,
      },

      // Watermarks: align HIGH with the threshold so green == CI pass.
      // LOW is set 15 pts below HIGH — yellow is "approaching the gate".
      watermarks: {
        statements: [70, 85],
        branches:   [60, 75],
        functions:  [70, 85],
        lines:      [70, 85],
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: misaligned watermarks produce habituation — developers stop reading the report because colors no longer convey actionable information. The cost of calibration is a one-time team discussion about what percentages are meaningful. Re-calibrate when the threshold gate is raised; stale watermarks that show everything green while thresholds have increased are more misleading than no colors at all. For monorepos with per-package thresholds, consider using `coverageProvider: 'v8'` and separate Vitest workspace configs so each package gets its own watermark calibration.

---

### Pattern 147 — Vitest `coverage.ignoreClassMethods`: excluding infrastructure boilerplate from coverage enforcement  [official]

Istanbul's class-method coverage includes every method name, including lifecycle hooks and abstract interface implementations that exist purely for framework conformance. In Angular applications, `ngOnInit` / `ngOnDestroy` are frequently empty stubs; in NestJS, `onApplicationBootstrap` / `onModuleDestroy` are often no-ops that satisfy the `OnApplicationBootstrap` interface. Counting these methods as uncovered functions lowers the reported function coverage metric without providing meaningful quality signal.

`coverage.ignoreClassMethods` accepts an array of method name strings. Any method matching a name in the list is excluded from the function coverage counter across all classes, regardless of which class defines it. The exclusion is name-based, not class-based — use precise names to avoid broad exclusions.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — ignoring lifecycle/infrastructure methods in NestJS application
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.module.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Exclude NestJS lifecycle hooks that are structural stubs.
      // These methods satisfy interface contracts but contain no testable logic.
      ignoreClassMethods: [
        'onModuleInit',
        'onModuleDestroy',
        'onApplicationBootstrap',
        'onApplicationShutdown',
        'beforeApplicationShutdown',
        // Angular lifecycle hooks (if mixing Angular + NestJS in a monorepo):
        'ngOnInit',
        'ngOnDestroy',
        'ngOnChanges',
      ],

      thresholds: {
        functions: 85,
        lines: 85,
        statements: 85,
        branches: 75,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `ignoreClassMethods` is name-based, so excluding `ngOnInit` silently removes ALL classes with that method name from function coverage — including a custom class where `ngOnInit` contains real business logic. For methods that sometimes contain logic (e.g., `constructor` body initialization), do NOT add them to this list; instead, add `/* istanbul ignore next */` comments in the specific empty implementations. Review the list quarterly to ensure no logic-bearing methods have been added to the exclusion set.

---

### Pattern 148 — Vitest `coverage.excludeAfterRemap`: fixing ghost coverage after TypeScript source-map remapping  [official]

V8 coverage collects raw byte-offset data keyed to compiled JavaScript files. When Vitest remaps that data through source maps back to TypeScript source locations, some compiled positions map to TypeScript lines that are already excluded by `coverage.exclude` patterns. Without `excludeAfterRemap: true`, these positions are remapped first and then the exclude patterns are checked against the TypeScript path — which may or may not match. With `excludeAfterRemap: true` (default since Vitest 4.x), exclude patterns are re-evaluated after remap, ensuring that TypeScript files excluded by pattern are fully absent from the coverage report even when their compiled counterparts had coverage data.

The issue manifests as ghost coverage: a file like `src/generated/schema.ts` appears in the HTML report with partial coverage even though `src/generated/**` is in `coverage.exclude`. Enabling `excludeAfterRemap` corrects this by re-filtering the remapped result.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — excludeAfterRemap for TypeScript generated-code exclusion
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],

      // These patterns are matched against the REMAPPED TypeScript path,
      // not the compiled JavaScript path.  excludeAfterRemap ensures the
      // pattern check runs on the final TypeScript path, not the intermediate.
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        'src/**/__mocks__/**',
        'src/generated/**',       // GraphQL / Prisma generated files
        'src/**/*.module.ts',     // NestJS DI wiring
        'src/**/index.ts',        // Re-export barrels
      ],

      // Reapply exclude patterns after source-map remapping.
      // Without this, generated files can appear in coverage if their
      // compiled counterparts had coverage recorded before remap.
      excludeAfterRemap: true,

      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      thresholds: { lines: 85, branches: 75 },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `excludeAfterRemap: true` adds a second filtering pass over the remapped coverage data, which adds a small processing overhead (typically < 2s for < 500 files). The tradeoff is always worth accepting: ghost coverage from generated files inflates reported percentages, producing false confidence. Projects with large amounts of generated code (Prisma schemas, GraphQL code-gen output) can see 5-10% coverage inflation without this setting, making thresholds meaningless for the files that actually matter.

---

### Pattern 149 — Jest `coverageProvider: 'v8'` with `collectCoverageFrom` all-files enforcement  [official]

Jest supports two coverage providers: `babel` (the default, which uses Istanbul's AST-based instrumentation) and `v8` (which uses Node.js's built-in V8 coverage engine). The V8 provider is faster because it requires no compile-time transformation of source files, but it reports raw byte-offset coverage rather than statement-level coverage. When `collectCoverageFrom` is specified without `coverageProvider: 'v8'`, Jest's babel provider instruments files at import time — files never imported by any test appear in the report only when `collectCoverageFrom` forces their inclusion.

Combining `coverageProvider: 'v8'` with a comprehensive `collectCoverageFrom` array is the fastest way to enforce all-files coverage in large Jest projects. The V8 provider does not require transforming every file; it uses V8's execution context to record which byte ranges were executed.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — V8 provider with forced all-files coverage reporting
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  coverageProvider: 'v8',

  // Collect coverage from all source files, not just imported ones.
  // Without this, files with zero imports appear in no report at all
  // rather than appearing as 0% — hiding coverage debt entirely.
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,js}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.{ts,js}',
    '!src/**/__mocks__/**',
    '!src/**/index.ts',
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',
  ],

  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  coverageDirectory: './coverage',

  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      lines: 80,
      branches: 70,
      functions: 80,
      statements: 80,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverageProvider: 'v8'` produces different branch coverage numbers than `babel` for the same test suite because V8 tracks execution at the bytecode level while Istanbul tracks AST-level branches. A project switching from `babel` to `v8` should treat the switch as a coverage baseline reset event: branch coverage numbers may change by ±5-15%, and previous thresholds may need recalibration. V8 is generally more accurate for async flows and generated class code (decorators, TypeScript abstract classes) where Istanbul's AST instrumentation sometimes over-counts branches.

---

### Pattern 150 — c8 v11 `--experimental-monocart` reporter: unified V8 + source-map coverage with console-detail  [official]

c8 v10.1.0 introduced an experimental Monocart reporter integration (`--experimental-monocart`) that produces a richer HTML coverage report directly from V8's byte-offset data without Istanbul remap. The Monocart renderer shows original V8 coverage data alongside source-mapped TypeScript, including per-function execution counts, uncovered byte ranges highlighted in the editor view, and a `console-details` summary with function-call histograms. Unlike the default Istanbul-remapped HTML, the Monocart output preserves V8's original byte-range fidelity — useful for debugging cases where Istanbul remap incorrectly attributes coverage to the wrong TypeScript line.

As of c8 v11.0.0 (February 2026), the Monocart integration requires Node 20 or >=22 (consistent with the v11 engine requirement) and must be opted into explicitly.

```typescript
// TypeScript wrapper for invoking c8 with monocart reporter via child_process
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';

interface C8MonocartOptions {
  includePattern: string;
  reportsDir: string;
  thresholds: { branches: number; lines: number; functions: number };
  testCommand: string;
}

function runCoverageWithMonocart(opts: C8MonocartOptions): void {
  const c8Args = [
    '--experimental-monocart',
    '--reporter=v8',
    '--reporter=html',
    '--reporter=text',
    `--reports-dir=${opts.reportsDir}`,
    '--all',
    `--include=${opts.includePattern}`,
    '--exclude=**/*.spec.ts',
    '--check-coverage',
    `--branches=${opts.thresholds.branches}`,
    `--lines=${opts.thresholds.lines}`,
    `--functions=${opts.thresholds.functions}`,
  ].join(' ');

  execSync(`npx c8 ${c8Args} ${opts.testCommand}`, {
    stdio: 'inherit',
    env: { ...process.env, NODE_OPTIONS: '--experimental-vm-modules' },
  });
}

runCoverageWithMonocart({
  includePattern: 'src/**/*.ts',
  reportsDir: './coverage-monocart',
  thresholds: { branches: 80, lines: 85, functions: 85 },
  testCommand: 'node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/jest',
});
```

**Tradeoff**: the Monocart integration is experimental — its API and output format may change between c8 minor releases. Do not depend on the Monocart HTML output format in CI pipelines that parse coverage HTML (e.g., coverage comment bots). Use `--reporter=json-summary` or `--reporter=lcov` for machine-readable output and reserve the Monocart reporter for developer-facing local reports. The `console-details` output adds 0.3-0.8s per run for large function inventories; disable it in fast-feedback CI jobs.

---

### Pattern 151 — NYC `watermarks` configuration: per-dimension red/yellow/green bands for legacy project dashboards  [official]

NYC's `watermarks` configuration key defines separate low/high percentage bounds for each coverage dimension, controlling the color coding in the text-table and HTML summary output. Like Vitest's watermarks, NYC's defaults (low 50%, high 80%) are often unsuitable for projects with strong or weak coverage cultures. A project that ships with 95% line coverage but 60% branch coverage may be set to all-green by default despite the branch coverage representing a real quality gap.

NYC accepts `watermarks` as a nested object in `.nycrc.json` or `package.json`. Each dimension key maps to a two-element array `[low, high]`.

```typescript
// TypeScript helper — programmatic nyc runner using calibrated watermarks
import Nyc from 'nyc';

// Matching .nycrc.json equivalent:
// { "branches": 70, "lines": 85, "functions": 85, "statements": 85,
//   "watermarks": { "lines": [70, 85], "statements": [70, 85],
//                  "functions": [70, 85], "branches": [55, 70] } }

async function runCoverageWithWatermarks(): Promise<void> {
  const nyc = new Nyc({
    cwd: process.cwd(),
    include:   ['src/**/*.ts'],
    exclude:   ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**', 'src/**/index.ts'],
    reporter:  ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
    reportDir: './coverage',
    branches:   70,
    lines:      85,
    functions:  85,
    statements: 85,

    // Align HIGH with the corresponding threshold value.
    // Files between LOW and HIGH appear yellow — "approaching the gate".
    // Files below LOW appear red — "failing the gate badly".
    watermarks: {
      lines:      [70, 85],
      statements: [70, 85],
      functions:  [70, 85],
      branches:   [55, 70],
    },
  });

  await nyc.reset();
  await nyc.wrap();
  // Run test suite here (spawn mocha or other runner as a child process)
  await nyc.writeCoverageFile();
  await nyc.report();
  const passed = nyc.checkCoverage();
  if (!passed) process.exit(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff**: NYC's programmatic API (`new Nyc(...)`) is lightly documented and the constructor options do not perfectly mirror `.nycrc.json` key names — some options use camelCase in the API and kebab-case in the config file (`report-dir` vs `reportDir`). Always validate the programmatic runner against the CLI output for a known test suite before trusting it in CI. For greenfield projects using Node 20+, prefer c8 v11 over nyc v18 for V8-native coverage; reserve NYC for legacy mocha/tap ecosystems where Istanbul's AST instrumentation is required.

---

### Pattern 152 — Stryker `disableBail` for complete survivor maps in mutation regression analysis  [official]

Stryker's default behaviour (`disableBail: false`) stops running tests for a mutant as soon as the first failing test is found — this is the "bail" optimization that makes mutation runs faster. However, in regression analysis workflows — where you want to understand which tests cover which mutants and how many tests catch each mutant — bailing early means you only ever see one covering test per mutant. Setting `disableBail: true` runs all tests against every mutant, producing a full coverage map that reveals whether a mutant is covered by one test or ten.

This complete coverage map is valuable for test suite health auditing: mutants caught by only one test indicate brittle coverage (remove that test and the mutant survives), while mutants caught by many tests may indicate redundant tests. The `json` reporter's `coveredBy` arrays are populated only when `disableBail` is active.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — disableBail for full mutation coverage map
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

export default {
  testRunner: 'vitest',

  // Must be perTest to populate coveredBy arrays in the JSON report.
  // 'all' or 'off' modes do not produce per-mutant test attribution.
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',

  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',
    '!src/**/index.ts',
  ],

  // Disable bail: run ALL covering tests per mutant (not just the first catcher).
  // This multiplies run time by the average test-per-mutant count.
  // Use ONLY in scheduled weekly health audits, not in per-commit CI gates.
  disableBail: true,

  reporters: ['json', 'progress'],
  jsonReporter: { fileName: 'reports/mutation/full-coverage-map.json' },

  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: 50 },
  timeoutMS: 15000,
  concurrency: 4,
  incremental: false,  // Disable incremental for accurate full-run baseline
} satisfies Config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `disableBail: true` multiplies total mutation run time by the average number of tests per mutant — for a project with 50 tests per module, a run that takes 10 minutes with bail may take 40-60 minutes without it. This makes `disableBail` unsuitable for every-commit CI. Use it in a scheduled weekly health job and store the resulting `full-coverage-map.json` as a build artifact. Diff it between sprints to detect coverage density regression — mutants moving from "covered by 5 tests" to "covered by 1 test" are a warning sign that test removal has degraded redundancy.

---

### Pattern 153 — Jest `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` vs `collectCoverageFrom` exclusion: precedence and interaction  [official]

Jest has two orthogonal mechanisms for excluding files from coverage: `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` (an array of regexp strings matched against file paths) and `collectCoverageFrom` (an array of micromatch glob patterns for files that should be collected). These mechanisms interact in a non-obvious way: `collectCoverageFrom` determines which files are instrumented, and `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` filters files from the final report. A file matching a `collectCoverageFrom` glob but also matching a `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` pattern is instrumented but excluded from the report — this wastes instrumentation overhead and causes confusing gaps in the HTML report.

The recommended pattern is to use `collectCoverageFrom` negation globs as the single source of truth and keep `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` only for node_modules or external paths that cannot be expressed as negation globs.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — explicit collectCoverageFrom negation globs, minimal coveragePathIgnorePatterns
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  coverageProvider: 'babel',

  // PREFERRED: use collectCoverageFrom negation globs for all exclusions.
  // Micromatch patterns are readable, auditable, and testable with micromatch.match().
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/__mocks__/**',
    '!src/**/index.ts',          // Re-export barrels: no logic to test
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',       // NestJS DI wiring
    '!src/generated/**',         // GraphQL/Prisma generated files
  ],

  // MINIMAL: only paths that cannot be expressed as collectCoverageFrom negations
  // (e.g., workspace symlinks that resolve outside the project root).
  coveragePathIgnorePatterns: [
    '/node_modules/',
    '/dist/',
  ],

  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: using `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` as the primary exclusion mechanism (as many legacy configs do) means exclusions are regexp-based rather than glob-based, making them harder to read and audit. Regexp exclusion patterns are not validated against the file tree — a typo in a regexp silently includes files you meant to exclude. Migrating to `collectCoverageFrom` negation globs is safer because micromatch patterns are easier to read, test with `micromatch.match()`, and document. Treat this migration as a coverage baseline reset: the first run after migration may show different file counts.

---

### Pattern 154 — Stryker `coverageAnalysis: 'all'` with NoCoverage budget: surfacing untested code without full `perTest` overhead  [official]

Stryker's `coverageAnalysis` option has three modes: `off` (run all tests for every mutant), `perTest` (run only tests that cover each mutant), and `all` (mark mutants with no test coverage as `NoCoverage` without running tests against them). The `all` mode is a middle ground: it runs the full test suite once to collect coverage data, marks uncovered mutants as `NoCoverage` immediately, and runs tests against covered mutants only. This is faster than `off` but less granular than `perTest`.

The key benefit of `all` over `perTest` is that it avoids the `singleThread: true` constraint — `perTest` requires Stryker to control test execution order and isolation, but `all` only needs a single coverage pass followed by per-mutant full runs.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — coverageAnalysis: 'all' for global-state test suites
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

export default {
  testRunner: 'vitest',

  // 'all' mode: single coverage pass, then full suite per covered mutant.
  // Safer than 'perTest' when tests share global state, in-memory caches,
  // or module-level singletons that cause perTest false survivors.
  coverageAnalysis: 'all',

  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',
    '!src/**/index.ts',
  ],

  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: 50 },
  reporters: ['html', 'progress', 'json'],
  timeoutMS: 10000,
  concurrency: '50%',
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: '.stryker-tmp/incremental.json',

  // allowEmpty: prevents hard exit when NoCoverage count exceeds zero.
  // Track NoCoverage ratio as a health metric: > 20% indicates coverage gaps.
  allowEmpty: true,
} satisfies Config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverageAnalysis: 'all'` reports `NoCoverage` for uncovered mutants but does not tell you which specific test would catch a given mutant (unlike `perTest`). The `disableBail` flag has no effect in `all` mode. For mutation score accuracy, `perTest` is still the gold standard; use `all` as a faster alternative when test suite isolation makes `perTest` unreliable. Projects where tests share global singletons frequently see false survivors with `perTest` that disappear with `all` or `off`.

---

### Pattern 155 — coverage.py `dynamic_context` with `test_function` for per-test file attribution  [official]

coverage.py's `dynamic_context` option records which test function was running when each line was executed, storing this information in the `.coverage` SQLite database. With `dynamic_context = test_function`, the database contains per-test attribution data that can be queried with `coverage debug data` or programmatically via the `CoverageData` API. This attribution enables test suite auditing workflows: finding lines covered by only one test, identifying tests that cover unexpectedly large code areas (potential sign of too-broad integration tests), and building per-test coverage reports.

The data is stored in the `.coverage` SQLite file as contexts — each context is a string like `test_module::test_function`. The `coverage report --contexts` flag filters the report to a specific context pattern.

```python
# .coveragerc — dynamic context attribution for per-test coverage analysis
[run]
source = src/
branch = True
dynamic_context = test_function
parallel = False            # parallel=True shards .coverage files; merge with combine first

[report]
exclude_also =
    if TYPE_CHECKING:
    \.\.\.
    @(abc\.)?abstractmethod
    @overload
precision = 2
show_missing = True

[html]
directory = htmlcov/
title = Coverage Report with Per-Test Context
```

```typescript
// TypeScript analogy — per-test coverage attribution concept
// (Actual usage is in Python; this illustrates the concept for cross-language teams)

type TestContext = {
  testName: string;
  coveredLines: Map<string, Set<number>>;
};

// After test run: coverage report --contexts="tests/unit/test_payment.py::*"
// shows only lines covered by tests in test_payment.py.
function findSinglyTestedLines(contexts: TestContext[]): Array<{ file: string; line: number }> {
  const lineToTests = new Map<string, string[]>();
  for (const ctx of contexts) {
    for (const [file, lines] of ctx.coveredLines) {
      for (const line of lines) {
        const key = `${file}:${line}`;
        lineToTests.set(key, [...(lineToTests.get(key) ?? []), ctx.testName]);
      }
    }
  }
  // Lines covered by exactly one test are brittle — removing that test = gap
  return [...lineToTests.entries()]
    .filter(([, tests]) => tests.length === 1)
    .map(([key]) => {
      const [file, lineStr] = key.split(':');
      return { file, line: Number(lineStr) };
    });
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `dynamic_context = test_function` increases the `.coverage` database size significantly — a project with 1000 tests and 500 source files can produce a `.coverage` file 10-20x larger than without dynamic contexts. This slows `coverage report` and `coverage html` generation proportionally. Limit dynamic context collection to local development or weekly scheduled audit runs; do not enable it in every-commit CI where coverage HTML generation is on the critical path. When using `parallel = True` for distributed test runs (pytest-xdist), each shard produces a `.coverage.N` file — merge them with `coverage combine` before querying contexts.

---

### Pattern 156 — Vitest `coverage.allowExternal`: measuring coverage in workspace packages from the consuming app  [official]

By default, Vitest only collects coverage for files within the project's root directory. In a monorepo workspace, if `packages/shared-utils` is a peer package resolved from `node_modules` or a workspace symlink, its files are considered "external" and excluded from coverage — even when tests in `apps/web` directly import and exercise those utilities. `coverage.allowExternal: true` removes this restriction and includes all instrumented files regardless of whether they live under the project root.

This is particularly valuable for monorepos where shared business logic lives in workspace packages that have no dedicated test suite; consumer-app tests become the primary coverage signal for shared code.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — allowExternal for monorepo workspace package coverage
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import path from 'node:path';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',

      // Allow coverage collection for files outside the project root.
      // This includes workspace packages resolved via node_modules symlinks.
      allowExternal: true,

      // Include both the app source and the shared workspace packages.
      // Use path.resolve to canonicalize symlink targets for consistent paths.
      include: [
        'src/**/*.ts',
        path.resolve(__dirname, '../../packages/shared-utils/src/**/*.ts'),
        path.resolve(__dirname, '../../packages/domain-models/src/**/*.ts'),
      ],

      exclude: [
        '**/*.spec.ts',
        '**/*.d.ts',
        '**/__mocks__/**',
        '**/index.ts',
        '**/node_modules/**',
      ],

      // With allowExternal, HTML report paths may become absolute.
      // Use reportsDirectory relative to the workspace root for consistent CI artifacts.
      reportsDirectory: path.resolve(__dirname, '../../coverage/web-app'),

      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary'],
      thresholds: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80 },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `allowExternal: true` can produce unexpected coverage inflation or deflation depending on which workspace packages are imported. If a shared utility is used in 5 apps and each app's test suite covers different paths, the coverage percentage per package will differ across app-level reports. Do not aggregate `allowExternal` coverage across multiple apps as a single quality signal — the same file will have different coverage in each consumer context. Use `allowExternal` for the consumer-app report only; maintain a dedicated test suite in the shared package for canonical coverage measurement.

---

### Pattern 157 — Jest `coverageThreshold` per-glob patterns with `global` fallback: two-tier threshold strategy  [official]

Jest's `coverageThreshold` supports both a `global` key (applying to all collected files by aggregate) and per-path glob keys (applying to files matching the pattern). A two-tier strategy uses high thresholds for critical business-logic paths and lower thresholds globally, ensuring that high-value code cannot hide behind aggregate coverage while allowing lower-value boilerplate to have relaxed requirements.

Since Jest 30.4, the `global` key applies only to files NOT matched by any per-pattern key. This means well-designed two-tier strategies become even more important: patterns must cover all critical files explicitly, and global acts as the safety net for uncategorized files.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — two-tier threshold: critical paths at 95%, global at 75%
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,js}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/index.ts',
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',
  ],
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',

  coverageThreshold: {
    // Critical business-logic paths: strict 95% across all dimensions.
    // Money, auth, and PII processing — quality bar is non-negotiable.
    './src/payments/': {
      branches: 95,
      functions: 95,
      lines: 95,
      statements: 95,
    },
    './src/auth/': {
      branches: 90,
      functions: 95,
      lines: 95,
      statements: 95,
    },

    // After Jest 30.4: 'global' applies ONLY to files not matched above.
    // Catches new files that don't fall under a critical-path pattern.
    global: {
      branches: 70,
      functions: 75,
      lines: 75,
      statements: 75,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: the two-tier strategy requires active maintenance — when a new critical feature is added (e.g., `src/compliance/`), a developer must remember to add a per-pattern threshold entry. Without it, the new critical code falls through to the global threshold. Mitigate this by adding a periodic CI check that lists files in known critical directories and verifies they have a per-pattern threshold entry in the config. Alternatively, use negative global thresholds (`branches: -5`) as the fallback rather than a percentage, so that any uncategorized file with low coverage adds to the global failure count rather than diluting a percentage.

---

### Pattern 158 — c8 `--all` flag with `--include` scoping: preventing zero-import files from escaping coverage gates  [official]

By default, c8 only records coverage for files that were actually loaded during test execution. A file with no imports in any test has no V8 execution record and thus no coverage data — it does not appear in the report at all, making it invisible to the threshold gate. The `--all` flag forces c8 to include all files matching the `--include` pattern in the coverage report, even those with zero imports, marking them as 0% covered.

Without `--all`, coverage gates can pass with high percentages while large chunks of untested code exist in the codebase. This is a silent failure mode that is easy to miss when new files are added.

```typescript
// TypeScript helper: generate c8 CLI command with --all enforcement
interface C8CoverageOptions {
  include: string[];
  exclude: string[];
  reporter: string[];
  thresholds: { branches: number; lines: number; functions: number; statements: number };
  reportsDir: string;
  testCommand: string;
}

function buildC8Command(opts: C8CoverageOptions): string {
  const includeArgs = opts.include.map(p => `--include="${p}"`).join(' ');
  const excludeArgs = opts.exclude.map(p => `--exclude="${p}"`).join(' ');
  const reporterArgs = opts.reporter.map(r => `--reporter=${r}`).join(' ');

  const thresholdArgs = [
    `--branches=${opts.thresholds.branches}`,
    `--lines=${opts.thresholds.lines}`,
    `--functions=${opts.thresholds.functions}`,
    `--statements=${opts.thresholds.statements}`,
  ].join(' ');

  return [
    'c8',
    '--all',               // Include all matched files, even those never imported
    '--check-coverage',    // Fail if thresholds are not met
    includeArgs,
    excludeArgs,
    reporterArgs,
    `--reports-dir="${opts.reportsDir}"`,
    thresholdArgs,
    opts.testCommand,
  ].join(' ');
}

const cmd = buildC8Command({
  include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
  exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**', 'src/**/index.ts'],
  reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  thresholds: { branches: 70, lines: 80, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
  reportsDir: './coverage',
  testCommand: 'node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/jest',
});

console.log('Running:', cmd);
```

**Tradeoff**: `--all` with a broad `--include` pattern adds overhead proportional to the number of files — c8 must load and parse every matched file to produce a 0% baseline entry. For large monorepos with thousands of source files, this can add 10-30 seconds to the coverage run. Mitigate by tightening `--include` to the package under test (e.g., `src/payments/**/*.ts` rather than `src/**/*.ts`). Always pair `--all` with `--include` scoping; without `--include`, c8's `--all` may traverse node_modules and produce enormous reports.

---

### Pattern 159 — Stryker `ignorePatterns` + `mutate` negation globs: layered exclusion for generated and infrastructure code  [official]

Stryker has two overlapping exclusion mechanisms: `ignorePatterns` (a top-level array of glob patterns for files Stryker should not read at all) and negation globs in the `mutate` array (prefixed with `!` to exclude files from mutation). Using both correctly avoids subtle differences in behavior: `ignorePatterns` prevents Stryker from even loading matched files (faster, but coarser), while `mutate` negation globs still cause Stryker to load and parse the file but skip generating mutants for it.

For large generated files (Prisma client, GraphQL schema types), `ignorePatterns` is the right tool — there is no value in parsing them. For source files that should be loaded (for coverage analysis) but not mutated (infrastructure wiring), `mutate` negation is correct.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — layered ignorePatterns + mutate negation
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

export default {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',

  // ignorePatterns: Stryker does not read these files at all.
  // Use for generated, large, or unrelated-to-source files.
  ignorePatterns: [
    'node_modules',
    'dist',
    'coverage',
    '.stryker-tmp',
    'src/generated',           // Prisma/GraphQL generated — never mutate or read
    '**/*.d.ts',               // TypeScript declarations: no runtime logic
    '**/*.json',               // Config/data files
    'stryker.config.*',
  ],

  // mutate: files to generate mutants for.
  // Negation globs (!) load the file (for coverage) but skip mutant generation.
  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',     // NestJS DI wiring: structural, not logic
    '!src/**/*.dto.ts',        // DTOs: validated by class-validator, not conditionals
    '!src/**/*.entity.ts',     // TypeORM entities: column definitions, not logic
    '!src/**/index.ts',
    '!src/**/migrations/**',   // DB migrations: idempotent, not unit testable
  ],

  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: 50 },
  reporters: ['html', 'progress'],
  timeoutMS: 10000,
  concurrency: '50%',
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: '.stryker-tmp/incremental.json',
  ignoreStatic: true,
} satisfies Config;
```

**Tradeoff**: over-broad `ignorePatterns` can prevent Stryker from calculating `NoCoverage` for files that should appear in the mutation score denominator. If a critical service file is accidentally placed in an `ignorePatterns` glob, it disappears from the mutation report entirely — the mutation score looks better than it is because the file's uncovered mutants are not counted. Audit `ignorePatterns` quarterly: run `stryker --dryRun` and examine the list of files Stryker considers; any missing critical file is a sign that `ignorePatterns` is too broad.

---

### Pattern 160 — Vitest `coverage.reporter` with `['json-summary']` for lightweight CI badge generation  [official]

Coverage badge generation (the shield.io-style "Coverage: 87%" badge in README files) requires a machine-readable coverage summary. Vitest's `json-summary` reporter produces a minimal `coverage-summary.json` file with total percentages for each dimension — it is far smaller than the full `json` reporter output and processes faster. Including `json-summary` as a reporter alongside `lcov` (for tools like Codecov/Coveralls) and `text` (for CI log output) gives all the outputs needed by different consumers without the overhead of the full JSON report.

The `coverage-summary.json` file follows the Istanbul `coverage-summary` schema and can be consumed by badge generators, PR comment bots, and custom CI scripts.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — multi-reporter setup for CI badge + upload + log
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],

      // Multi-reporter: each serves a different consumer.
      // json-summary: badge generators and PR comment bots (1-5 KB, fast)
      // lcov:         Codecov, Coveralls, SonarQube upload
      // text:         CI log output (human-readable table)
      reporter: [
        'json-summary',
        'lcov',
        'text',
      ],

      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      thresholds: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
    },
  },
});

// ci/post-coverage.ts — read json-summary and generate badge URL
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

interface CoverageSummaryEntry {
  total: number; covered: number; skipped: number; pct: number;
}
interface CoverageSummary {
  total: {
    lines:      CoverageSummaryEntry;
    statements: CoverageSummaryEntry;
    functions:  CoverageSummaryEntry;
    branches:   CoverageSummaryEntry;
  };
}

function getBadgeUrl(summaryPath: string): string {
  const summary: CoverageSummary = JSON.parse(readFileSync(summaryPath, 'utf-8'));
  const pct = Math.round(summary.total.lines.pct);
  const colour = pct >= 80 ? 'brightgreen' : pct >= 60 ? 'yellow' : 'red';
  return `https://img.shields.io/badge/coverage-${pct}%25-${colour}`;
}

console.log(getBadgeUrl('./coverage/coverage-summary.json'));
```

**Tradeoff**: `json-summary` only reports aggregate (total) coverage percentages, not per-file data. If your CI badge script or PR comment bot needs per-file data (e.g., to comment on which changed files dropped below threshold), you must use the full `json` reporter instead. The `json` reporter output can be 10-100x larger than `json-summary` depending on codebase size; for large codebases (>500 files), parse only the `total` key and discard per-file entries to keep PR comment generation fast.

## Cycle 40 Community Gotchas

### G124 — Vitest `coverage.watermarks` defaults silently make all files appear yellow until you calibrate  [community]

Vitest inherits Istanbul's default watermarks of `[50, 80]` for all coverage dimensions. A project that has recently raised its threshold to 90% will now have files in the 80-89% range appearing yellow — even though they were previously green and the tests have not degraded. Developers see unexpected yellow files in the HTML report and interpret them as a quality regression when no regression occurred. **WHY it matters**: habituation to false signals destroys the usefulness of the coverage report. Developers stop checking the report because "it always shows yellow" or "it always shows red for those files." The fix: calibrate `watermarks[*][1]` to match the corresponding `thresholds.*` value immediately when threshold values change. Add a CI lint step that reads the Vitest config and validates that `watermarks[*][1]` equals the corresponding `thresholds.*` value; if they diverge, the lint step fails with a message prompting recalibration.

### G125 — Jest `coverageProvider: 'v8'` produces different branch numbers than `babel` for decorated TypeScript classes  [community]

TypeScript decorators (and `emitDecoratorMetadata` metadata emission) compile to `__decorate` and `__metadata` helper calls with conditional expressions. Istanbul's babel provider counts these conditions as branches (increasing the denominator); V8's provider counts executed byte ranges, which often excludes the conditional short-circuits in `__decorate` wrappers. The result: the same test suite run with `coverageProvider: 'babel'` shows 72% branch coverage, while `coverageProvider: 'v8'` shows 81% for the same code. **WHY it matters**: teams migrating from `babel` to `v8` to gain speed treat the coverage increase as "free improvement" when it is actually a measurement artifact. Threshold gates may need recalibration downward after the switch. Always run both providers on the same codebase for a comparison sprint before treating the v8 numbers as canonical, and note that `experimentalDecorators: true` vs `useDefineForClassFields` produces different compiled output with different coverage numbers between TypeScript 4.x and 5.x for the same decorator code.

### G126 — c8 `--all` with workspace symlinks reports absolute symlink targets, breaking per-package coverage aggregation  [community]

In a Yarn or pnpm workspaces monorepo, packages in `packages/` are symlinked into `node_modules/@scope/package`. When `c8 --all --include="src/**/*.ts"` is run from an app package that imports a workspace sibling, V8 records coverage for the symlink target (the real path under `packages/sibling/src/`). c8 then maps this to a path relative to the real directory — not the symlink — which may be outside the `--include` pattern evaluated from the app's cwd. **WHY it matters**: the workspace sibling's files appear in the coverage report with paths like `../../packages/sibling/src/foo.ts`, which do not match the `--include` glob anchored at the app cwd. The files are included with confusing paths, and the threshold computation may be skewed because their real paths are absolute. The fix: use `path.resolve` to canonicalize `--include` patterns from the monorepo root, or use Vitest's `coverage.allowExternal: true` with explicit `include` absolute paths resolved via `path.resolve`.

### G127 — NYC `--foreground-child` and Jest `--forceExit`: SIGTERM forwarding races with coverage file write  [community]

NYC uses `foreground-child` to wrap the test runner process, forwarding signals from nyc to the child. When Jest's `--forceExit` flag is used (common in integration test suites that hold database connections open), Jest sends SIGTERM to its own workers and then exits. NYC's `foreground-child` receives the SIGTERM forwarded from Jest's exit, which may race with nyc's coverage file write (`nyc.writeCoverageFile()`). **WHY it matters**: coverage `.nycrc` files (the raw JSON coverage dumps) may be partially written or missing entirely when this race occurs. The symptom is `nyc report` producing reports with unexpectedly low coverage (or 0%) after test runs that appear successful. The race is non-deterministic and more likely under load. The fix: avoid `--forceExit` in Jest configs that use nyc coverage; instead, ensure test teardown properly closes all async resources (database connections, HTTP servers) so Jest exits naturally, giving nyc time to complete the coverage write lifecycle.

### G128 — Stryker incremental mode `force: true` left in config permanently disables the incremental optimization  [community]

Stryker's `force: true` option (or `--force` CLI flag) discards the existing incremental baseline and runs a full mutation test. This is useful for periodic full-baseline refreshes but catastrophic if accidentally left in a CI configuration. A CI pipeline with `force: true` hardcoded in `stryker.config.ts` runs a full mutation suite on every commit — the incremental optimization is completely disabled. **WHY it matters**: teams that add `force: true` during a debugging session, commit it, and forget to revert will see mutation CI times jump from 3-5 minutes (incremental) back to 30-60 minutes (full). The symptom is subtle because the run succeeds — it just takes much longer. The fix: never hardcode `force: true` in `stryker.config.ts`; instead, use an environment variable override: `force: process.env.STRYKER_FORCE === 'true'`. Run the force baseline refresh via a scheduled weekly job that sets `STRYKER_FORCE=true` in the environment, leaving the default config in incremental mode.

### G129 — coverage.py `dynamic_context` with pytest-xdist `--dist=load`: contexts recorded per worker, not per test function  [community]

When pytest-xdist is used for parallel test execution with `dynamic_context = test_function` in `.coveragerc`, each xdist worker collects its own coverage data to a separate `.coverage.N` file. The context names in these per-worker files are correct when `--dist=loadfile` or `--dist=loadscope` is used, but with the default `--dist=load` (work stealing), tests may be interrupted and resumed on different workers mid-collection. In some pytest-xdist versions, an interrupted context write leaves a partial context record that combines multiple test function names in the same context entry. **WHY it matters**: per-test context queries like `coverage report --contexts="tests/unit/test_payment.py::*"` may miss coverage that was recorded under a malformed combined-context key, producing incomplete per-test attribution reports. The fix: always use `--dist=loadscope` (group by module) when using `dynamic_context = test_function` with xdist, and after merging coverage files with `coverage combine`, run `coverage debug data` to verify that all context names follow the expected `module::function` format before trusting context-filtered reports.
