### Pattern 161 — Vitest `coverage.thresholds.perFile` combined with negative thresholds: per-file uncovered-item budget  [official]

Vitest's threshold system supports two complementary strategies for per-file enforcement. When `coverage.thresholds.perFile: true` is set, every individual file must independently meet all threshold values — the aggregate total no longer hides weak files. Combining this with **negative threshold values** (which cap the maximum number of uncovered items rather than enforcing a percentage) creates a budget-style gate: a new file is allowed up to 5 uncovered lines, not 0%, which is realistic for files still under active development.

The negative-value syntax uses the same four dimensions (`lines`, `branches`, `functions`, `statements`) but accepts integers ≤ 0. A value of `-5` means "no more than 5 uncovered items of this type." This is especially useful for legacy files that are too expensive to bring to 100% immediately but should not regress.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — per-file threshold with uncovered-item budgets
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      thresholds: {
        // Per-file enforcement: every file must independently pass
        perFile: true,

        // Percentage gate for all normal source files
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  80,
        statements: 80,

        // Per-glob overrides: legacy adapter files allow uncovered-item budgets
        './src/adapters/legacy/**': {
          lines:      -10,   // max 10 uncovered lines per legacy adapter file
          branches:   -5,    // max 5 uncovered branches
          functions:  -3,    // max 3 uncovered functions
          statements: -10,
        },

        // Critical payment path: strict 100% enforcement
        './src/payments/**': {
          lines:      100,
          branches:   100,
          functions:  100,
          statements: 100,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `perFile: true` dramatically increases CI noise because a single poorly-covered file fails the entire suite regardless of aggregate health. Teams should combine it with the negative-budget approach for files in active migration. Note that Vitest's per-glob threshold applies the pattern check independently — the `global` threshold does NOT serve as a fallback for pattern-matched files, unlike Jest's behavior. Document the intentional budgets in a comment block so reviewers understand why specific files have relaxed thresholds instead of treating them as accidental misconfigurations.

---

### Pattern 162 — Vitest `coverage.cleanOnRerun`: preserving historical coverage data across watch-mode iterations  [official]

By default Vitest deletes the `coverage/` directory at the start of each run (`cleanOnRerun: true`). In watch mode during active development, this means every file save triggers a complete coverage recalculation — files not affected by the changed module are re-instrumented unnecessarily. Setting `cleanOnRerun: false` preserves the previous run's coverage data: Vitest only writes new coverage for files actually rerun, leaving unchanged file entries intact.

This is most beneficial in large codebases where running the full test suite in watch mode takes 30+ seconds. With `cleanOnRerun: false`, incremental watch runs update only the changed module's coverage file, and the HTML report reflects a composite of the latest coverage data across all files.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — watch-mode optimized configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],
      reporter: ['html', 'text'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // In watch mode: keep previous coverage; only update changed files.
      // In CI: always starts fresh (cleanOnRerun defaults to true in --run mode).
      cleanOnRerun: process.env.CI === 'true' ? true : false,

      // Only show files with coverage below the threshold in text reporter
      skipFull: true,

      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: stale coverage data can accumulate when `cleanOnRerun: false` is used and tests are deleted. A file that had 95% coverage and whose tests are later removed will still show 95% in the report because no new coverage data was written for it. Always run a clean full pass (`vitest run --coverage`) in CI even if watch mode uses `cleanOnRerun: false`. The risk is highest when deleting test files — deleted tests silently leave stale-high coverage for the module they tested.

---

### Pattern 163 — Jest `coverageReporters` with per-reporter options: `skipFull` for the text reporter only  [official]

Jest's `coverageReporters` array supports a two-element tuple format `[reporterName, options]` that passes reporter-specific options without affecting other reporters. The most common application is enabling `skipFull: true` on the `text` reporter while leaving `json` and `lcov` fully detailed. Without this, a large codebase's text coverage table floods CI logs with hundreds of green-100%-coverage lines, obscuring the files that actually need attention.

The `skipFull` option tells the text reporter to omit any file with 100% across all dimensions. This produces a focused report showing only files with partial coverage — exactly the actionable information teams need during a coverage improvement sprint.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — selective skipFull on text reporter only
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  collectCoverage: true,
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/__mocks__/**',
    '!src/generated/**',
  ],
  coverageDirectory: './coverage',
  coverageProvider: 'babel',

  coverageReporters: [
    // Text table: hide fully-covered files to focus on gaps
    ['text', { skipFull: true }],

    // JSON summary for badge generation — always complete
    'json-summary',

    // LCOV for Codecov upload — always complete
    'lcov',

    // HTML for browsable report — always complete
    'html',
  ],

  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      lines:      80,
      branches:   70,
      functions:  80,
      statements: 80,
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `skipFull` on the text reporter only affects the human-readable CI log; JSON, LCOV, and HTML outputs are unaffected and retain all file entries. The risk is that developers who rely solely on the CI text output may not notice when a previously non-full file reaches 100% (it disappears from the output). This is usually desirable behaviour — a file graduating to 100% and vanishing from the report is a success signal — but can be surprising. Document the behaviour in the project's contributing guide so developers understand why some files appear to be missing from the coverage table.

---

### Pattern 164 — Stryker `maxTestRunnerReuse`: preventing memory-leak-driven false survivors in long mutation runs  [official]

StrykerJS runs a test runner process per worker and reuses it across multiple mutants to amortize process startup cost. In test suites that leak memory (e.g., Sinon stubs not properly restored, Angular modules that accumulate listeners, or database connection pools that grow under test), the worker process can accumulate enough heap pressure over hundreds of mutants to cause test flakiness — tests start timing out or producing incorrect results, which Stryker records as "mutant killed" when the kill was spurious.

`maxTestRunnerReuse` caps the number of mutants a single worker process handles before Stryker tears it down and spawns a fresh process. Setting it to 50-100 in leak-prone test suites dramatically reduces flaky mutation results. The cost is a small fixed overhead per process restart.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — memory-leak mitigation with process reuse cap
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: {
    configFile: 'vitest.config.ts',
  },
  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/__mocks__/**',
  ],

  // Cap reuse to prevent test flakiness from memory-leaking test suites.
  // Tune downward (to 50 or 25) if false survivors still appear after restart.
  maxTestRunnerReuse: 100,

  // Performance options
  concurrency: '50%',
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  ignoreStatic: true,

  // Incremental to avoid re-running clean mutants
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: 'reports/stryker-incremental.json',

  reporters: ['html', 'progress'],
  htmlReporter: { fileName: 'reports/mutation.html' },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: lower `maxTestRunnerReuse` values reduce flakiness but increase total runtime because process restarts have overhead (framework initialization, module loading). Setting it to `1` effectively disables reuse — each mutant gets a fresh process, which is the safest but slowest option. Measure your process startup time with a dry run (`--dryRun`): if startup is under 500ms, setting `maxTestRunnerReuse` to 25–50 is low-cost. If startup takes 3+ seconds (common with NestJS or large Angular modules), tune reuse higher and instead fix the memory leaks in teardown hooks.

---

### Pattern 165 — NYC `extends` preset with `@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript`: one-line TypeScript source-map wiring  [official]

TypeScript projects using NYC require several non-obvious configuration settings: enabling source maps, specifying `.ts` and `.tsx` extensions, pointing at the compiled output for instrumentation, and configuring a TypeScript-capable require hook. The `@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript` preset encapsulates all of these into a single `extends` declaration in `.nycrc.json`, avoiding the common trap of missing one setting and getting coverage mapped to compiled `.js` lines instead of original `.ts` source.

The preset sets `extension: ['.ts', '.tsx']`, `require: ['ts-node/register']`, `sourceMap: true`, and `instrument: true`. It also enables `inlineSourceMap` fallback, which handles TypeScript's `--inlineSourceMap` compiler option for projects that emit source maps inline rather than as separate `.map` files.

```typescript
// .nycrc.json — TypeScript NYC configuration using the official preset
{
  "extends": "@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript",
  "all": true,
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": [
    "src/**/*.spec.ts",
    "src/**/*.d.ts",
    "src/**/__mocks__/**",
    "src/generated/**"
  ],
  "reporter": ["text", "html", "lcov", "json-summary"],
  "report-dir": "./coverage",
  "check-coverage": true,
  "lines": 80,
  "branches": 70,
  "functions": 80,
  "statements": 80,
  "watermarks": {
    "lines":      [65, 80],
    "branches":   [55, 70],
    "functions":  [65, 80],
    "statements": [65, 80]
  },
  "skip-full": false,
  "temp-dir": ".nyc_output",
  "cache": true
}
```

```typescript
// tsconfig.json excerpt — required for nyc + ts-node to agree on source maps
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "sourceMap": true,
    "inlineSourceMap": false,
    "declarationMap": false
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript` uses `ts-node/register` as its require hook, which means every instrumented file is transpiled at test-time. For large TypeScript projects (500+ files), this is significantly slower than pre-compiling and running coverage against compiled output. Projects on a build-and-run workflow (compile TypeScript, then run `nyc node dist/index.js`) should use `nyc --extension .ts --source-map` flags with pre-compiled output rather than the `ts-node` preset, since `ts-node` bypasses the compiled output entirely.

---

### Pattern 166 — c8 `--exclude-after-remap` flag: preventing phantom coverage from compiled helper functions  [official]

V8 coverage operates at byte-offset granularity against compiled JavaScript. When TypeScript is compiled to JavaScript, helper functions like `__awaiter`, `__generator`, `__decorate`, and `__extends` appear in the compiled output at positions that may not correspond to any TypeScript source line. c8's source-map remapping attempts to attribute these byte ranges back to original TypeScript positions, but for positions that map outside the declared source range, c8 falls back to reporting them at line 1 of the source file.

The `--exclude-after-remap` flag (or `excludeAfterRemap: true` in `.c8rc`) re-applies the `--include`/`--exclude` glob patterns after source-map remapping completes. Without this, a helper that maps outside its source range may end up attributed to a file that should be excluded (e.g., a `.d.ts` declaration file), inflating or deflating coverage numbers.

```typescript
// package.json — c8 configuration with exclude-after-remap
{
  "c8": {
    "all": true,
    "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
    "exclude": [
      "src/**/*.spec.ts",
      "src/**/*.d.ts",
      "src/**/__mocks__/**",
      "src/generated/**"
    ],
    "excludeAfterRemap": true,
    "reporter": ["text", "html", "lcov", "json-summary"],
    "reportsDirectory": "./coverage",
    "checkCoverage": true,
    "lines": 80,
    "branches": 70,
    "functions": 80,
    "statements": 80
  }
}
```

```typescript
// ci/run-coverage.ts — programmatic c8 invocation with excludeAfterRemap
import { createCoverageMap } from 'istanbul-lib-coverage';
// For direct V8 usage, run via CLI:
// npx c8 --exclude-after-remap --all --include="src/**/*.ts" \
//         --reporter=text --reporter=lcov \
//         node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/jest

// Verification: check that no .d.ts files appear in coverage output
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

function verifyNoDTsFiles(summaryPath: string): void {
  const summary = JSON.parse(readFileSync(summaryPath, 'utf-8'));
  const phantomFiles = Object.keys(summary).filter(k => k.endsWith('.d.ts'));
  if (phantomFiles.length > 0) {
    console.error('Phantom .d.ts files in coverage (excludeAfterRemap may be disabled):', phantomFiles);
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

verifyNoDTsFiles(join(process.cwd(), 'coverage/coverage-summary.json'));
```

**Tradeoff**: `excludeAfterRemap` is a post-processing step that runs after the coverage map is built. For very large codebases (1000+ source files), the remap + re-exclude cycle adds measurable overhead (1-3 seconds). The trade-off is worth it in TypeScript projects that use `tsconfig` paths, project references, or `outDir` + `rootDir` configurations — these are the most likely to produce out-of-range source-map entries that pollute the coverage report.

---

### Pattern 167 — Vitest `coverage.instrumenter` custom factory: edge-runtime and non-Node environments  [official]

Vitest 4.1.5 introduced the `coverage.instrumenter` option for the Istanbul provider, accepting a factory function that returns a `CoverageInstrumenter` interface implementation. This allows replacing the default Istanbul instrumenter with a custom one, which is primarily useful for edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno) that do not support all Node.js APIs that Istanbul uses internally, or for custom instrumentation schemes like coverage over WebAssembly boundaries.

The factory receives the `instrumenterOptions` configuration object (the same one normally passed to `@istanbuljs/schema`) and must return an object implementing `instrumentSync(code, filename, options)` and optionally `instrument(code, filename, options)`.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — custom instrumenter factory for edge-compatible coverage
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import type { CoverageInstrumenter } from 'vitest/coverage';

// Custom instrumenter that wraps Istanbul but replaces the `path` module
// usage with edge-compatible equivalents (no require('path') calls).
function createEdgeCompatibleInstrumenter(): CoverageInstrumenter {
  // Dynamic import of Istanbul to avoid top-level require() in edge contexts
  return {
    instrumentSync(code: string, filename: string, opts?: object): string {
      // Use the @istanbuljs/istanbul-lib-instrument package directly
      // with edge-safe options (no auto-detection of paths)
      const { instrumenter } = require('@istanbuljs/istanbul-lib-instrument');
      const inst = instrumenter({
        produceSourceMap: true,
        autoWrap: false,
        ...opts,
      });
      return inst.instrumentSync(code, filename);
    },

    async instrument(code: string, filename: string, opts?: object): Promise<string> {
      return this.instrumentSync(code, filename, opts);
    },
  };
}

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      instrumenter: createEdgeCompatibleInstrumenter,
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      thresholds: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: custom instrumenters bypass Vitest's internal validation of the instrumentation output. If the custom instrumenter produces invalid source-map entries, coverage remapping will silently fail with incorrect line attributions rather than throwing an error. This option is intended for advanced use cases where the default Istanbul instrumenter is genuinely incompatible with the target environment. For standard Node.js projects, always use the default instrumenter; the performance and correctness benefits of the custom path are only realized when targeting non-standard runtimes.

---

### Pattern 168 — Stryker `coverageAnalysis: 'all'` with `ignoreStatic: true`: the optimal balance for class-heavy TypeScript  [official]

StrykerJS offers three `coverageAnalysis` modes that dramatically affect mutation run time. `'perTest'` (the default since v5) runs only tests that cover each mutant, but requires a coverage collection overhead run first. `'off'` runs all tests for every mutant — correct but O(mutants × tests). `'all'` is the middle ground: it identifies which mutants are covered at all, marks uncovered ones as `NoCoverage` without running tests, and then runs all tests only for covered mutants.

`ignoreStatic: true` pairs naturally with `'all'` mode: it additionally skips mutants that are only executed during module load (static class properties, top-level expressions), marking them as `Ignored`. This eliminates an entire category of slow mutants — the ones that require a fresh process start to test. The combination of `coverageAnalysis: 'all'` + `ignoreStatic: true` typically reduces mutation run time by 30-50% compared to `'off'` while being more reliable than `'perTest'` for codebases with shared global state.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — optimized for TypeScript class-heavy NestJS application
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'jest',
  jest: {
    configFile: 'jest.config.ts',
    projectType: 'custom',
    enableFindRelatedTests: true,
  },
  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.module.ts',   // NestJS module files are pure wiring
    '!src/**/*.dto.ts',      // DTOs: class-validator decorators, not business logic
    '!src/**/*.entity.ts',   // TypeORM entities: schema definitions
    '!src/main.ts',
  ],

  // Coverage analysis: mark NoCoverage without running tests (faster than 'off')
  coverageAnalysis: 'all',

  // Skip mutants that only execute during file loading (static class fields)
  ignoreStatic: true,

  // TypeScript checker to eliminate type-error mutants before running tests
  checkers: ['typescript'],
  tsconfigFile: 'tsconfig.json',
  disableTypeChecks: false,   // v7 changed default to true; re-enable for accuracy

  concurrency: '50%',
  reporters: ['html', 'progress', 'dots'],
  htmlReporter: { fileName: 'reports/mutation/index.html' },
  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: null },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverageAnalysis: 'all'` runs ALL tests for each covered mutant (unlike `'perTest'` which only runs relevant tests). For test suites where a small percentage of tests cover most mutants, `'perTest'` is faster. For test suites with heavy global state setup (shared database fixtures, module-level singletons), `'perTest'` can produce false survivors when a mutant's covering tests depend on state set up by non-covering tests. The `'all'` mode is the safe default for NestJS, Angular, and TypeScript class-heavy applications.

---

### Pattern 169 — Istanbul `ignore start` / `ignore stop` block directives: excluding multi-line regions from coverage  [official]

Istanbul (and by extension Vitest's Istanbul provider, Jest with Babel, and NYC) supports block-level ignore directives using `/* istanbul ignore start */` and `/* istanbul ignore stop */` comment pairs. Unlike the `/* istanbul ignore next */` directive (which applies to the immediately following statement), the start/stop directives wrap an entire code region, allowing multi-line exclusions for platform-specific polyfills, environment detection blocks, or feature-flag switches that are not exercisable in the test environment.

These directives were restored in Vitest 4.1 after a regression in earlier Vitest 4.x builds. When using esbuild as the TypeScript transpiler (the default in Vitest), the `-- @preserve` suffix is mandatory for both directives: `/* istanbul ignore start -- @preserve */`.

```typescript
// src/platform/node-compat.ts — multi-line block ignore for platform detection
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

export function hashString(input: string): string {
  return createHash('sha256').update(input).digest('hex');
}

/* istanbul ignore start -- @preserve */
// The following block handles environments where Node crypto is unavailable
// (e.g., browser-like test environments or edge workers). This path is not
// reachable in the standard test environment and is verified via E2E testing only.
export const cryptoFallback: typeof hashString = (input: string): string => {
  // Simple djb2 hash as a fallback — not cryptographically secure
  let hash = 5381;
  for (let i = 0; i < input.length; i++) {
    hash = ((hash << 5) + hash) + input.charCodeAt(i);
  }
  return (hash >>> 0).toString(16).padStart(8, '0');
};
/* istanbul ignore stop -- @preserve */

// Test environment only: export a function to verify which implementation is active
export const getHashImplementation = (): 'crypto' | 'fallback' =>
  typeof process !== 'undefined' && process.versions?.node ? 'crypto' : 'fallback';
```

**Tradeoff**: block-level ignore directives are invisible in the coverage HTML report — they vanish completely from the coverage table. This makes it impossible to audit how much code is excluded without examining the source directly. Maintain a project-level registry of all `ignore start/stop` blocks with justifications (a simple markdown table or a comment in a central config file) so coverage exclusions are reviewable during code review. Never use `ignore start/stop` for code that contains business logic — reserve them strictly for environment-specific shims that cannot be tested in the unit test environment.

---

### Pattern 170 — V8 coverage `ignore file` directive: whole-file exclusion without config changes  [official]

Vitest's V8 provider supports a `/* v8 ignore file */` directive (and Istanbul supports `/* istanbul ignore file */`) that excludes the entire file from the coverage report when placed anywhere in the file. This is the canonical way to exclude generated files, declaration shims, or re-export barrel files that pollute coverage metrics, especially when the file is generated by a tool and cannot be excluded via glob patterns at the configuration level (e.g., because it lives in `src/` alongside source files).

The directive must survive TypeScript compilation. With esbuild (Vitest default), use `/* v8 ignore file -- @preserve */`. The directive is checked at coverage-report generation time, not at instrumentation time — the file is still instrumented, but all its coverage data is discarded during report generation.

```typescript
/* v8 ignore file -- @preserve */
// THIS FILE IS AUTO-GENERATED. DO NOT EDIT.
// Generated by: scripts/gen-routes.ts at build time.
// Regenerate with: npm run gen:routes
//
// Excluding from coverage because:
// 1. The file is 100% generated from route definitions in routes.config.ts
// 2. routes.config.ts is independently covered
// 3. The generator script (gen-routes.ts) has its own test suite

export * from './routes/auth.generated';
export * from './routes/users.generated';
export * from './routes/products.generated';
export * from './routes/orders.generated';

export type { RouteHandler, RouteMiddleware } from './routes/types.generated';

// Convenience re-exports with renamed types for consumer ergonomics
export type {
  AuthRouteConfig as AuthConfig,
  UserRouteConfig as UserConfig,
} from './routes/auth.generated';
```

**Tradeoff**: file-level ignore directives are harder to discover than glob-based exclusions in `coverage.exclude`. A new team member reading the config file will not see these exclusions — they are in the source files themselves. The advantage is that the exclusion travels with the file: if the file is moved or copied, the directive moves with it, whereas config-level glob patterns may silently fail to match after a rename. For generated files, the directive in the file is the right approach; for stable source files you want to exclude (e.g., a `src/dev-tools.ts` debug module), prefer the config-level `exclude` glob for discoverability.

---

### Pattern 171 — Stryker `disableTypeChecks` default change in v7: re-enabling for payment and security logic  [official]

StrykerJS v7 changed the default of `disableTypeChecks` from `false` to `true`. The rationale: the TypeScript checker eliminates type-error mutants (mutations that produce code that would fail tsc compilation), but this check doubles or triples mutation run time in large codebases. For most applications, type-error mutants are not practically relevant — the TypeScript compiler would catch them at compile time anyway.

However, for **payment processing**, **authentication**, and **security-critical** modules, type-error mutants matter: a mutant that causes a type error in the TypeScript checker might still be valid JavaScript at runtime (TypeScript types are erased), and if your tests do not exercise the runtime behavior, the mutation survives. Re-enabling `disableTypeChecks: false` for these specific modules closes this gap.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — conditional type checking based on file scope
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';
import { globSync } from 'glob';

// Determine if this run targets payment/security modules
const isSecurityRun = process.env.STRYKER_SCOPE === 'security';

// Security-critical file patterns
const securityFiles = globSync('src/{payments,auth,security}/**/*.ts').filter(
  f => !f.endsWith('.spec.ts')
);

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: { configFile: 'vitest.config.ts' },

  // Target: either all files or security-critical files only
  mutate: isSecurityRun
    ? securityFiles
    : ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.spec.ts'],

  // For security runs: enable TypeScript type checking to catch type-error mutants.
  // For regular runs: keep disabled for speed (v7 default).
  disableTypeChecks: !isSecurityRun,

  // Only enable TypeScript checker when type checks are enabled
  checkers: isSecurityRun ? ['typescript'] : [],

  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  ignoreStatic: true,
  concurrency: isSecurityRun ? 2 : '50%', // Lower concurrency for type-check overhead
  reporters: ['html', 'progress'],
  thresholds: {
    high: isSecurityRun ? 90 : 80,
    low: isSecurityRun ? 75 : 60,
    break: isSecurityRun ? 70 : null,
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: re-enabling `disableTypeChecks: false` (which means type checking IS enabled) runs every mutant through the TypeScript compiler. This adds a compile step per mutant — typically 50-200ms each — which multiplies total run time by 2-5x. The performance cost is justified only for modules where runtime type safety matters: payment handlers, JWT validation, cryptographic operations, and authorization logic. For UI components, utilities, and data-transformation code, the v7 default (`disableTypeChecks: true`) is appropriate.

---

### Pattern 172 — Jest `collectCoverageFrom` negation glob ordering: left-to-right evaluation pitfall  [official]

Jest's `collectCoverageFrom` evaluates glob patterns strictly left-to-right, and a later negation pattern OVERRIDES a prior positive match only if it appears after in the array. This creates a non-obvious trap: if you place a broad positive glob first and a negation second, the negation works as expected. But if negation patterns appear before the positive glob they are supposed to negate, the positive glob re-admits those files.

The canonical safe ordering is: list all positive inclusion patterns first, then list all negation patterns last. Every negation that appears before its corresponding positive glob is silently ineffective — the files are included because the later positive pattern re-matches them.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — correct negation ordering for collectCoverageFrom
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  collectCoverage: true,
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  coverageDirectory: './coverage',

  // CORRECT ordering: all positive globs first, negations after
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    // 1. Positive: include all TypeScript source files
    'src/**/*.ts',
    'src/**/*.tsx',

    // 2. Negative: exclude test files, generated, and declarations
    //    (MUST come after the positive patterns to be effective)
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.tsx',
    '!src/**/*.test.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/__mocks__/**',
    '!src/generated/**',
    '!src/**/*.stories.tsx',  // Storybook stories: excluded from unit coverage
    '!src/**/index.ts',       // Barrel re-exports: excluded as pure re-exports
  ],

  coverageReporters: [
    ['text', { skipFull: true }],
    'json-summary',
    'lcov',
  ],

  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      lines: 80,
      branches: 70,
      functions: 80,
      statements: 80,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: the left-to-right evaluation rule is not explicitly documented in most versions of the Jest docs — teams discover it empirically when a negation "stops working" after a refactoring that moved patterns around. A CI lint step that checks the ordering (using a script that verifies all `!` patterns appear after non-`!` patterns) catches regressions. Note that this behavior is consistent with standard glob libraries (`micromatch`, `picomatch`) — it is not a Jest quirk, but it is unfamiliar to developers coming from tools like Webpack's `module.rules` where ordering semantics differ.

---

### Pattern 173 — Vitest `coverage.skipFull` AI-agent auto-detection: understanding automatic reporter configuration  [official]

When Vitest detects it is running inside an AI coding agent environment (via environment variable checks), it automatically enables two behaviours: adds the `text-summary` reporter to the reporter list and sets `skipFull: true`. The `text-summary` reporter produces a compact single-paragraph coverage summary rather than a file-by-file table, reducing token consumption. `skipFull: true` additionally suppresses 100%-covered files from the text report.

This auto-detection is useful to know about because it can produce unexpected CI behaviour when AI-assisted workflows are used in CI pipelines: if the CI job runs under an AI agent environment with those variables set, the text output will look different from a standard run, which can confuse log parsers that expect the full table format.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — explicit override to suppress AI-agent auto-detection in CI
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],

      // Explicitly set reporter list so AI-agent auto-detection cannot add text-summary.
      // CI log parsers depend on the full text table format.
      reporter: [
        ['text', { skipFull: false }],  // Full table in CI logs
        'json-summary',                  // For badge generation
        'lcov',                          // For Codecov upload
        'html',                          // For browsable artifact
      ],

      // Explicitly disable skipFull so no files are hidden from CI log
      skipFull: false,

      // Thresholds: enforce at CI
      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: the AI-agent auto-detection is designed to reduce noise in agentic workflows where coverage output is fed directly to a language model. Overriding it in CI ensures deterministic, parseable output but may produce verbose logs in AI-assisted PR review pipelines. The safe default for production CI is to always explicitly specify the `reporter` array — do not rely on Vitest's auto-detection for CI-critical reporter configuration. The auto-detection is best treated as a developer-experience convenience in local AI-assisted development sessions, not as a CI configuration strategy.

---

### Pattern 174 — Stryker VS Code plugin inline mutation results: integrating mutation coverage into the editor development loop  [official]

The StrykerJS VS Code extension uses the Mutation Server Protocol (MSP) to display inline mutation results directly in the editor. After a mutation run produces a JSON report, the extension reads it and overlays surviving mutants as inline annotations in the relevant source files — yellow decorations for surviving mutants, green for killed ones, gray for `NoCoverage`. The developer sees exactly which code paths are under-tested without leaving the editor.

The workflow is: run Stryker once to generate `reports/mutation.json`, then activate the VS Code plugin (it reads the report file), then continue developing. As code changes, a watch-mode mutation run can update the report incrementally (via `--incremental`), and the plugin refreshes the inline annotations. This eliminates the context-switch of opening a browser to review HTML mutation reports.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — configured for VS Code plugin integration
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: { configFile: 'vitest.config.ts' },
  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
  ],

  // JSON reporter is required for VS Code plugin to read mutation results
  // 'html' provides the browser-based fallback view
  reporters: ['json', 'html', 'progress'],

  // Incremental for fast subsequent runs during development
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: 'reports/stryker-incremental.json',

  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  ignoreStatic: true,
  concurrency: '50%',

  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: null },

  // MSP server configuration (used by the VS Code extension)
  // The plugin automatically discovers the mutation.json at the default path
  htmlReporter: { fileName: 'reports/mutation/index.html' },
};

// .stryker-vscode.json (workspace settings for VS Code plugin):
// {
//   "mutationTestReportJsonFilePath": "reports/mutation.json"
// }

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: the VS Code plugin reads a static JSON snapshot, not a live server. The inline annotations are only as fresh as the last Stryker run. In fast-moving development sessions, annotations become stale quickly — a developer refactors a function, the annotations still point to old line numbers, and the experience degrades. The MSP watch mode partially solves this but requires `--incremental` mode and adds background CPU usage. Teams with slow mutation runs (> 10 minutes) should use the plugin only after PR-stage full runs rather than in the inner development loop.

---

### Pattern 175 — NYC `--all` flag with `skip-full` for legacy project coverage auditing  [official]

NYC's `--all` flag forces the tool to instrument every file matching the `include` patterns, even those that are never `require`'d or `import`'ed by any test. Without this flag, a file that has no tests at all does not appear in the coverage report — its absence is invisible. With `--all`, those files appear with 0% coverage across all dimensions, making untested code visible and measurable in threshold gates.

Pairing `--all` with `skip-full: false` (the default) ensures the full coverage table is visible. For a legacy audit where the goal is to find completely untested files, use `--all` with the `text` reporter and filter the output for `0 |` entries — these are completely uncovered files.

```typescript
// package.json — legacy audit workflow using nyc --all
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:coverage": "nyc --all mocha",
    "test:coverage:audit": "nyc --all --reporter=json-summary mocha && node ci/audit-untested.js",
    "test:coverage:report": "nyc report --reporter=html"
  },
  "nyc": {
    "extends": "@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript",
    "all": true,
    "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
    "exclude": [
      "src/**/*.spec.ts",
      "src/**/*.d.ts",
      "src/**/__mocks__/**"
    ],
    "reporter": ["text", "json-summary"],
    "check-coverage": false,
    "skip-full": false
  }
}
```

```typescript
// ci/audit-untested.ts — extract completely untested files from json-summary
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

interface CoverageEntry {
  lines: { pct: number }; statements: { pct: number };
  branches: { pct: number }; functions: { pct: number };
}
interface CoverageSummary {
  total: CoverageEntry;
  [filename: string]: CoverageEntry;
}

const summary: CoverageSummary = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync('./coverage/coverage-summary.json', 'utf-8')
);

const untestedFiles = Object.entries(summary)
  .filter(([key]) => key !== 'total')
  .filter(([, entry]) => entry.lines.pct === 0)
  .map(([key]) => key)
  .sort();

console.log(`Completely untested files (${untestedFiles.length}):`);
untestedFiles.forEach(f => console.log(`  ${f}`));

if (untestedFiles.length > 0) {
  process.exit(1); // Fail CI if any completely untested files exist
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `--all` significantly increases coverage run time and output size because every source file is instrumented and reported, regardless of whether tests touch it. For a large codebase with 500 source files but only 200 tested, the coverage report will contain 300 zero-coverage entries. This is exactly the point for an audit, but it produces very long CI logs in routine runs. Use `--all` in a dedicated nightly or weekly audit job, not in every PR run. Gate the nightly job on zero 0%-coverage files as a quality baseline, separate from the PR gate which enforces aggregate thresholds.

---

## Cycle 41 Community Gotchas

### G130 — Vitest `coverage.thresholds.perFile` masks file-count changes: new files start at 0 % and immediately fail CI  [community]

When `perFile: true` is enabled and a developer adds a new source file without any corresponding tests, that file appears in the coverage report with 0% across all dimensions and immediately fails the per-file threshold gate. This is technically correct behavior but creates a frustrating development experience: a PR that adds a new utility module fails CI before the developer has written any tests for it. **WHY it matters**: teams react to this friction by disabling `perFile` entirely or by pre-populating new files with `/* istanbul ignore file */` to silence the gate — both reactions undermine the purpose of per-file enforcement. The fix: combine `perFile: true` with the `coverage.changed` option so that per-file thresholds only apply to files that were already present in the previous run's baseline. New files get a grace period (one complete PR cycle) before they are subject to per-file gates. This requires Vitest 4.1+ with the `coverage.changed` option available.

### G131 — Jest `coverageProvider: 'v8'` with TypeScript 5.5+ `using` declarations: branch counts inflate unexpectedly  [community]

TypeScript 5.5 introduced explicit resource management via the `using` keyword (part of the TC39 proposal). When `using` declarations are compiled to JavaScript, they generate try/finally blocks with conditional cleanup calls. Jest's V8 provider records these generated branches separately from the original source, producing branch counts that are higher than expected. A file with 3 `using` declarations can see its branch count jump from 10 to 16, all attributed to lines in the original TypeScript source. **WHY it matters**: teams see their branch coverage drop after upgrading TypeScript without changing any tests, which triggers threshold failures and wastes debugging time. The branches are real (the finally-block conditionals execute based on whether the resource was actually initialized), but they are not independently testable without explicitly testing exceptional teardown paths. The workaround: add `using` declaration teardown paths to the `ignoreClassMethods` list (if `using` appears inside class methods) or use `/* v8 ignore next */` on the compiler-generated `Symbol.dispose` calls.

### G132 — Stryker incremental JSON becomes a persistent source of false negatives after mutation operator changes  [community]

Stryker's incremental file (`stryker-incremental.json`) stores per-mutant results including the mutant's operator type and source hash. When you add or remove mutators from the `excludedMutations` list, Stryker does not automatically invalidate the incremental baseline — it continues to reuse cached results from the previous operator set. The result: newly-enabled operators are not tested because Stryker sees the file hash as unchanged and reuses the old results that predate those operators. **WHY it matters**: teams that progressively enable more mutation operators (a common adoption pattern) get a false sense of completion because the mutation score reflects old, partial runs rather than the new operator set. The fix: always run with `force: true` (or set `STRYKER_FORCE=true`) when the `excludedMutations` list changes, and document operator list changes in the commit that modifies `stryker.config.ts` to prompt baseline resets during code review.

### G133 — c8 `--all` with TypeScript path aliases: aliased imports not resolved to source files  [community]

When TypeScript projects use `tsconfig.paths` aliases (e.g., `@domain/feature` mapped to `./src/domain/feature`), the compiled JavaScript uses path aliases that Node.js cannot resolve without a path-alias resolver plugin (like `tsconfig-paths` or `module-alias`). c8's `--all` flag instruments files based on glob patterns against the filesystem, not against what TypeScript's module resolver would discover. Files that are only reachable via aliased imports may be missing from the `--all` report if the glob patterns do not match their actual filesystem path. **WHY it matters**: a file at `src/domain/feature/index.ts` that is only ever imported as `@domain/feature` will appear in the `--all` report correctly (the glob matches it). But if the compiled output emits `require('@domain/feature')` and the test runner cannot resolve the alias, the file's coverage is recorded as an alias path, not a source path, producing two separate entries in the report: the real file with 0% coverage and a phantom entry at the alias path. The fix: ensure the test runner has `tsconfig-paths/register` in its require array and that c8's `--include` patterns match the actual source paths, not alias paths.

### G134 — coverage.py `omit` and `include` patterns are evaluated relative to the current working directory, not the config file  [community]

When `.coveragerc` or `pyproject.toml` contains `[coverage:run] omit = tests/*`, the pattern is evaluated relative to the process's current working directory at the time `coverage run` is invoked — not relative to the location of the `.coveragerc` file. In monorepos where the config file lives in a sub-package but `coverage run` is invoked from the monorepo root, `omit = tests/*` silently fails to exclude anything because the `tests/` directory is at `packages/my-service/tests/`, not `tests/`. **WHY it matters**: the coverage report includes test files themselves as source files, inflating the covered-file count and potentially triggering false 0% branch coverage on empty `__init__.py` test fixtures. The fix: always use absolute paths or paths anchored with `${configdir}` (supported in coverage.py 7.x) in `omit` and `include` patterns when the config file may not be at the working directory root. Alternatively, invoke `coverage run` from the same directory as the config file using `cd packages/my-service && coverage run`.

### G135 — Vitest `coverage.changed` + `--reporter=blob` sharding: changed-file detection is scoped to the shard, not the full repo  [community]

Vitest's blob reporter enables sharded parallel CI by collecting coverage from each shard independently and merging them with `vitest merge-coverage`. When `coverage.changed` is used alongside sharding, each shard independently computes its list of "changed" files (via `git diff`) and applies per-file thresholds only to the changed files it processes. In a sharded setup where changed files are distributed across shards by test path rather than source path, a changed source file may land in a shard that runs no tests for it — the shard sees it as changed but with 0 coverage, applying the threshold and failing. **WHY it matters**: the failure is non-deterministic across shards (it depends on how changed files map to test files in the sharding algorithm) and may only manifest when specific combinations of changed files are present in the same PR. The fix: disable `coverage.changed` in sharded CI setups and instead use a post-merge step that runs the full coverage suite on the merged blob report and applies changed-file thresholds at that stage.

### Pattern 176 — Vitest `coverage.processingConcurrency`: tuning parallel source-map resolution for large TypeScript projects  [official]

Vitest resolves source maps for coverage reports in parallel using a worker pool. The `coverage.processingConcurrency` option controls how many source-map resolution tasks run simultaneously. For large TypeScript codebases with hundreds of files, the default concurrency (based on available CPU cores) can overwhelm memory in CI environments with constrained RAM, causing the coverage post-processing step to OOM-fail after the tests themselves pass cleanly.

Setting `processingConcurrency` to a lower fixed value (e.g., `4` or `8`) on memory-constrained runners trades slightly longer post-processing time for reliable completion. The option is distinct from the test runner's own concurrency — `coverage.processingConcurrency` applies only to the source-map resolution phase that runs after all tests finish, not to test execution itself.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — processingConcurrency tuned for CI memory constraints
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import os from 'node:os';

// In CI with constrained RAM (e.g. GitHub Actions 2-core runner), cap concurrency.
// Locally, use all cores for full speed.
const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';
const coverageConcurrency = isCI ? 4 : os.cpus().length;

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Cap source-map resolution workers. Default: os.cpus().length.
      // Reduce to 2-4 on memory-constrained CI runners to prevent OOM kills
      // during the post-processing phase that follows test execution.
      processingConcurrency: coverageConcurrency,

      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: lowering `processingConcurrency` increases the wall-clock time of the coverage post-processing step proportionally. On a 500-file TypeScript project, the difference between concurrency 1 and 8 can be 20–40 seconds. In a PR gate where total CI time matters, use the highest concurrency that stays under the memory limit. Profile by running with `--reporter=verbose` and monitoring peak RSS during the coverage phase; if it spikes past 80% of available RAM, halve `processingConcurrency` until stable.

### Pattern 177 — Node 24 built-in test runner `--experimental-test-coverage`: zero-dependency coverage for simple TypeScript CLIs  [official]

Node 24 ships a built-in test runner (`node:test`) with integrated coverage via `--experimental-test-coverage`. This eliminates the need for Vitest, Jest, c8, or Istanbul for small TypeScript utilities where adding a full testing framework feels disproportionate. The runner emits LCOV output and supports `--test-coverage-include` and `--test-coverage-exclude` glob patterns, making it immediately compatible with Codecov and Coveralls upload actions.

Coverage thresholds can be enforced via `--test-coverage-lines`, `--test-coverage-branches`, `--test-coverage-functions`, and `--test-coverage-statements` flags — the process exits with code 1 when any threshold is breached, which integrates cleanly into CI pipelines without custom scripts.

```typescript
// package.json — zero-dependency coverage using Node 24 built-in test runner
// Requires Node 24+ and ts-node or tsx for TypeScript transpilation at test time.
// {
//   "scripts": {
//     "test": "node --experimental-strip-types --experimental-test-coverage
//              --test-coverage-include='src/**/*.ts'
//              --test-coverage-exclude='src/**/*.spec.ts'
//              --test-coverage-lines=80
//              --test-coverage-branches=70
//              --test-coverage-functions=80
//              --test-reporter=tap
//              --test-reporter-destination=./reports/tap.txt
//              $(find src -name '*.spec.ts')"
//   }
// }

// src/math.spec.ts — example test using node:test
import { describe, it } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { add, subtract } from './math.js';

describe('math utilities', () => {
  it('adds two integers', () => {
    assert.strictEqual(add(2, 3), 5);
  });

  it('subtracts second from first', () => {
    assert.strictEqual(subtract(10, 4), 6);
  });

  it('handles negative numbers', () => {
    assert.strictEqual(add(-1, -2), -3);
    assert.strictEqual(subtract(-5, -3), -2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Node 24's built-in coverage is still experimental (`--experimental-test-coverage`) and has several limitations compared to Vitest/Jest: no HTML reporter (LCOV only), no per-file threshold support, no mutation testing integration, and no watch mode. The `--experimental-strip-types` flag for TypeScript support is also RC-quality in Node 24 and does not support TypeScript decorators or some advanced generic patterns. Use this pattern for simple utility packages, internal scripts, and CI tooling — not for application test suites where coverage visualization, per-file thresholds, and mutation testing are required.

### Pattern 178 — Vitest `coverage.htmlDir` with custom reporter: separating HTML output from the default reports directory  [official]

By default, Vitest places the HTML coverage report alongside other report formats in `coverage.reportsDirectory`. For teams that publish the HTML coverage report as a CI artifact or serve it from an internal documentation site, co-locating HTML with JSON and LCOV files creates path ambiguity in artifact upload configurations. The `coverage.htmlDir` option (available for custom HTML reporters) allows specifying a separate output path for the human-readable report while keeping machine-consumable formats in the standard `reportsDirectory`.

The `html-spa` reporter (available since Vitest 4.1) produces a single-file HTML report that embeds all assets inline — ideal for email attachments, Confluence uploads, and artifact storage where multi-file directories are inconvenient.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — html-spa single-file report + separated directory layout
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import path from 'node:path';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],

      // Machine-readable formats go here (uploaded to S3, read by badge bots)
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      reporter: [
        // Lightweight CI log output
        ['text', { skipFull: true }],

        // JSON summary: badge generation and PR comments
        'json-summary',

        // LCOV: Codecov / Coveralls upload
        'lcov',

        // Single-file HTML: attach to PR, upload to Confluence, email to stakeholders
        // html-spa embeds all assets inline; no multi-file directory needed
        ['html-spa', { outDir: path.resolve('./coverage-report') }],
      ],

      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: the `html-spa` single-file reporter produces a larger file than the standard multi-file HTML report because all JavaScript, CSS, and data are inlined. For a 300-file TypeScript codebase, the single-file report can be 2–5 MB versus 500 KB for the multi-file version. This is acceptable for email/Confluence uploads but can slow CI artifact upload steps if stored as a build artifact on every PR. Reserve `html-spa` for scheduled nightly reports and use the standard `html` reporter for PR-stage artifacts where the smaller size matters.

### Pattern 179 — Stryker `logLevel` and `allowEmpty` for no-mutation module whitelisting without silent failures  [official]

When Stryker encounters a `mutate` glob pattern that matches zero files, it defaults to silently succeeding with a 100% mutation score for that pattern. This silent-success behavior can mask misconfigured glob patterns (e.g., a typo in `mutate: ['src/paymennts/**']`) — the CI gate passes, but no mutations were tested. The `allowEmpty: false` option (added in StrykerJS 7+) makes Stryker fail with an explicit error when a configured `mutate` pattern matches no files.

Combining this with `logLevel: 'info'` (the default) vs `logLevel: 'debug'` allows tuning how much mutation run detail appears in CI logs. For large runs in CI, `logLevel: 'info'` suppresses per-mutant progress noise; for debugging false survivors locally, `logLevel: 'debug'` shows the exact test that killed (or failed to kill) each mutant.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — allowEmpty and logLevel configuration
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: { configFile: 'vitest.config.ts' },

  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/generated/**',
    // Payment module: separate strict run defined in stryker.payments.config.ts
    '!src/payments/**',
  ],

  // Fail if any pattern matches zero files — catches typos immediately.
  // Without this, a mistyped pattern silently scores 100% on zero mutants.
  allowEmpty: false,

  // CI: use 'info' to suppress per-mutant progress noise.
  // Debugging locally: switch to 'debug' to see individual mutant test results.
  logLevel: process.env.STRYKER_DEBUG === 'true' ? 'debug' : 'info',

  reporters: ['html', 'json', 'progress'],
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: 'reports/stryker-incremental.json',
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  ignoreStatic: true,
  concurrency: '50%',
  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: null },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `allowEmpty: false` is a breaking change for teams that intentionally configure `mutate` patterns with zero matches (e.g., patterns that apply only to feature branches where a module does not yet exist). If your repository conditionally includes source directories, `allowEmpty: false` will fail on branches that do not include those directories. The fix: use environment variables to conditionally build the `mutate` array rather than static patterns: `mutate: process.env.INCLUDE_PAYMENTS === 'true' ? ['src/payments/**/*.ts'] : []`. This makes optional patterns explicit rather than allowing them to silently match nothing.

### Pattern 180 — c8 v11 `--experimental-monocart` reporter: execution-count visualization without source-map remapping  [official]

c8 v11 introduced an experimental integration with the Monocart coverage reporter, which renders V8's raw byte-range coverage data as a human-readable HTML report with per-function execution counts. Unlike the Istanbul-backed HTML reporter (which must remap V8 byte ranges through source maps back to TypeScript lines), the Monocart reporter works directly with V8's native format — this eliminates the remap step that is responsible for the largest fraction of coverage post-processing time.

The practical benefit: for TypeScript projects with complex mapped code (decorators, async generators, template literals), Monocart shows exact execution counts per expression rather than per-line aggregates, making it possible to identify which path through a complex branch expression was executed and how many times.

```typescript
// package.json — c8 with --experimental-monocart reporter
// Requires c8 >= 11.0.0 and monocart-coverage-reports installed separately.
// {
//   "devDependencies": {
//     "c8": "^11.0.0",
//     "monocart-coverage-reports": "^2.0.0"
//   },
//   "scripts": {
//     "test:coverage": "c8 --experimental-monocart node --test src/**/*.spec.ts",
//     "test:coverage:html": "c8 --experimental-monocart --reporter=v8 --reporter=lcov node --test src/**/*.spec.ts"
//   }
// }

// c8.config.cjs — c8 configuration file
module.exports = {
  'experimental-monocart': true,
  all: true,
  include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
  exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
  reporter: ['v8', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  reportsDir: './coverage',
  // Thresholds enforced via --lines/--branches/--functions/--statements CLI flags
  // or programmatically via coverage-summary.json in post-coverage.ts script
  lines: 80,
  branches: 70,
  functions: 80,
  statements: 80,
};
```

**Tradeoff**: `--experimental-monocart` is explicitly experimental as of c8 v11 — the API and output format may change in minor versions without a deprecation cycle. The Monocart renderer is a separate package (`monocart-coverage-reports`) that adds approximately 3 MB to dev dependencies and has its own update cadence independent of c8. For production CI pipelines where stability matters more than richer visualization, prefer the standard Istanbul-remapped HTML reporter. Use `--experimental-monocart` in development and debugging workflows where execution-count data provides actionable insight, and gate it behind an environment variable so CI uses the stable reporter by default.

### Pattern 181 — Jest `fakeTimers` interaction with Istanbul branch coverage: timer-guarded branches remain uncovered  [community]

Jest's `fakeTimers` replaces `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Date`, and related APIs with synchronous simulation. When a function under test guards a code path based on elapsed time (e.g., `if (Date.now() - lastRun > threshold)`) and the test uses `jest.useFakeTimers()`, the branch can only be exercised by explicitly advancing fake time with `jest.advanceTimersByTime()`. Teams that forget this step produce test suites that execute the timer-guarded code but always take the same time-based branch — Istanbul records both branches as "covered" if the guard evaluates to both true and false across the test suite, but if only one branch is ever taken, the other shows as uncovered.

The coverage report's red branch indicator on a `Date.now()` comparison line is often the first clue that a time-based branch has never been exercised in the "threshold exceeded" state.

```typescript
// src/rate-limiter.ts — rate limiter with time-based branch
export class RateLimiter {
  private lastCallAt = 0;

  constructor(private readonly windowMs: number) {}

  isAllowed(): boolean {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - this.lastCallAt < this.windowMs) {
      return false; // within window: reject
    }
    this.lastCallAt = now;
    return true; // outside window: allow and update timestamp
  }
}

// src/rate-limiter.spec.ts — correctly exercising both time branches with fakeTimers
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { RateLimiter } from './rate-limiter.js';

describe('RateLimiter', () => {
  beforeEach(() => { jest.useFakeTimers(); });
  afterEach(() => { jest.useRealTimers(); });

  it('allows a call when window has not started', () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter(1000);
    expect(limiter.isAllowed()).toBe(true);   // covers: return true branch
  });

  it('rejects a call within the rate-limit window', () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter(1000);
    limiter.isAllowed();                       // first call: sets lastCallAt
    expect(limiter.isAllowed()).toBe(false);   // covers: return false branch (within window)
  });

  it('allows a call after the window expires', () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter(1000);
    limiter.isAllowed();
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(1001);            // advance past window
    expect(limiter.isAllowed()).toBe(true);    // covers: return true branch (window elapsed)
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: using `jest.useFakeTimers()` in every test file introduces setup/teardown overhead and requires explicit `jest.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach` to prevent timer leakage between tests. Forgetting `useRealTimers()` causes subsequent test files (run in the same worker process) to inherit fake timers, producing subtle ordering-dependent failures that are very hard to diagnose. Use `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pairs rather than module-level calls, and ensure your Jest config includes `fakeTimers: { legacyFakeTimers: false }` to use the modern `@sinonjs/fake-timers` implementation, which intercepts more timer APIs and produces more predictable branch coverage.

### Pattern 182 — Stryker `checkerNodeArgs` for TypeScript checker performance tuning in large monorepos  [official]

StrykerJS runs a TypeScript type-checker alongside mutation testing to filter out type-invalid mutations before executing them (avoiding test suite runs for code that would never compile). In large TypeScript monorepos with composite projects or `project references`, the type-checker startup time can dominate total mutation run time. The `checkerNodeArgs` option passes additional Node.js flags to the TypeScript checker worker, enabling V8 flags like `--max-old-space-size` and `--experimental-specifier-resolution` without affecting the test runner workers.

For projects with `disableTypeChecks: false` (re-enabled for payment/security modules per Pattern 171), tuning `checkerNodeArgs` is the primary lever for controlling checker memory and speed independently of the test runner.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — TypeScript checker tuning for large monorepo
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: { configFile: 'vitest.config.ts' },
  mutate: ['src/payments/**/*.ts', '!src/payments/**/*.spec.ts'],

  // Re-enable type checking for security-critical payment module
  disableTypeChecks: false,

  // Pass Node.js flags to the TypeScript checker worker process.
  // --max-old-space-size: prevents OOM in large composite projects.
  // --expose-gc: allows explicit GC calls between checker batches (advanced).
  checkerNodeArgs: [
    '--max-old-space-size=4096',
  ],

  // Batch mutations to checker in larger groups to amortize startup overhead.
  // Default is 10; increase to 50-100 for large files with many mutations.
  // (Available as 'checkerConcurrency' in StrykerJS 8+)
  concurrency: 2,        // 2 parallel mutation test workers
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  ignoreStatic: true,
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: 'reports/stryker-payments-incremental.json',

  reporters: ['html', 'json', 'progress'],
  thresholds: { high: 90, low: 70, break: 70 },

  allowEmpty: false,
  logLevel: 'info',
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: increasing `--max-old-space-size` for the checker worker allocates more heap to the TypeScript language service, which can significantly improve checker performance for large projects (reducing OOM restarts that silently slow runs) but increases the total memory footprint of the Stryker process. On a 4-core CI runner with 8 GB RAM running 2 mutation workers plus a checker worker, allocating 4 GB to the checker leaves limited headroom for the workers themselves. Profile with `logLevel: 'debug'` to see checker time vs. test time before tuning; if checker time is under 10% of total run time, `checkerNodeArgs` optimization will have minimal impact.
