### Pattern 183 — Vitest `coverage.changed` combined with `thresholds.perFile`: scoping per-file gates to changed files only  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `coverage.changed`, which limits coverage collection and threshold evaluation to files that differ from a specified git ref (default: `HEAD`). When combined with `thresholds.perFile: true`, this creates a "new-code quality gate" pattern: only files touched in the current PR must meet per-file thresholds. Legacy files with known coverage debt are excluded from the gate, which eliminates the "can't touch legacy code without fixing all its coverage" friction that blocks incremental improvement.

The `changed` option accepts a git ref string: `HEAD` (staged vs last commit), `origin/main` (PR branch vs main), or a specific commit SHA. In CI, `origin/main` is the most useful reference for PR gates.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — per-file thresholds scoped to PR-changed files
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Only evaluate thresholds for files changed vs main branch.
      // Unchanged legacy files are collected but not gated.
      // Set to 'HEAD' for staged-changes-only mode (local development).
      changed: process.env.CI === 'true' ? 'origin/main' : 'HEAD',

      thresholds: {
        // Per-file enforcement: each changed file must independently pass.
        perFile: true,

        // These thresholds apply only to changed files when 'changed' is set.
        lines:      85,
        branches:   75,
        functions:  85,
        statements: 85,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverage.changed` with `origin/main` requires the CI runner to have the full git history available — shallow clones (`--depth=1`) break the `git diff` operation that powers this feature, producing empty changed-file lists and silently skipping all threshold checks. Always ensure your CI checkout step uses `fetch-depth: 0` (full history) when using `coverage.changed`. Additionally, rebasing a PR branch before running coverage can cause `git diff origin/main` to produce different results than `git diff --merge-base origin/main HEAD`, potentially including files from unrelated commits. Use `git diff origin/main...HEAD` (three dots) for the most precise PR-scope diff.

---

### Pattern 184 — NYC `watermarks` in `.nycrc.json`: calibrating the red/yellow/green HTML report bands  [official]

NYC's HTML coverage report uses three color bands to communicate file health: red (below the low watermark), yellow (between low and high), and green (above the high watermark). The default watermarks are `[50, 80]` for all dimensions — a project with thresholds set to 90% will see files at 85% as yellow, suggesting they need work when they are actually 5 percentage points above the threshold. This visual mismatch erodes trust in the report over time.

The `watermarks` config object accepts per-dimension `[low, high]` arrays. Setting both values to align with your threshold (e.g., low at 70%, high at 90%) means yellow indicates "approaching the threshold" and red indicates "below threshold" — exactly the semantics developers expect.

```typescript
// .nycrc.json — watermarks aligned with coverage thresholds
{
  "extends": "@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript",
  "all": false,
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": [
    "src/**/*.spec.ts",
    "src/**/*.d.ts",
    "src/**/__mocks__/**",
    "src/generated/**"
  ],
  "reporter": ["text", "html", "json-summary", "lcov"],
  "check-coverage": true,
  "lines": 80,
  "branches": 70,
  "functions": 80,
  "statements": 80,
  "watermarks": {
    "lines":      [70, 80],
    "branches":   [60, 70],
    "functions":  [70, 80],
    "statements": [70, 80]
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: watermarks are purely cosmetic — they affect the HTML report color-coding only and have no effect on the `--check-coverage` threshold enforcement. Teams often set watermarks once and forget to update them when thresholds are raised. A CI lint check that reads both the watermarks and check-coverage values from `.nycrc.json` and verifies alignment (watermarks high == check-coverage value) prevents drift. Note that watermarks apply per-file in the HTML report; the coverage table row for a file turns red if that file's line coverage is below the `lines[0]` watermark, independent of whether the project-level threshold is met.

---

### Pattern 185 — Jest `projects` array with unified `coverageThreshold`: fixing multi-project coverage aggregation  [official]

Jest's `projects` configuration enables monorepo-style multi-package test runs from a single `jest.config.ts`. A subtle behavior (documented and fixed in Jest 30.4): when `collectCoverageFrom` is specified in individual project configs and the project's `rootDir` differs from the global `rootDir`, coverage glob patterns were previously resolved against the project's `rootDir` but reported against the global `rootDir` — causing glob mismatches where patterns like `src/**/*.ts` matched no files because the project's source lived at `packages/my-lib/src/`. Jest 30.4 fixed this by resolving `collectCoverageFrom` globs against `globalRootDir` consistently.

The correct post-30.4 pattern is to define `collectCoverageFrom` in the global config using workspace-relative paths, and use per-project `coverageThreshold` for module-level enforcement.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — multi-project setup with Jest 30.4+ aggregation fix
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Global config: coverage is aggregated here.
  // Post-Jest 30.4: collectCoverageFrom is resolved against globalRootDir.
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'packages/*/src/**/*.ts',
    '!packages/*/src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!packages/*/src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!packages/*/src/generated/**',
  ],
  coverageDirectory: './coverage',
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  coverageReporters: [['text', { skipFull: true }], 'json-summary', 'lcov'],

  // Global threshold: applies to all files not matched by project patterns.
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      lines: 80,
      branches: 70,
      functions: 80,
      statements: 80,
    },
    // Critical business logic modules require higher coverage
    'packages/payments/src/': {
      lines: 95,
      branches: 90,
    },
    'packages/auth/src/': {
      lines: 90,
      branches: 85,
    },
  },

  projects: [
    '<rootDir>/packages/payments',
    '<rootDir>/packages/auth',
    '<rootDir>/packages/api',
    '<rootDir>/packages/shared',
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff**: the Jest 30.4 fix for `collectCoverageFrom` resolution changes behavior — upgrading from Jest 30.3 or earlier may cause previously-passing coverage gates to fail if glob patterns were accidentally working due to the old path resolution bug. Before upgrading, audit your `collectCoverageFrom` patterns with `jest --collectCoverage --verbose` to verify the full set of files being reported. If per-project patterns relied on the old (incorrect) resolution, update them to use `globalRootDir`-relative paths as part of the upgrade.

---

### Pattern 186 — Istanbul `/* istanbul ignore if */` and `/* istanbul ignore else */`: branch-selective exclusion  [official]

Istanbul supports two branch-selective ignore directives that exclude only one branch of a conditional: `/* istanbul ignore if */` excludes the true branch of the next `if` statement, and `/* istanbul ignore else */` excludes the false branch. These are more precise than `/* istanbul ignore next */`, which suppresses the entire next statement or block including both branches.

In TypeScript applications, the most common use case is platform shims where one branch is always taken in the test environment but the other executes only in a specific runtime (e.g., a Node.js version check, a browser-only code path, or an environment detection guard). Suppressing only the untestable branch keeps the testable branch in the coverage report.

```typescript
// src/platform-utils.ts — branch-selective Istanbul ignore directives
// Using /* istanbul ignore else */ to suppress the browser-only branch
// that is never executed in Node.js test environments.

export function getStorageAdapter(): Storage | Map<string, string> {
  /* istanbul ignore else -- @preserve */
  if (typeof localStorage !== 'undefined') {
    // Node.js test environment: this else branch is always taken,
    // localStorage is always undefined in Node.
    return new Map<string, string>();
  } else {
    // Browser-only: localStorage is available.
    // This branch is unreachable in test environments.
    return localStorage;
  }
}

export function getWorkerThreadCount(): number {
  /* istanbul ignore if -- @preserve */
  if (typeof navigator !== 'undefined' && navigator.hardwareConcurrency > 0) {
    // Browser-only: navigator.hardwareConcurrency is undefined in Node.
    return navigator.hardwareConcurrency;
  }
  // Node.js path: always taken in tests.
  return require('node:os').cpus().length;
}
```

**Tradeoff**: branch-selective ignores require the `-- @preserve` suffix when using Vitest with esbuild (see Principle 6 in this guide). Without it, esbuild strips the comment before Istanbul instruments the code and both branches are reported as uncovered, defeating the purpose of the directive. Additionally, `/* istanbul ignore if */` and `/* istanbul ignore else */` apply to the next `if` statement, not to arbitrary expressions — they cannot selectively suppress one side of a ternary operator (`condition ? a : b`). For ternary branches, use `/* istanbul ignore next */` on the full expression or refactor to an explicit `if/else`.

---

### Pattern 187 — c8 `checkCoverage` with CLI threshold flags: enforcing thresholds without a config file  [official]

c8 supports coverage threshold enforcement via four CLI flags: `--lines`, `--branches`, `--statements`, and `--functions`. When any metric falls below its threshold, c8 exits with code 1. This approach is useful for projects that manage coverage configuration through environment variables, CI pipeline parameters, or scripting layers that cannot easily write config files.

Combining `--check-coverage` (the flag that activates enforcement) with threshold values as separate flags avoids the need for a `.c8rc` or `c8` section in `package.json`. This makes the threshold values visible and overridable directly in CI pipeline definitions without editing source files.

```typescript
// .github/workflows/coverage.yml (excerpt, commented as TypeScript documentation)
// The following CI step uses c8 with inline threshold flags for clean override:
//
// - name: Run tests with coverage
//   run: |
//     npx c8 \
//       --check-coverage \
//       --lines ${{ vars.COVERAGE_LINES_THRESHOLD || '80' }} \
//       --branches ${{ vars.COVERAGE_BRANCHES_THRESHOLD || '70' }} \
//       --functions ${{ vars.COVERAGE_FUNCTIONS_THRESHOLD || '80' }} \
//       --statements ${{ vars.COVERAGE_STATEMENTS_THRESHOLD || '80' }} \
//       --reporter=text \
//       --reporter=lcov \
//       --reporter=json-summary \
//       --include='src/**/*.ts' \
//       --exclude='src/**/*.spec.ts' \
//       node --test src/**/*.spec.ts

// ci/parse-coverage-thresholds.ts — helper to read threshold flags from env
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

interface Thresholds {
  lines: number;
  branches: number;
  functions: number;
  statements: number;
}

export function readThresholdsFromEnv(defaults: Thresholds): Thresholds {
  return {
    lines:      parseInt(process.env.COVERAGE_LINES_THRESHOLD      ?? String(defaults.lines),      10),
    branches:   parseInt(process.env.COVERAGE_BRANCHES_THRESHOLD   ?? String(defaults.branches),   10),
    functions:  parseInt(process.env.COVERAGE_FUNCTIONS_THRESHOLD  ?? String(defaults.functions),  10),
    statements: parseInt(process.env.COVERAGE_STATEMENTS_THRESHOLD ?? String(defaults.statements), 10),
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff**: storing threshold values as CI environment variables makes them easy to override per-environment (e.g., stricter thresholds on main branch, looser on feature branches) but harder to track in version control. A threshold change that should be committed alongside test improvements can silently exist only as a CI variable update, losing the commit-history traceability that code reviews rely on. The best practice: keep default thresholds in a config file (`.c8rc.json`) and allow CI variables to override only upward (strict) — never downward — to prevent coverage regression through pipeline configuration drift.

---

### Pattern 188 — Vitest V8 `/* v8 ignore if */` and `/* v8 ignore else */`: branch-selective V8 ignore directives  [official]

Vitest 4.1 extended V8 coverage ignore directives with branch-selective variants: `/* v8 ignore if */` and `/* v8 ignore else */`. These suppress only one branch of the immediately following conditional, analogous to Istanbul's `ignore if` / `ignore else` directives. Since the V8 provider tracks branches at coarser granularity than Istanbul, these directives are particularly useful for Node.js version guards and environment-detection branches that structurally cannot be exercised in a test environment.

The directives require the `-- @preserve` suffix when using Vitest's default esbuild transpiler (same as all other Vitest ignore directives). Without it, esbuild strips the comment before the V8 instrumentation layer sees it.

```typescript
// src/async-iterator-utils.ts — V8 branch-selective ignore for Node version guard
// Node 22+ has native ReadableStream.from(); older Node requires a polyfill.
// The polyfill branch is not tested in CI (always Node 22+).

import { Readable } from 'node:stream';

const nodeMajor = parseInt(process.versions.node.split('.')[0], 10);

export function streamFrom<T>(iterable: AsyncIterable<T>): Readable {
  /* v8 ignore if -- @preserve */
  if (nodeMajor < 22) {
    // Polyfill path: not tested in CI (Node 22+ required by CI pipeline)
    return Readable.from(iterable as AsyncIterable<unknown>);
  }
  // Native path: always taken in test environment
  return Readable.from(iterable as AsyncIterable<unknown>);
}

export function supportsStructuredClone(): boolean {
  /* v8 ignore else -- @preserve */
  if (typeof structuredClone === 'function') {
    return true;
  } else {
    // Node < 17: structuredClone undefined. Only the true branch is tested.
    return false;
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `/* v8 ignore if */` and `/* v8 ignore else */` are only available in Vitest 4.1+ — they are not part of the underlying V8 coverage API and are implemented as a Vitest-layer annotation. Projects using c8 directly, Istanbul, or NYC cannot use this syntax. The directives also do not work with Jest's V8 provider — Jest does not implement the Vitest annotation layer. For cross-tool compatibility, use `/* istanbul ignore if -- @preserve */` / `/* istanbul ignore else -- @preserve */` instead, which Vitest recognizes regardless of provider (Istanbul handles these natively; Vitest's V8 layer maps them to V8 branch suppression via its AST remapper).

---

### Pattern 189 — Stryker `testableMutations` for fine-grained operator-level control within a mutator  [official]

StrykerJS's `excludedMutations` option removes entire mutator categories (e.g., `ArithmeticOperator`, `ConditionalExpression`). For teams that want to exclude specific sub-patterns within a mutator category without disabling the whole category, Stryker 8+ introduced `mutatorConfig` (formerly `testableMutations` in plugin form) which allows specifying a replacement whitelist per mutator. This prevents the coarse-grained problem where disabling `StringLiteral` to avoid template-string mutations also disables meaningful string-equality mutations.

The most common use case is `ConditionalExpression` mutations in code-generated files — disabling the whole operator suppresses valuable logical-operator mutations in hand-written code. Fine-grained control allows suppressing only code-gen patterns while keeping the operator active for business logic.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — fine-grained mutator configuration
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Partial<Config> = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: { configFile: 'vitest.config.ts' },
  mutate: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/generated/**',
  ],

  // Coarse-grained exclusion: suppress entire operator categories.
  // Use for generated code patterns that cannot be excluded by file path alone.
  excludedMutations: [
    // RegExp mutations rarely map to meaningful faults in business code;
    // they generate large numbers of low-signal surviving mutants.
    'Regex',
  ],

  // Fine-grained: restrict which replacements a mutator may produce.
  // Available in StrykerJS 8+ via mutatorConfig plugin.
  // Example: only allow ConditionalExpression to flip boolean conditions,
  // not replace complex expressions with literals.
  // (Exact API depends on installed mutator plugin version)
  // mutatorConfig: {
  //   ConditionalExpression: { replacements: ['false', 'true'] },
  //   StringLiteral: { excludePatterns: [/^generated/] },
  // },

  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  ignoreStatic: true,
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: 'reports/stryker-incremental.json',
  reporters: ['html', 'json', 'progress'],
  concurrency: '50%',
  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: null },
  allowEmpty: false,
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: fine-grained `mutatorConfig` is a StrykerJS 8+ feature that was added as a plugin-layer capability — the exact configuration API differs from the core `excludedMutations` array and is less well-documented. Teams on StrykerJS 7 or earlier must use the coarse-grained `excludedMutations` approach or scope exclusions via `mutate` pattern negations at the file level. When in doubt, use file-path negation (`'!src/generated/**'`) to remove generated files from mutation scope entirely — this is always the cleanest approach and does not risk suppressing meaningful mutations in non-generated code.

---

### Pattern 190 — Vitest `coverage.autoUpdate`: automatically ratcheting thresholds to prevent regression  [official]

Vitest 4.0 introduced `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate: true`, which automatically updates threshold values in `vitest.config.ts` when the current coverage run exceeds the configured thresholds. This implements a ratchet pattern without manual intervention: after every successful coverage improvement, the threshold locks in at the new (higher) level, making it impossible to regress silently.

The auto-update mechanism writes updated threshold values directly to the config file — a local-only feature designed for developer workflows, not CI. In CI, `autoUpdate` should be `false` (or absent), and the config file's committed thresholds should be the enforced baseline.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage ratchet with autoUpdate
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      thresholds: {
        lines:      82,   // Auto-updated: was 80, coverage improved to 82
        branches:   71,   // Auto-updated: was 70, coverage improved to 71
        functions:  83,   // Auto-updated: was 80, coverage improved to 83
        statements: 82,

        // autoUpdate: true causes Vitest to overwrite these values in-file
        // when the current run exceeds them. Disable in CI to prevent config
        // drift (CI should enforce the committed thresholds, not self-update).
        autoUpdate: !isCI,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `autoUpdate` writes to the `vitest.config.ts` file in the working directory, which creates a git diff on every local run that improves coverage. Developers must remember to commit the updated thresholds alongside their coverage-improving test changes — otherwise the ratchet resets to the committed value on the next clone. The risk is that `autoUpdate` produces config changes that appear trivial ("just bumped some numbers") but represent meaningful quality commitments; reviewers may approve them without understanding their significance. Mitigate by adding a commit template or PR description template note that explains the coverage ratchet pattern, so reviewers know to check that the bumped thresholds are backed by genuine test improvements and not by adding ignore directives.

## Cycle 42 Community Gotchas

### G136 — Vitest `coverage.changed` with shallow CI checkouts silently skips all threshold checks  [community]

Vitest's `coverage.changed` option runs `git diff` against a reference branch to determine which files changed. When a CI runner checks out a repository with `--depth=1` (the default for most CI providers including GitHub Actions without explicit configuration), the local repository has no knowledge of commits on `origin/main` beyond the merge base — and `git diff origin/main...HEAD` produces an empty diff. Vitest interprets an empty changed-file list as "no files changed" and skips all per-file threshold checks entirely, reporting a successful run even when new code has zero test coverage. **WHY it matters**: the empty diff is a silent false-positive — CI passes, coverage looks fine, and no one notices that the per-file threshold gate was completely bypassed. The fix: in your CI checkout step, set `fetch-depth: 0` (GitHub Actions) or the equivalent full-history checkout option for your CI provider. Alternatively, use `coverage.changed: 'HEAD'` (diff against the previous commit rather than a remote branch ref), which works with shallow checkouts but only gates on the last commit's changes, not the full PR diff.

### G137 — Jest `fakeTimers` with `advanceTimersByTime` leaves `Date` stubs active if `useRealTimers` is forgotten: coverage appears correct but assertions are wrong  [community]

When a test uses `jest.useFakeTimers()` and advances time with `jest.advanceTimersByTime()` to exercise timer-guarded branches, the fake `Date.now()` returns a value that reflects the advanced clock. If `jest.useRealTimers()` is not called in `afterEach`, subsequent test files that run in the same Jest worker inherit the stale fake clock. Tests in those files that call `Date.now()` get the fake advanced value instead of real wall-clock time. The coverage report shows those branches as covered (they were, in the faked-time test), but the assertions pass for the wrong reason — the branch was taken based on a fake timestamp that would never occur in production. **WHY it matters**: the coverage report and test results appear healthy, but the tests are testing incorrect behavior under a clock that is permanently advanced. The canonical symptom is "tests pass but the feature fails in production when deployed on a server where `Date.now()` returns real time." The fix: always use `beforeEach`/`afterEach` symmetry for fake timer setup/teardown; consider using Jest's `restoreMocks: true` and `resetMocks: true` global config options to automatically clean up all mocks (including fake timers) between tests.

### G138 — c8 `--exclude-after-remap` with `.d.ts` re-exports: declaration files included in coverage report despite exclusion  [community]

c8's `--exclude-after-remap` flag re-applies `--exclude` glob patterns after source-map remapping. However, when a TypeScript module re-exports its public API through a barrel `.d.ts` file (a pattern common in library packages using `declaration: true` and `declarationDir`), some V8 coverage entries are recorded with the `.d.ts` path rather than the implementation `.ts` path. After remap, these entries appear as `.d.ts` file coverage rows in the report. If the `--exclude` pattern only matches `*.d.ts` at the top level (`*.d.ts`) rather than recursively (`**/*.d.ts`), declaration files in subdirectories are not excluded. **WHY it matters**: `.d.ts` files have 0% coverage by definition (they contain no executable code), and their presence in the report inflates the "uncovered files" count, can trigger `--check-coverage` failures, and produces confusing 0% rows in the HTML report that developers waste time investigating. The fix: ensure `--exclude` patterns use `**/*.d.ts` (recursive glob) not `*.d.ts` (root-only glob), and run `--exclude-after-remap` in combination to catch both pre-remap and post-remap phantom entries.

### G139 — Stryker `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` with Vitest `describe.concurrent`: mutant test attribution is incorrect for concurrent test blocks  [community]

Stryker's `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` mode records which tests cover each mutant — this per-test attribution enables Stryker to run only the tests that cover a mutant when testing it, dramatically speeding up mutation runs. The attribution is computed during an initial "dry run" where each test is run individually and its coverage is recorded. Vitest's `describe.concurrent` blocks run their tests in parallel within the same worker, which causes the per-test coverage attribution to conflate all concurrent tests into a single coverage record. Stryker records all tests in a concurrent block as "covering" every line that any of them covered, over-attributing coverage and causing Stryker to run all concurrent tests for mutants that only one test actually covers. **WHY it matters**: the mutation run takes significantly longer than expected because Stryker runs unnecessarily large test subsets per mutant. Worse, if the concurrent tests have shared state side effects, false "mutant killed" results can appear because an unrelated concurrent test happens to catch a side effect of the mutation. The fix: avoid `describe.concurrent` in files that contain code exercised by Stryker; use sequential `describe` blocks or split concurrent tests into separate top-level `it` blocks that Stryker can attribute individually.

### G140 — NYC `foreground-child` and ESM loaders: `--require` hook does not apply to ESM test files, producing 0% coverage for ESM modules  [community]

NYC instruments CommonJS modules at load time by wrapping `require()` with a coverage hook. For projects that mix ESM (`import`/`export`) and CommonJS, NYC's `--require=ts-node/register` hook instruments `.ts` files that are loaded via `require()` but has no effect on `.ts` files loaded via `import`. When an ESM test file (`describe`/`it` using ES module syntax with `"type": "module"` in `package.json`) imports a TypeScript module, NYC never instruments it because the ES module loader bypasses the CommonJS `require()` hook. The result: every ESM module in the project shows 0% coverage despite being extensively tested. **WHY it matters**: teams migrating from CommonJS to ESM often see their coverage drop catastrophically after adding `"type": "module"` to `package.json` — not because tests were deleted but because NYC's instrumentation mechanism no longer reaches the code. The fix: migrate from NYC to c8 for ESM TypeScript projects (c8 uses V8's native coverage API, which works regardless of module system) or configure NYC with `--loader=ts-node/esm` and ensure your Node.js version supports the `--loader` experimental ESM hooks (Node 18.19+ with `--experimental-vm-modules` or Node 20+ ESM loader hooks).

## Cycle 43 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 191 — Jest `coverageThreshold` with negative values: capping maximum uncovered item counts instead of minimum percentages  [official]

Jest's `coverageThreshold` object accepts both positive and negative numeric values. Positive values are interpreted as minimum percentage requirements (e.g., `statements: 80` means at least 80% of statements must be covered). Negative values flip the semantics entirely: they specify the maximum number of uncovered items allowed (e.g., `statements: -10` means at most 10 uncovered statements are permitted, regardless of total statement count). This is especially useful for large legacy codebases where percentage thresholds are impractical at launch but an absolute cap on regressions is achievable from day one. The negative threshold mode is an official Jest feature that predates v29 and remains unchanged through Jest 30.

A common phased adoption strategy: start with `statements: -500` (no more than 500 uncovered statements) and reduce the cap by 50 each sprint until the codebase stabilises around a meaningful percentage threshold. This gives teams a concrete improvement target without requiring a percentage gate they cannot currently meet.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — negative threshold as absolute uncovered-item cap
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  collectCoverage: true,
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/__mocks__/**',
    '!src/**/index.ts', // barrel re-exports add noise to uncovered counts
  ],
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],

  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      // Positive: minimum percentage required
      lines:      70,
      branches:   60,
      functions:  75,
      // Negative: maximum uncovered statement COUNT allowed.
      // 250 uncovered statements is the current baseline; reduce by 50 per sprint.
      statements: -250,
    },
    // Critical payment path: 100% coverage required regardless of global cap
    './src/payments/**/*.ts': {
      lines:      100,
      branches:   100,
      functions:  100,
      statements: 100,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: negative thresholds are invisible in the HTML coverage report — you only see the pass/fail in CI terminal output. Teams unfamiliar with the pattern will see `Jest: "global" coverage threshold for statements (-250) not met: -263` and misread the negative as "negative coverage" rather than "cap exceeded." Document the negative-threshold convention prominently in your `CONTRIBUTING.md` and add a comment in `jest.config.ts` (as shown above) to prevent confusion. Additionally, negative thresholds do not encourage improvement the way percentage thresholds do: a team that adds new tested code while also adding untested code can stay within the negative-threshold cap without making any proportional progress. Combine with periodic percentage-threshold reviews to ensure the absolute cap is actually decreasing over time.

---

### Pattern 192 — Vitest `coverage.ignoreEmptyLines`: eliminating blank-line false-negatives in Istanbul branch maps  [official]

Istanbul's line-level coverage map includes blank lines and comment-only lines in its `uncovered lines` count under certain transpiler configurations — specifically when the transpiler emits source-map entries pointing at blank lines in the original TypeScript source. Vitest's `coverage.ignoreEmptyLines: true` option (Istanbul provider only) instructs Istanbul to skip any source line that contains only whitespace or comment text when counting uncovered lines. This reduces the "uncovered lines" number to reflect only genuinely unexecuted code, removing the noise from empty lines that Istanbul incorrectly attributes as executable. The option is distinct from `coverage.skipFull` (which controls report verbosity) and does not affect branch or function coverage counts.

Projects that enforce strict per-file line thresholds (via `thresholds.perFile`) benefit the most from this option: a single comment block at the bottom of a file can inflate the uncovered-line count by 10-20 lines, potentially triggering a threshold failure on a file that is otherwise well-tested.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — ignoreEmptyLines to prevent blank-line false failures
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/__mocks__/**',
      ],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Eliminate blank lines and comment-only lines from the uncovered
      // lines count.  Without this, Istanbul may count JSDoc comment blocks
      // as uncovered lines when source maps point at whitespace.
      ignoreEmptyLines: true,

      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  82,
        statements: 80,
        // Per-file gate: each file must meet these thresholds independently.
        // ignoreEmptyLines is critical here — without it, comment-heavy files
        // fail this gate even when all executable code is covered.
        perFile: true,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `ignoreEmptyLines` is an Istanbul-provider-only option — it has no equivalent for the V8 provider because V8's coverage data is statement-based and does not include blank-line entries in the first place. Switching from Istanbul to V8 automatically eliminates blank-line noise without any configuration, so teams planning a provider migration should not rely on `ignoreEmptyLines` as a long-term solution. The option also silently ignores lines that are exclusively `//` comments — this means a large commented-out code block is excluded from coverage, which may mask the fact that dead code has been left in the file. Use `ignoreEmptyLines` together with a lint rule (e.g., `no-commented-out-code`) to prevent the option from hiding genuinely problematic commented-out logic.

---

### Pattern 193 — c8 `/* c8 ignore start */` and `/* c8 ignore stop */`: block-range V8 coverage suppression  [official]

c8's single-line ignore directive (`/* c8 ignore next */` or `/* c8 ignore next N */`) only suppresses the immediately following line(s). For multi-line blocks that are structurally untestable — such as complex error-handling chains, platform-detection switch statements, or Node.js version polyfill shims — c8 provides block-range directives: `/* c8 ignore start */` opens a suppression block and `/* c8 ignore stop */` closes it. All lines between the directives are excluded from V8 coverage counts. These directives work identically to Istanbul's `/* istanbul ignore next */` applied repeatedly but are cleaner and less error-prone for blocks exceeding three lines. The block directives were introduced in c8 v7.4 and are fully supported in all subsequent versions including c8 v11.

The directives survive esbuild and tsc transpilation without requiring `-- @preserve` suffixes because they are processed by c8 post-execution during source-map remapping — they are not consumed by the TypeScript compiler pipeline.

```typescript
// src/platform/process-exit-shim.ts — block ignore for platform detection
// Node.js 18 lacks process.exitCode setter in some edge environments.
// This block is untestable in standard CI (always Node 22+).

export function safeExit(code: number): never {
  /* c8 ignore start */
  if (typeof process.exitCode !== 'undefined') {
    process.exitCode = code;
    process.exit();
  } else {
    // Older Node path: exitCode property not available
    process.exit(code);
  }
  /* c8 ignore stop */
}

// Testable path: platform string detection
export function getPlatformLabel(): string {
  switch (process.platform) {
    case 'win32':  return 'Windows';
    case 'darwin': return 'macOS';
    case 'linux':  return 'Linux';
    /* c8 ignore start */
    default:       return `Unknown(${process.platform})`;
    /* c8 ignore stop */
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `/* c8 ignore start */` / `/* c8 ignore stop */` blocks are not recognised by Istanbul or Vitest's Istanbul provider — they are c8-specific annotations. Projects using Vitest with the Istanbul provider must use `/* istanbul ignore next */` (applied repeatedly) or switch to `/* v8 ignore start */` / `/* v8 ignore stop */` for Vitest 4.1+ with the V8 provider. This creates a divergence risk: a project that starts with c8 directly and later migrates to Vitest + Istanbul provider will have hundreds of silent c8 annotations that no longer suppress anything. Maintain a policy: either use only Istanbul-compatible annotations (`/* istanbul ignore next */`) everywhere, or adopt c8/V8-specific annotations and document the provider lock-in explicitly in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

---

### Pattern 194 — Jest `coverageProvider: 'v8'` with `sourceMap: true` in tsconfig: ensuring accurate TypeScript line mapping  [official]

Jest's V8 coverage provider (`coverageProvider: 'v8'`) collects coverage data directly from Node.js's V8 engine and then remaps it to TypeScript source lines using the source maps generated during transpilation. If `tsconfig.json` does not include `"sourceMap": true` (or `"inlineSourceMap": true`), V8 has no source-map data to remap and reports coverage against the compiled JavaScript output rather than the original `.ts` files. The resulting coverage report shows `.js` file paths with coverage percentages that do not correspond to any file the developer recognises. This is particularly confusing in monorepos where each package has its own `tsconfig.json` — a single package missing `sourceMap: true` causes that package's coverage to report against its build output, while all other packages report correctly against TypeScript source.

The fix is straightforward but easy to miss: verify that every `tsconfig.json` in the project tree — including `tsconfig.base.json`, workspace-level configs, and any `tsconfig.build.json` variants — includes `"sourceMap": true` or `"inlineSourceMap": true`.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — V8 provider with source map verification
import type { Config } from 'jest';
import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

// Helper: verify tsconfig has sourceMap enabled.
// Run this check at config-load time to catch misconfiguration early.
function assertSourceMapEnabled(tsconfigPath: string): void {
  if (!existsSync(tsconfigPath)) return;
  const raw = readFileSync(tsconfigPath, 'utf8');
  // Strip JSON comments (tsconfig allows comments)
  const cleaned = raw.replace(/\/\/.*$/gm, '').replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, '');
  const parsed = JSON.parse(cleaned);
  const co = parsed?.compilerOptions ?? {};
  if (!co.sourceMap && !co.inlineSourceMap) {
    throw new Error(
      `[jest.config] ${tsconfigPath} must set "sourceMap": true or ` +
      `"inlineSourceMap": true for V8 coverage provider to map to .ts files.`
    );
  }
}

assertSourceMapEnabled('./tsconfig.json');

const config: Config = {
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  collectCoverage: false, // Enable via --coverage CLI flag only
  coverageProvider: 'v8', // Requires sourceMap: true in tsconfig
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
  ],
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: the `assertSourceMapEnabled` guard runs at Jest config-load time (i.e., for every `jest` invocation including non-coverage runs), adding a small filesystem read overhead. For large monorepos with many packages, checking all `tsconfig.json` files at startup can add 50-100ms to test startup time. A lighter approach is to add the check only to a dedicated CI lint step (e.g., `tsc --noEmit` already validates tsconfig correctness) rather than the Jest config. Additionally, `inlineSourceMap: true` embeds source-map data directly in the compiled `.js` files rather than emitting `.js.map` files, which increases the size of built artifacts — use `sourceMap: true` (external map files) for library packages where artifact size matters and `inlineSourceMap: true` only for test-only transpilation flows.

---

### Pattern 195 — Vitest `coverage.reportOnFailure`: ensuring coverage artifacts are written even when tests fail  [official]

By default, Vitest suppresses coverage report generation when the test run exits with failures. This means a CI run where tests fail produces no coverage report artifact — making it impossible to diagnose which tests were covering which lines before the failure occurred. Vitest's `coverage.reportOnFailure: true` option overrides this behaviour and writes coverage artifacts to `reportsDirectory` regardless of test outcome. This is essential in two scenarios: (1) triage workflows where the coverage report helps identify which test failure corresponds to which code path, and (2) coverage-gate enforcement where the threshold check should still run and report how far the failing build is from the target, not just silently skip.

The option does not affect whether Vitest exits with a non-zero code — test failures still cause the process to exit with code 1. It only ensures the coverage artifact (HTML, JSON, LCOV) is written before exit.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — write coverage even on test failure for CI triage
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: isCI
        ? ['json-summary', 'lcov', 'text']   // CI: machine-readable + text for logs
        : ['html', 'text'],                   // local: HTML for browser inspection
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Write coverage artifacts even when tests fail.
      // Without this, a single failing test prevents coverage from being
      // uploaded as a CI artifact, losing the diagnostic information.
      reportOnFailure: true,

      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  82,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `reportOnFailure: true` means coverage reports from failing builds are uploaded as CI artifacts alongside passing-build reports, which can create ambiguity: is the uploaded `coverage/index.html` from a green run or a red run? Mitigate by including a `pass/fail` metadata file in the `reportsDirectory` (e.g., a `coverage-summary.json` with a `"testsPassed": false` field written by a custom reporter or a `vitest globalTeardown` hook) so that any system consuming the artifact can distinguish the two cases. Also be aware that on a failing run, the coverage percentages in the report may be misleadingly low because failed tests do not exercise their full code paths — the report reflects coverage up to the point of failure, not the coverage the suite would achieve if all tests passed.

---

### Pattern 196 — c8 `.c8rc.json` centralised configuration: moving all threshold and reporter options out of package.json scripts  [official]

c8 reads configuration from a `.c8rc.json` (or `.c8rc`) file in the project root, similar to `.nycrc.json` for Istanbul. Moving all c8 options out of `package.json` scripts (where they are easy to accidentally alter in a rebase or merge conflict) and into a dedicated config file brings several benefits: the config is version-controlled as a distinct file, changes to thresholds appear as clear diffs in code review, and the same config is used regardless of which script invokes c8 (test, coverage, CI). The `.c8rc.json` format mirrors the CLI flag names (without the `--` prefix) and supports all options including `include`, `exclude`, `reporter`, `check-coverage`, `lines`, `branches`, `functions`, and `statements`.

An important nuance: `all: true` in `.c8rc.json` causes c8 to include all files matching `include` patterns in the coverage report, even files that were never imported during the test run. This is the correct setting for catching completely untested files (0% coverage), which threshold checks would otherwise miss since uncovered files default to 100% coverage when absent from the report.

```json
{
  "all": true,
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": [
    "src/**/*.spec.ts",
    "src/**/*.d.ts",
    "src/**/__mocks__/**",
    "src/**/index.ts"
  ],
  "extension": [".ts"],
  "reporter": ["text", "html", "json-summary", "lcov"],
  "reports-dir": "./coverage",
  "exclude-after-remap": true,
  "check-coverage": true,
  "lines": 80,
  "branches": 70,
  "functions": 82,
  "statements": 80,
  "per-file": false,
  "skip-full": false
}
```

```typescript
// Helper: validate .c8rc.json at build time (run in pre-commit hook)
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

interface C8Rc {
  lines?: number;
  branches?: number;
  functions?: number;
  statements?: number;
  all?: boolean;
}

export function validateC8Config(path = '.c8rc.json'): C8Rc {
  const cfg: C8Rc = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'));
  if (!cfg.all) {
    console.warn(
      '[c8] WARNING: "all: true" not set — untested files will be ' +
      'excluded from threshold checks'
    );
  }
  return cfg;
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `.c8rc.json` is processed by c8 only when c8 is invoked directly (e.g., `c8 vitest run` or `c8 node test.js`). If the project also uses Vitest with the V8 provider, Vitest does not read `.c8rc.json` — it reads `vitest.config.ts` coverage options. Maintaining both a `.c8rc.json` (for direct c8 invocations) and `vitest.config.ts` coverage settings introduces duplication risk: a threshold change in one file may not be reflected in the other, leading to different pass/fail outcomes depending on which tool runs. The cleanest resolution is to pick one tool and one config location: use Vitest exclusively (with `vitest.config.ts`) or use c8 directly (with `.c8rc.json`), not both.

---

### Pattern 197 — Jest `collectCoverageFrom` glob ordering: later negation patterns override earlier inclusions  [official]

Jest evaluates `collectCoverageFrom` glob patterns left-to-right using micromatch semantics, where later patterns override earlier ones when a file path matches multiple entries. A common mistake is placing exclusion negations before positive inclusion patterns, causing the negations to be overridden. For example, `['!**/__fixtures__/**', '**/*.ts']` will include fixture files because the later `**/*.ts` pattern matches them and overrides the earlier negation. The correct order is always: positive (include) patterns first, negation (exclude) patterns last. This is the opposite of `.gitignore` semantics (where specific rules override general ones regardless of order), and developers with strong git background frequently make this mistake.

A secondary issue: the `<rootDir>` token in `collectCoverageFrom` resolves differently than in `testMatch` or `testPathIgnorePatterns` when `rootDir` is not explicitly set — it defaults to the directory containing `jest.config.ts`, which may differ from the project root in monorepo setups.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — correct glob ordering for collectCoverageFrom
import type { Config } from 'jest';
import path from 'node:path';

const config: Config = {
  rootDir: path.resolve(__dirname),  // Explicit rootDir prevents <rootDir> surprises
  collectCoverage: false,
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    // CORRECT ORDER: inclusions first, then exclusions.
    // Later patterns override earlier ones (micromatch semantics).
    '<rootDir>/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',        // Include all source files
    '!<rootDir>/src/**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}',  // Exclude test files (after inclusion)
    '!<rootDir>/src/**/*.d.ts',           // Exclude declaration files
    '!<rootDir>/src/**/__mocks__/**',     // Exclude mock modules
    '!<rootDir>/src/**/__fixtures__/**',  // Exclude fixture data
    '!<rootDir>/src/**/index.ts',         // Exclude barrel re-exports

    // WRONG (do NOT put negations before the inclusion pattern):
    // '!<rootDir>/src/**/__fixtures__/**',  // overridden by src/**/*.ts below
    // '<rootDir>/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',        // re-includes fixture files
  ],
  coverageDirectory: '<rootDir>/coverage',
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: the left-to-right override semantics are specific to Jest's use of micromatch and are not universally shared by other tools. Vitest's `coverage.exclude` is a separate array (additive exclusions on top of a fixed default list), c8's `--include`/`--exclude` flags use their own evaluation order, and Istanbul's `nyc.include`/`nyc.exclude` behave differently again. Teams maintaining coverage configuration across multiple tools should add explicit comments explaining the semantics of each config file, since "why does this order matter?" is not intuitive and the micromatch documentation is not commonly consulted by QA engineers.

---

### Pattern 198 — Vitest `coverage.all` with `include` globs: catching zero-coverage files excluded from the default report  [official]

By default, Vitest's coverage report only includes files that were imported (directly or transitively) during the test run. A newly added module that has no corresponding test file will not appear in the coverage report at all — it will not show as 0% covered, it simply will not exist in the output. This is a silent coverage gap: `coverageThreshold` checks pass because the uncovered file is not counted, and the HTML report provides no indication that the file exists. Vitest's `coverage.all: true` option forces all files matching `coverage.include` patterns to appear in the report, including files with 0% coverage, ensuring that threshold checks account for completely untested code.

The `coverage.all` option must be combined with an explicit `coverage.include` glob — without it, Vitest does not know which files to scan and `coverage.all` has no effect. The include glob should match the same files as the project's `tsconfig.json` `include` configuration to avoid scanning files that are not part of the compilation.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage.all to catch zero-coverage files
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',

      // Force ALL matching files into the report, even if never imported.
      // Without this, a new module with no test file silently passes threshold checks.
      all: true,

      // The include glob must be explicit when using coverage.all — without it,
      // Vitest cannot determine which files to scan.
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}',
        'src/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}',
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/__mocks__/**',
        'src/**/__fixtures__/**',
        'src/**/index.ts',
      ],

      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  82,
        statements: 80,
        // perFile: true combined with coverage.all will flag every
        // zero-coverage file individually — useful for new code gates.
        perFile: false,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverage.all: true` can dramatically inflate the number of files in the coverage report for projects with large `src/` trees containing configuration files, type-only modules, or re-export barrels. Every `index.ts` barrel file will appear as 0% covered (since it contains only `export` statements, which the V8 provider may not count as executable lines) unless the barrel is explicitly excluded. The best practice is to maintain a precise `exclude` list that mirrors your `collectCoverageFrom` negations, removing known-zero files before they inflate the "uncovered" count and trigger false threshold failures. When `coverage.all` is first enabled on an established project, expect the coverage percentage to drop significantly — budget for a cleanup sprint to either add tests for the newly-visible untested files or explicitly exclude files that are genuinely untestable (configuration, type stubs, generated code).

---

### Pattern 199 — Istanbul `/* istanbul ignore file */` whole-file exclusion: co-located reason visible to code reviewers  [official]

Istanbul supports a `/* istanbul ignore file */` comment at the top of a source file to exclude the entire file from coverage instrumentation. This is the Istanbul equivalent of adding the file to `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` — but it is co-located with the code rather than buried in the Jest or Vitest config, making the exclusion reason visible to code reviewers. The comment must appear before any executable code in the file (typically as the first line or immediately after `'use strict'`). For files using the V8 provider (Jest `coverageProvider: 'v8'` or Vitest `provider: 'v8'`), the equivalent is `/* c8 ignore file */` which suppresses all V8 coverage entries for the file.

Istanbul's `/* istanbul ignore file */` is supported by Vitest's Istanbul provider without the `-- @preserve` suffix because it is processed by Istanbul post-instrumentation rather than being a transpiler directive — it survives esbuild transformation.

```typescript
/* istanbul ignore file */
// This file is auto-generated by the OpenAPI code generator.
// Manual edits will be overwritten on next generation run.
// Coverage is not meaningful for generated client boilerplate.

// src/generated/api-client.ts — OpenAPI generated REST client

export interface UserResponse {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  createdAt: string;
}

export interface ApiError {
  code: number;
  message: string;
  details?: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export async function getUser(
  baseUrl: string,
  userId: string,
  token: string,
): Promise<UserResponse> {
  const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/users/${userId}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const err: ApiError = await res.json();
    throw new Error(`API error ${err.code}: ${err.message}`);
  }
  return res.json() as Promise<UserResponse>;
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `/* istanbul ignore file */` co-locates the exclusion reason with the code, which is excellent for readability, but it introduces a maintenance risk: if the file is no longer auto-generated but the comment is not removed, it silently hides coverage gaps permanently. Config-level exclusions (`coveragePathIgnorePatterns`) are centrally auditable — you can see all exclusions in one place. File-level exclusion comments are scattered across the codebase and harder to audit. Best practice: use `/* istanbul ignore file */` only for files that carry a machine-verifiable marker (e.g., a `@generated` JSDoc tag) and add a CI check (e.g., a lint rule) that ensures `/* istanbul ignore file */` comments appear only in files that also carry the `@generated` tag.

---

### Pattern 200 — Jest `coverageThreshold` glob patterns: applying per-directory and per-file thresholds alongside global defaults  [official]

Jest's `coverageThreshold` object supports three levels of specificity: `global` (applies to the aggregate across all files), directory globs (apply to the aggregate of files within a directory), and exact file paths (apply to a single file). These levels are evaluated independently — a file matching a directory glob uses that glob's threshold, not the global threshold. Files not matched by any glob key fall back to the `global` threshold. This allows teams to enforce stricter coverage on critical modules (payments, authentication, data validation) while maintaining a lower baseline for utility code, generated code, and UI components.

An important subtlety: Jest applies directory-level thresholds to the aggregate of all files in the matched directory, not per-file. To enforce per-file thresholds via `coverageThreshold`, you must specify the exact file path (or a glob that matches exactly one file). Vitest's `thresholds.perFile` is the cleaner solution for per-file enforcement across an entire directory.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — multi-level coverageThreshold with per-domain tuning
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.ts',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/generated/**',
  ],
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],

  coverageThreshold: {
    // Global: aggregate across all non-glob-matched files
    global: {
      lines:      75,
      branches:   65,
      functions:  78,
      statements: 75,
    },

    // Critical paths: aggregate threshold across entire directory (not per-file)
    './src/auth/**/*.ts': {
      lines:      95,
      branches:   90,
      functions:  95,
      statements: 95,
    },
    './src/payments/**/*.ts': {
      lines:      100,
      branches:   100,
      functions:  100,
      statements: 100,
    },

    // Specific high-value module: exact-file threshold
    './src/core/validation/schema-validator.ts': {
      lines:      100,
      branches:   95,
      functions:  100,
      statements: 100,
    },

    // Lower bar for generated OpenAPI client (still visible in report)
    './src/generated/api-client.ts': {
      lines:      0,
      branches:   0,
      functions:  0,
      statements: 0,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: per-glob `coverageThreshold` keys can create confusion when a file matches both a directory glob and the `global` key. Jest uses the most specific matching key: an exact file path beats a directory glob beats `global`. However, when two directory globs both match the same file (e.g., `./src/auth/**` and `./src/**`), Jest's behaviour is not clearly documented — in practice, the first matching key wins. Avoid overlapping glob keys by making them mutually exclusive (using disjoint directories). Also note that adding a zero-threshold entry like `'./src/generated/**': { statements: 0 }` does not exclude the file from the global aggregate — the file still contributes its (potentially low) coverage to the global percentage calculation. Use `collectCoverageFrom` negations to truly exclude files from all threshold calculations.

---

### Pattern 201 — Vitest `coverage.clean` and `coverage.cleanOnRerun`: managing stale coverage artifacts between runs  [official]

Vitest writes coverage artifacts to `reportsDirectory` (default `./coverage`) and by default removes the directory contents before each run (`coverage.clean: true`). This prevents stale data from previous runs from persisting in the report when test files are deleted or renamed. However, in workflows where coverage is run incrementally (e.g., running coverage on a subset of files, then merging) or where the HTML report is used as a long-lived build artifact, automatic cleaning causes data loss. `coverage.clean: false` disables pre-run cleanup entirely. The finer-grained option `coverage.cleanOnRerun: true` (the default when using Vitest's watch mode) cleans the coverage directory only when tests are explicitly re-run (keyboard `r` in watch mode), not on every file-save change re-run — preserving coverage data across incremental watch-mode runs.

Understanding the difference between `clean` and `cleanOnRerun` is critical for watch-mode workflows where incremental coverage feedback is desired without the overhead of a full coverage pass on each file save.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — clean and cleanOnRerun for CI vs watch-mode workflows
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

const isCI      = process.env.CI    === 'true';
const isWatchCI = process.env.WATCH === 'true'; // custom env var for watch CI jobs

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include:  ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude:  ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // clean: true (default) — delete reportsDirectory before each run.
      // Set false ONLY for incremental merge workflows (e.g., shard merging).
      clean: true,

      // cleanOnRerun: controls watch-mode cleanup.
      // true (default): clean when 'r' is pressed in watch mode.
      // false: preserve coverage across watch iterations (incremental feedback).
      cleanOnRerun: isWatchCI ? false : true,

      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  82,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: disabling `coverage.clean` in CI to preserve artifacts across parallel sharded test runs is a legitimate pattern for combining shard-level LCOV files into a merged report (using `lcov --add-tracefile`). However, if `clean: false` is accidentally left enabled on a CI job that re-uses a persistent workspace (a common pattern in Jenkins and TeamCity), the merged report may contain data from previous commits — creating phantom coverage for code that was deleted. Always ensure CI workspaces are fresh (or explicitly clean the coverage directory in a pre-step) when relying on `clean: false` for shard-merge workflows.

### Pattern 202 — c8 `--per-file` combined with `--check-coverage`: per-file threshold enforcement without Vitest  [official]

c8's `--per-file` flag changes `--check-coverage` behaviour from aggregate-level threshold enforcement to per-file enforcement. Without `--per-file`, a single well-tested file can offset a poorly-tested file in the aggregate, masking individual low-coverage modules. With `--per-file`, c8 checks each included file individually against the threshold values and fails if any single file falls below the threshold. This is the c8 equivalent of Vitest's `thresholds.perFile: true` and Jest's per-file `coverageThreshold` glob entries. The `--per-file` flag was added in c8 v7.0 and is supported in all subsequent versions including c8 v11.

The per-file check is particularly valuable for library packages where every exported module should have high coverage independently — not just in aggregate — because consumers import individual modules, not the entire library.

```typescript
// Helper: read per-file failures from json-summary and surface as annotations
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

interface FileSummary {
  lines:      { pct: number };
  branches:   { pct: number };
  functions:  { pct: number };
  statements: { pct: number };
}
type CoverageSummary = Record<string, FileSummary>;

// .c8rc.json equivalent (shown as TypeScript comment for context):
// {
//   "all": true,
//   "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
//   "exclude": ["src/**/*.spec.ts", "src/**/*.d.ts", "src/**/index.ts"],
//   "reporter": ["text", "html", "json-summary", "lcov"],
//   "check-coverage": true,
//   "per-file": true,
//   "lines": 80, "branches": 70, "functions": 82, "statements": 80
// }

export function findLowCoverageFiles(
  summaryPath: string,
  threshold: number,
): string[] {
  const summary: CoverageSummary = JSON.parse(
    readFileSync(summaryPath, 'utf8')
  );
  return Object.entries(summary)
    .filter(([filePath, data]) =>
      filePath !== 'total' &&
      (data.lines.pct      < threshold ||
       data.branches.pct   < threshold ||
       data.functions.pct  < threshold)
    )
    .map(([filePath]) => filePath);
}

// Example usage: surface low-coverage files as GitHub Actions annotations
export function emitGitHubAnnotations(
  summaryPath: string,
  threshold: number,
): void {
  for (const file of findLowCoverageFiles(summaryPath, threshold)) {
    console.log(`::warning file=${file}::Coverage below ${threshold}%`);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: `--per-file` with a strict threshold (e.g., 80%) on a legacy project will immediately surface many threshold violations that the aggregate threshold was hiding. This is the correct outcome — the violations were real, just invisible — but it creates a large remediation backlog that can be demoralising if introduced abruptly. The recommended migration strategy: (1) run `c8 report --per-file` without `--check-coverage` to enumerate all per-file violations, (2) add the worst offenders to an exception list with a corresponding ticket number, (3) enforce `--per-file` only on files not in the exception list, and (4) work through the exception list over successive sprints. Never use a low global threshold as a permanent substitute for per-file enforcement — it is a migration tool, not a long-term policy.

### Pattern 203 — Vitest `coverage.watermarks`: calibrating HTML report colour bands for meaningful visual feedback  [official]

Vitest inherits Istanbul's watermark system for colouring coverage percentages in the HTML report. By default, lines below 50% are coloured red, lines between 50%-80% are yellow, and lines above 80% are green. For teams with a coverage threshold of 80%, this means that files at exactly 80% (just passing) appear yellow — the "caution" colour — despite meeting the threshold. This creates a misleading visual signal: the report looks like it has many warnings even when all thresholds are met. Configuring `coverage.watermarks` to align the green threshold with the team's enforced threshold eliminates this false-yellow noise. `watermarks.lines: [80, 85]` means: red below 80%, yellow between 80%-85%, green above 85% — which accurately represents "failing," "passing but tight," and "comfortably covered."

The watermarks are a purely visual configuration — they do not affect `--check-coverage` pass/fail outcomes or threshold enforcement in any way.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — watermarks aligned with coverage thresholds
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

// Coverage policy for this project:
const THRESHOLD = { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 82, statements: 80 };

// Watermark strategy:
// - Low watermark = threshold value (red below threshold = failing)
// - High watermark = threshold + 10 (yellow = recently passing, needs attention)
// - Above high watermark = green (comfortably covered)
const WATERMARKS = {
  lines:      [THRESHOLD.lines,      THRESHOLD.lines      + 10] as [number, number],
  branches:   [THRESHOLD.branches,   THRESHOLD.branches   + 10] as [number, number],
  functions:  [THRESHOLD.functions,  THRESHOLD.functions  + 10] as [number, number],
  statements: [THRESHOLD.statements, THRESHOLD.statements + 10] as [number, number],
};

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      watermarks: WATERMARKS,

      thresholds: {
        ...THRESHOLD,
        perFile: false,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverage.watermarks` is an Istanbul-provider-only option in Vitest — the V8 provider does not support custom watermarks (the HTML output uses hardcoded 50%/80% bands). If your team uses the V8 provider and needs custom colour bands, the only option is to post-process the HTML report (a fragile approach) or switch to the Istanbul provider for reporting purposes while using V8 for the actual coverage collection (a hybrid approach that requires running the suite twice). Additionally, aligning the low watermark with the enforced threshold means a threshold increase (e.g., from 80% to 85%) requires updating both `thresholds` and `watermarks` — the shared `THRESHOLD` constant pattern shown above prevents this from becoming a two-file update footgun.

### Pattern 204 — Jest `forceCoverageMatch`: including test-file-adjacent inline source files in coverage reports  [official]

Jest normally excludes test files (files matching `testMatch` patterns) from coverage collection because test files themselves are not production code and their coverage is not meaningful. `forceCoverageMatch` overrides this exclusion, allowing test files matching specific patterns to be included in `collectCoverageFrom` collection. The primary use case is "spec-adjacent" or "colocated test" patterns where production code and tests exist in the same file — for example, Rust-style inline unit tests in TypeScript files, or `*.t.ts` files that contain both the implementation and its tests in a single module. A secondary use case is testing framework integration verification: ensuring that coverage instrumentation reaches test helper utilities (`src/test-utils/*.ts`) that are tested indirectly via other test files.

`forceCoverageMatch` accepts an array of glob patterns (the same format as `testMatch`) and adds matched files back into the coverage collection pool even if they would otherwise be excluded.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — forceCoverageMatch for colocated test files
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // Standard test file patterns
  testMatch: [
    '**/__tests__/**/*.ts',
    '**/*.spec.ts',
    '**/*.test.ts',
    // Inline test files: *.t.ts contain both implementation and tests
    '**/*.t.ts',
  ],

  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.test.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    // *.t.ts files are excluded here because they match testMatch
    '!src/**/*.t.ts',
  ],

  // forceCoverageMatch re-includes *.t.ts files into coverage collection
  // even though they match testMatch.  The production code in *.t.ts is
  // instrumented; the test-only functions within the same file are
  // not meaningful to cover (they are test infrastructure).
  forceCoverageMatch: ['**/*.t.ts'],

  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `forceCoverageMatch` is a niche option that is primarily useful for Rust-inspired colocated-test patterns, which are uncommon in TypeScript projects. Misusing it (e.g., forcing coverage on all `*.spec.ts` files) inflates the coverage report with test infrastructure code that is never meaningful to cover and distorts threshold calculations. The result: a project appears to have high coverage but the coverage is partly of test code (which, by definition, is 100% exercised by the test runner itself). If the goal is to include test utility helpers in coverage, the cleaner solution is to ensure those helpers are in non-test-suffixed files (e.g., `src/test-utils/builders.ts`) and include them in `collectCoverageFrom` directly.

### Pattern 205 — Vitest workspace coverage merging: aggregating per-package reports into a single root-level report  [official]

Vitest's workspace mode (configured via `vitest.workspace.ts`) runs tests across multiple packages in a monorepo but by default generates separate per-package coverage reports in each package's `reportsDirectory`. For monorepos where a single aggregate coverage report is required (e.g., for a repository-level coverage badge or a PR comment showing total coverage across all packages), Vitest supports coverage merging via the `coverage.mergeReports` option. Each package workspace emits `json` coverage data to a shared directory, and the root Vitest config then merges and reports from that directory.

The merge workflow requires two Vitest invocations: first run each workspace with `reporter: ['json']` to a shared output directory, then run the root config with `mergeReports: './shared-coverage'` and the desired reporters. Alternatively, use `lcov --add-tracefile` to merge LCOV files at the OS level outside of Vitest.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts — per-package coverage with shared JSON output
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    test: {
      name: 'core',
      root: './packages/core',
      coverage: {
        provider: 'v8',
        include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
        exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
        // Each package emits JSON to a shared directory at the repo root.
        reporter: ['json'],
        reportsDirectory: '../../coverage-data/core',
        all: true,
      },
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'api',
      root: './packages/api',
      coverage: {
        provider: 'v8',
        include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
        exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
        reporter: ['json'],
        reportsDirectory: '../../coverage-data/api',
        all: true,
      },
    },
  },
]);
```

```typescript
// vitest.config.root.ts — merge all package JSON reports into a single report
// Run with: vitest --config vitest.config.root.ts --coverage --run
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // mergeReports: directory containing per-package JSON coverage files.
      // Vitest 2.0+ only — not available in Vitest 1.x.
      mergeReports: './coverage-data',
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 82, statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Vitest's `mergeReports` expects all JSON coverage files to have been generated by the same provider (V8 or Istanbul) — mixing providers across workspace packages produces a merge error. If different packages use different providers (V8 for Node-only packages, Istanbul for browser-compatible packages), the LCOV-based merge strategy is more robust. Also note that `coverage.mergeReports` is a Vitest 2.0+ feature — projects on Vitest 1.x must use external LCOV merging or upgrade. The two-invocation workflow complicates CI pipelines: if any package's test run fails, the merge step receives incomplete data and the merged threshold check may pass or fail for the wrong reason; always run the merge step only after all package test runs have completed successfully.
