## Cycle 43 Community Gotchas

### G141 — Jest `coverageThreshold` with directory globs matches more files than expected when paths contain symlinks  [community]

Jest resolves `coverageThreshold` glob keys using the real filesystem path after symlink resolution. In monorepos that use `npm link`, `yarn link`, or `pnpm link` to create symlinks between local packages, a file at `packages/auth/src/login.ts` may be symlinked into `node_modules/@company/auth/src/login.ts`. When Jest collects coverage, it records coverage under the real path (e.g., `packages/auth/src/login.ts`) but the `coverageThreshold` glob key `'./src/auth/**'` may not match the full path prefix. Conversely, if the real path is inside `node_modules`, the default `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` (`['/node_modules/']`) excludes it entirely, causing the auth package's coverage to vanish from the report. **WHY it matters**: teams using workspace-protocol monorepos with linked packages regularly report that coverage for shared packages inexplicably drops to 0% or disappears from the report after adding `npm link` entries — the real path goes through `node_modules` and is excluded by default. The fix: add `'<rootDir>/packages/*/src/**'` to `collectCoverageFrom` explicitly and add each linked package's real path to a custom `coveragePathIgnorePatterns` exception list that restores them; or avoid symlinked packages in coverage runs by using `jest --testPathPattern` to test each package independently.

### G142 — c8 `--all` with TypeScript project references: coverage includes compiled output from referenced projects  [community]

c8's `--all` flag scans all files matching `--include` patterns at startup, before any tests run. In TypeScript projects using project references (`tsconfig.json` with `references` arrays), the `outDir` of each referenced project may be inside the main project's `src/` directory (a common pattern when `declarationDir` and `outDir` overlap). When `--include` is set to `src/**/*.ts`, c8 may scan `.ts` files in those `outDir` subdirectories — including compiled `.d.ts` declaration files that have been placed alongside source files. These declaration files appear as 0% covered and pollute the report with phantom entries. **WHY it matters**: a project with 10 referenced sub-packages, each emitting declarations into `src/generated/`, will have hundreds of 0% `.d.ts` rows in the c8 report, dragging down aggregate coverage percentages and potentially triggering `--check-coverage` failures on files that contain no executable code. The fix: ensure all project-reference `outDir` paths are explicitly listed in `--exclude` patterns, and use `--exclude-after-remap` to catch declaration entries that survive the pre-remap exclusion step.

### G143 — Vitest `coverage.thresholds.perFile: true` with re-export barrel files: `index.ts` files always fail per-file thresholds  [community]

Vitest's `perFile: true` threshold enforcement checks every file in `coverage.include` individually. TypeScript barrel files (`index.ts` that contain only `export { ... } from './module'` statements) are included in coverage reports but have no executable statements — they consist entirely of re-export declarations, which the V8 provider records as uncovered lines. When `perFile: true` is enabled, every `index.ts` barrel file fails the per-file line threshold because its line coverage is 0% (no executable lines were ever run — re-exports are resolved at module load time, not at statement execution time). **WHY it matters**: a project with 50 barrel files and `perFile: true` will have 50 threshold violations that are entirely false positives, obscuring genuine per-file coverage issues in business logic modules. The fix: add `'src/**/index.ts'` to `coverage.exclude` to remove all barrel files from per-file threshold checks, or use `/* v8 ignore file */` (V8 provider, Vitest 4+) at the top of each barrel to suppress V8 coverage entries for that file entirely.

### G144 — Istanbul `/* istanbul ignore next */` suppresses the wrong line when applied above a multi-line arrow function expression  [community]

Istanbul's `/* istanbul ignore next */` directive is intended to suppress the immediately following statement, expression, or branch. However, when applied immediately above a multi-line arrow function that spans three or more lines, Istanbul's AST walk may suppress only the opening line of the function (the `const fn = (` line) rather than the entire function body. The remaining lines of the function body appear as uncovered in the report despite the developer's intention to ignore the entire function. This behaviour is Istanbul-version-dependent: Istanbul 0.4 (used by Istanbul 1.x / nyc) exhibits this bug; Istanbul 2.x (used by Vitest's Istanbul provider) corrects it for most cases but still exhibits it for some complex nested arrow expressions. **WHY it matters**: developers who add `/* istanbul ignore next */` above an untestable multi-line arrow function believe they have suppressed the coverage gap, but the report continues to show red lines, causing CI threshold failures. The diagnostic symptom is "I added the ignore comment but coverage still fails." The fix: use `/* istanbul ignore next N */` (where N is the line count of the function including braces) to explicitly span the suppression, or restructure the code to use a `function` declaration (which Istanbul handles more reliably than multi-line arrow expressions) for the untestable path.

### G145 — Stryker incremental mode (`incremental: true`) with renamed test files: stale attribution causes survivors to not be re-tested  [community]

Stryker's `incremental: true` mode stores per-mutant test attribution and result data in `incrementalFile` (default `reports/stryker-incremental.json`) between runs. On subsequent runs, mutants that were already tested and killed are skipped — only untested or previously-surviving mutants are re-run. When a test file is renamed (a common occurrence during refactoring), Stryker cannot match the old test attribution record to the new filename. Stryker treats the renamed test's attributed mutants as "no longer covered by any test" and marks those mutants as surviving (not killed) even though the renamed test still covers and kills them. **WHY it matters**: a mutation score that was 85% can drop to 70% after a rename refactoring — not because test coverage regressed but because Stryker's incremental cache is stale. The false surviving mutants also appear in the HTML report, wasting engineer time on investigation. The fix: delete `incrementalFile` whenever test files are renamed, moved, or significantly restructured; add this cleanup to your rename refactoring checklist or pre-commit hook. Stryker will then perform a full dry-run on the next invocation and rebuild the attribution map from scratch.

### Pattern 206 — Vitest `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate`: self-healing threshold ratchets  [official]

Vitest's `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate` (introduced in Vitest 2.0) automatically rewrites the threshold values in your configuration file whenever the measured coverage exceeds the currently configured minimums. The update is performed in-place to the config file on disk, so a CI run that improves coverage will commit the tightened thresholds back to the repository when combined with a `git add vitest.config.ts && git commit -m "chore: ratchet coverage thresholds"` post-run step. By default `autoUpdate` accepts a boolean; passing a formatter function instead lets you control decimal precision — `(n) => Math.floor(n)` rounds down and avoids meaningless micro-fluctuations (e.g. `82.857` → `82`). The feature works alongside per-file and glob-pattern thresholds and only ever increases values, never decreases them.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — self-healing threshold ratchet
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  82,
        statements: 80,
        // autoUpdate rewrites the four numbers above in this file
        // whenever measured coverage exceeds them.
        // Pass a formatter to control rounding (floor = never overshoot).
        autoUpdate: (newValue: number) => Math.floor(newValue),
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `autoUpdate` writes directly to the config file at test-run time — this means CI jobs that run in read-only filesystems or inside Docker containers with immutable bind-mounts will fail with a filesystem write error, not a coverage failure. Additionally, when thresholds are written back to disk and the CI pipeline stages `vitest.config.ts` automatically, a commit that was "green" in terms of tests will produce an unexpected uncommitted-file diff that blocks subsequent steps expecting a clean working tree. The recommended pattern is to use `autoUpdate` only in pre-commit hooks or in a dedicated "ratchet" CI job that runs after all other jobs succeed and whose sole responsibility is to commit threshold bumps.

---

### Pattern 207 — Vitest `coverage.changed`: diff-scoped coverage for PR feedback loops  [official]

`coverage.changed` restricts coverage collection to files that are modified relative to a git reference. Setting it to `true` uses staged and unstaged local changes; passing a string (e.g., `'main'` or a commit SHA) compares against that specific ref. This is distinct from the `--changed` flag (which filters *which tests* to run) — `coverage.changed` runs *all* tests but only emits coverage data for the diff-touched files. The result is a focused coverage report in pull-request workflows: instead of a full project report where a single changed file's gap is drowned out by thousands of green lines, the developer sees only the coverage delta for the files they actually modified. When combined with `coverage.thresholds.perFile: true`, each modified file must independently meet the per-file threshold, turning every PR into a coverage gate for the specific files it touches.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — PR-scoped coverage using coverage.changed
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

// In CI, compare against the merge base; locally compare against HEAD.
const changedRef = process.env.CI
  ? (process.env.BASE_SHA ?? 'main')
  : true;

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary'],
      // Only report coverage for files modified since changedRef.
      changed: changedRef,
      thresholds: {
        // Per-file threshold applies only to the changed-file subset.
        perFile: true,
        lines:    80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverage.changed` requires a git repository at the project root and a valid git history — shallow clones (`git clone --depth 1`) in CI pipelines may not have the base branch ref available, causing Vitest to fall back to full coverage or throw a git error. The `BASE_SHA` approach shown above mitigates this by using the explicit merge-base SHA that most CI systems expose (e.g., `${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}` in GitHub Actions). Additionally, `coverage.changed` does not catch untested new files that have never been committed — a newly created file that is staged but was never added to `include` patterns will still be invisible to the coverage report even though it is "changed".

---

### Pattern 208 — Vitest `coverage.excludeAfterRemap`: post-sourcemap exclusion for transpiled codebases  [official]

When Vitest collects V8 coverage, the raw V8 data references transpiled file paths (`.js`, `.jsx`, compiled `.ts` output). Source maps then remap those paths back to the original `.ts` source files. The standard `coverage.exclude` patterns are applied to the *pre-remap* paths — which means an exclusion like `'src/generated/**'` may never match if the V8 layer reports those files as `dist/generated/**` before remapping occurs. `coverage.excludeAfterRemap` (boolean, default `false`) re-applies the `exclude` pattern list a second time against the *post-remap* source file paths. Enabling it ensures that generated files, build outputs, and declaration files that appear under their original source path after remapping are correctly excluded from threshold calculations and HTML output.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — excluding generated files that survive source-map remapping
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: [
        // These patterns are applied BEFORE remapping (pre-remap exclusions).
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        // Generated code lives here in source; the pre-remap path may be
        // 'dist/generated/**' — the pattern below catches it post-remap.
        'src/generated/**',
        'src/**/*.generated.ts',
      ],
      // Re-apply exclusions against post-sourcemap paths so that generated
      // source files that survive the V8 → source-map remap are also excluded.
      excludeAfterRemap: true,
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `excludeAfterRemap: true` adds a second exclusion pass over every file in the coverage map, which has a small but non-zero performance cost proportional to the number of source files (typically negligible for projects with fewer than 10,000 files). The more significant issue is that enabling it can cause previously-passing thresholds to fail: if generated files were silently leaking into the coverage report (recorded as 0% covered) and inflating the "total files" denominator, their removal after enabling `excludeAfterRemap` may *increase* the measured coverage percentage (fewer uncovered files in the denominator), which is generally desirable. However, in pathological cases where generated files happened to be 100% "covered" (because all their generated code was exercised), removing them decreases aggregate coverage and may trigger threshold failures until thresholds are recalibrated.

---

### Pattern 209 — Vitest `coverage.processingConcurrency`: tuning parallel coverage file processing  [official]

After all tests complete, Vitest processes the collected V8 or Istanbul coverage data for each test worker file asynchronously. `coverage.processingConcurrency` (integer, default: `Math.min(20, os.availableParallelism())`) controls how many coverage files are processed in parallel during this post-test phase. On machines with high CPU core counts (e.g., a 32-core CI runner), the default can be 20 concurrent workers all reading and transforming coverage JSON, which spikes memory usage and can cause OOM kills on memory-constrained agents. Conversely, on resource-starved environments (shared CI runners with 2 vCPUs), the default 20 causes excessive context switching that prolongs the coverage processing phase. Explicitly setting `processingConcurrency` to `os.availableParallelism()` or a fixed low value (e.g., `4`) aligns coverage processing with actual available resources.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — explicit coverage processing concurrency
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import os from 'node:os';

// Detect CI environment: use a conservative ceiling to protect shared runners.
const coverageConcurrency = process.env.CI
  ? Math.min(4, os.availableParallelism())   // CI: cap at 4 to avoid OOM
  : os.availableParallelism();               // Local dev: use all cores

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary'],
      processingConcurrency: coverageConcurrency,
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `processingConcurrency` only affects the *post-test processing phase* — it has no impact on how many test workers run in parallel (controlled by `maxWorkers`). On a large monorepo test suite running 200+ test files, a `processingConcurrency` of 4 may extend the coverage processing phase from 8 seconds to 30 seconds compared to the default of 20 — this is an acceptable trade-off on memory-constrained CI runners but would be a poor choice for a developer's local machine where memory is ample and speed matters more. Profile the coverage phase duration separately from the test phase duration (use `--reporter=verbose` and observe the "Coverage" timing line) before deciding whether to tune this option.

---

### Pattern 210 — Vitest `coverage.allowExternal`: capturing coverage for code outside the project root  [official]

By default, Vitest's coverage providers only record coverage for files inside `process.cwd()` (the project root). Files imported from outside the root — such as symlinked packages in monorepos, packages linked via `npm link` during development, or shared utilities installed as file-protocol dependencies (`"@company/utils": "file:../utils"`) — are excluded from coverage data even when they are executed during tests. Setting `coverage.allowExternal: true` removes this root-boundary restriction and allows coverage to be collected for any file that is imported during the test run, regardless of its location on disk. This is especially useful when testing a package against a locally-developed dependency to verify that the dependency's code paths are actually exercised.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage for externally-linked monorepo packages
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import path from 'node:path';

// The 'ui-components' package is linked locally for development.
// Its source lives outside this package's root.
const externalPackageRoot = path.resolve(__dirname, '../ui-components/src');

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // Allow coverage for files outside the project root.
      allowExternal: true,
      include: [
        'src/**/*.ts',
        // Explicitly include the external package's source files.
        `${externalPackageRoot}/**/*.ts`,
      ],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        `${externalPackageRoot}/**/*.spec.ts`,
        '**/node_modules/**',
      ],
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary'],
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `allowExternal: true` without a tightly-scoped `include` list will pull in coverage data for *all* external files exercised during the test run — including framework internals, polyfills, and node_modules code that happens to be executed. This explodes the coverage report with thousands of irrelevant files and makes threshold calculations meaningless (framework code is usually 10–30% "covered" because most code paths are never triggered in unit tests). Always pair `allowExternal: true` with an explicit `include` array that names only the specific external paths you want to track. The HTML report also becomes very large when external paths are included — consider using `reporter: ['json-summary']` for CI threshold checks and reserving `html` for local investigation.

---

### Pattern 211 — Node.js built-in test runner coverage: `--experimental-test-coverage` and `/* node:coverage */` directives  [official]

Node.js 20+ ships a built-in test runner with native V8 coverage collection, accessible via the `--experimental-test-coverage` flag (stability level 1 — experimental). The built-in runner eliminates the need for c8 or Istanbul in simple Node.js scripts and CLI tools. Coverage thresholds are set programmatically via the `run()` API's `lineCoverage`, `branchCoverage`, and `functionCoverage` options, or via `--test-coverage-lines`, `--test-coverage-branches`, and `--test-coverage-functions` CLI flags. Inline suppression uses the `/* node:coverage disable */` / `/* node:coverage enable */` block form or `/* node:coverage ignore next [N] */` for single-line or N-line suppression. The `lcov` reporter generates a standard `lcov.info` file compatible with Codecov, Coveralls, and SonarQube.

```typescript
// Programmatic Node.js test runner coverage (Node 20+)
// run-tests.mjs
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { spec as SpecReporter } from 'node:test/reporters';
import { createWriteStream } from 'node:fs';

// Run all *.spec.ts files with coverage enforced programmatically.
const runner = run({
  files: ['src/**/*.spec.ts'],
  coverage: true,
  coverageExcludeGlobs: ['**/*.spec.ts', '**/node_modules/**'],
  coverageIncludeGlobs: ['src/**/*.ts'],
  // Threshold options (Node 22+): fail if not met.
  lineCoverage: 80,
  branchCoverage: 70,
  functionCoverage: 80,
});

// Emit human-readable output to stdout and LCOV to file.
runner.compose(SpecReporter).pipe(process.stdout);
runner.pipe(
  // LCOV reporter writes lcov.info for CI upload.
  // Use alongside SpecReporter — LCOV suppresses test output.
  createWriteStream('coverage/lcov.info'),
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Node.js built-in coverage remains marked "Stability 1 — Experimental" as of Node 26, meaning the API surface can change in minor releases without a semver major bump. The built-in runner does not support Istanbul-style branch-granularity coverage (it uses raw V8 coverage semantics), so `||`/`&&` short-circuit paths and optional-chaining branches are counted differently than in Istanbul-instrumented projects. Projects that mix Istanbul (Vitest/Jest) and Node built-in coverage across packages will produce inconsistent branch coverage numbers for the same logical branches, making side-by-side comparisons misleading. Use the built-in runner for standalone scripts and CLI tools; keep Vitest or Jest for application code where Istanbul's AST-accurate branch semantics are required.

---

### Pattern 212 — Vitest `coverage.skipFull`: de-noising CI text reports  [official]

`coverage.skipFull` (boolean, default `false`) omits files that have reached 100% across all four metrics (statements, branches, functions, lines) from the text reporter output. In a project with 500 source files where 460 are at 100%, the default text output is 460 lines of noise that obscures the 40 files that actually need attention. Setting `skipFull: true` reduces the text output to only the files with gaps, making the console report immediately actionable. As of Vitest 4.1.4, the text reporter *automatically* sets `skipFull: true` when it detects an agent or automation environment (via `process.env.CI` and related heuristics), so CI pipelines benefit from this behaviour without explicit configuration — though teams can override it by explicitly setting `skipFull: false`.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — explicit skipFull plus text reporter configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      reporter: [
        // Text reporter: skip fully-covered files for a concise console output.
        // The 'skipFull' option is passed as the second element of the tuple.
        ['text', { skipFull: true }],
        // Also emit JSON summary and LCOV for CI upload and badge generation.
        'json-summary',
        'lcov',
      ],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `skipFull: true` only affects the *text* reporter output — all other reporters (`html`, `json`, `lcov`) still include all files regardless of this setting. This means the HTML report remains complete and navigable for local development, while CI logs remain terse. However, teams using CI log-scraping tools that parse the text reporter output (e.g., custom Slack bots or dashboard scripts that regex-parse `vitest --reporter=text` output) will need to update their parsers to handle the case where fully-covered files are absent from the output. Additionally, `skipFull` at the reporter level is distinct from `coverage.watermarks` — `skipFull` omits files from output; watermarks colour-code them. Both can be used simultaneously: files above the high watermark and at 100% are the candidates for `skipFull` omission.

---

### Pattern 213 — Vitest V8 `ignore start` / `ignore stop` block directives: multi-line suppression restored in Vitest 4.1  [official]

Vitest 4.1 restored support for block-level coverage ignore directives for both the V8 and Istanbul providers. The V8 provider now recognises `/* v8 ignore start */` and `/* v8 ignore stop */` to suppress an arbitrary multi-line block from V8 coverage, while Istanbul recognises `/* istanbul ignore start */` / `/* istanbul ignore stop */`. These block forms were temporarily removed during the Vitest 4.0 migration and are back as of 4.1.x. The block form is superior to stacking individual `/* v8 ignore next */` lines because it survives code reformatting (prettier may merge or reorder lines, invalidating per-line directives) and is easier to audit — a single paired open/close comment makes the suppression boundary immediately visible in code review.

```typescript
// src/platform/os-specific.ts — block-form ignore directives (Vitest 4.1+)
import { platform } from 'node:os';

export function getPlatformLabel(): string {
  const p = platform();

  // Standard path: always tested.
  if (p === 'linux') return 'Linux';
  if (p === 'darwin') return 'macOS';

  /* v8 ignore start */
  // Windows-specific branch: not exercised in Linux CI.
  // The block form ensures ALL lines in this branch are suppressed,
  // even if the formatter reflows the if/else into a single line.
  if (p === 'win32') {
    const edition = process.env.WIN_EDITION ?? 'Standard';
    return `Windows (${edition})`;
  }
  // Truly unknown platform: defensive fallback.
  return `Unknown (${p})`;
  /* v8 ignore stop */
}
```

**Tradeoff**: Block-form ignore directives suppress all coverage metrics (lines, branches, functions) for every statement within the block — there is no way to suppress only branch coverage while keeping line coverage active within the same block. If you need finer-grained suppression (e.g., suppress only the `else` branch of a conditional, not the `if` branch), you must use the branch-selective `/* v8 ignore else */` or `/* v8 ignore if */` directives (introduced in Vitest 4+ via `ast-v8-to-istanbul`) rather than the block form. Additionally, mismatched `start`/`stop` pairs (e.g., a `start` inside a function that is never followed by a `stop`) will suppress coverage for the entire remainder of the file after the unclosed `start` — a silent, wide-area suppression that is very difficult to diagnose.

---

### Pattern 214 — Vitest `coverage.htmlDir`: integrating custom coverage reporters with Vitest UI  [official]

Vitest UI (the browser-based test dashboard, `vitest --ui`) can display HTML coverage reports inline if the report is placed in the directory specified by `coverage.htmlDir`. This option (added in Vitest 4.1) is primarily intended for *custom* coverage providers (configured via `coverage.customProviderModule`) that generate their own HTML output format — it allows them to register where their HTML lives so Vitest UI can find and serve it. Standard reporters (`html`, `html-spa`, `lcov`) auto-infer `htmlDir` from their output directories. For teams building a custom coverage provider (e.g., integrating a commercial coverage tool or generating a custom dashboard format), `htmlDir` is the registration point that connects the custom provider's output to the Vitest UI iframe.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — custom coverage provider with htmlDir registration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      // Custom provider: a local module that wraps a commercial coverage tool.
      provider: 'custom',
      customProviderModule: './coverage-provider/my-custom-provider.ts',

      // Tell Vitest UI where the custom provider writes its HTML output,
      // so the Vitest UI iframe can display it directly.
      htmlDir: './coverage/custom-html',

      // The custom provider is responsible for writing to htmlDir.
      // Standard reporters can be specified alongside a custom provider
      // to also emit json-summary for threshold checks.
      reporter: ['json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverage.htmlDir` is only consulted by the Vitest UI browser interface — it has no effect on CLI output or CI pipelines. Teams that do not use `vitest --ui` gain nothing from setting it. For standard Vitest usage with the built-in `html` reporter, `htmlDir` is automatically inferred from `reportsDirectory` and does not need to be set explicitly. The primary risk of setting `htmlDir` incorrectly (pointing to a non-existent or wrong directory) is that the Vitest UI coverage tab shows a blank iframe without a helpful error message, making the misconfiguration difficult to diagnose without checking the Vitest UI server console.

---

### Pattern 215 — Stryker `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` vs `'all'` vs `'off'`: mutation performance vs accuracy trade-offs  [official]

Stryker's `coverageAnalysis` option controls how it determines which tests to run for each mutant. `'perTest'` (the default since Stryker 5+) instruments the test suite to record which tests exercise each source file, then for each mutant runs only the subset of tests that cover the mutated code — dramatically reducing the number of test invocations needed. `'all'` marks any mutant with *any* test coverage as needing re-run (all covering tests run, not just the most specific ones). `'off'` disables coverage-based pruning entirely and re-runs the full test suite for every mutant — the most accurate but slowest option. The choice between `perTest` and `off` matters most for slow integration tests: `perTest` may attribute a mutant to only unit tests, leaving integration tests that also exercise the mutant absent from the kill attempt, causing the mutant to falsely survive.

```typescript
// stryker.config.ts — perTest configuration with timeout tuning
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Config = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  // perTest: only the tests that cover a mutant are re-run.
  // Reduces test invocations from O(mutants × full-suite) to O(mutants × covering-tests).
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',

  // ignoreStatic: skip mutants that are only executed at module load time
  // (static class fields, top-level initialisers). These require a full reload
  // to detect and are expensive with perTest analysis.
  ignoreStatic: true,

  // Timeout multiplier: perTest runs fewer tests per mutant,
  // but the baseline timeout is recalibrated per-test rather than per-suite.
  timeoutMS: 10_000,
  timeoutFactor: 1.5,

  // Sandbox configuration: symlink node_modules to avoid repeated installs.
  symlinkNodeModules: true,
  tempDirName: '.stryker-tmp',

  mutate: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.spec.ts'],
  reporters: ['html', 'progress'],
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` requires an additional "dry run" of the entire test suite before mutation testing begins — Stryker runs all tests once to build the test-to-file attribution map. This adds fixed overhead (proportional to full test suite duration) to every Stryker run. For a project where the full test suite takes 60 seconds, the dry run adds 60 seconds to the total Stryker runtime regardless of how many mutants are tested. For small projects with fast test suites (< 10 seconds), `coverageAnalysis: 'off'` may actually be faster end-to-end because the dry-run overhead exceeds the savings from test pruning. The break-even point is approximately when the per-mutant test savings across all mutants exceed the dry-run cost — rule of thumb: use `perTest` when the test suite takes > 30 seconds and there are > 500 mutants.

---

### Pattern 216 — c8 `--experimental-monocart`: richer V8 coverage reports without Istanbul remapping  [official]

c8's `--experimental-monocart` flag enables the [monocart-coverage-reports](https://github.com/cenfun/monocart-coverage-reports) engine as an alternative to Istanbul for processing raw V8 coverage data. The monocart engine offers richer HTML output (tree-map views, per-function heat maps), supports additional reporter formats (cobertura, codecov JSON, clover), and crucially performs its own source-map remapping independently of Istanbul's `@istanbuljs/schema` pipeline. For projects where Istanbul's source-map remapping produces inaccurate line numbers (a common issue with double-transpiled code: TypeScript → esbuild → source map), monocart's remapping engine may produce more accurate reports. The flag is still experimental and the output format differs from standard Istanbul HTML, so existing tooling that scrapes Istanbul HTML (e.g., coverage badge generators) may need adaptation.

```typescript
// package.json — c8 with monocart reporter via .c8rc.json
// .c8rc.json (project root)
const c8Config = {
  "all": true,
  "src": ["src"],
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["src/**/*.spec.ts", "src/**/*.d.ts", "node_modules/**"],
  "extension": [".ts", ".tsx"],
  "reporter": ["v8"],           // monocart replaces the html reporter
  "experimental-monocart": true,
  "reports-dir": "./coverage",
  "check-coverage": true,
  "lines": 80,
  "branches": 70,
  "functions": 80,
  "statements": 80
};
```

```typescript
// Alternatively: invoke c8 programmatically from a Node script
// scripts/run-coverage.ts
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';

execSync(
  'c8 --experimental-monocart --all --src src ' +
  '--include "src/**/*.ts" ' +
  '--exclude "src/**/*.spec.ts" ' +
  '--reporter v8 ' +
  '--check-coverage --lines 80 --branches 70 ' +
  'vitest run',
  { stdio: 'inherit' }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: `--experimental-monocart` is explicitly labelled experimental — c8's maintainers may promote, modify, or remove it in a future major version without following semver pre-announcement conventions. The monocart engine also has its own dependency tree (adding ~500 KB to the install footprint) and its own source-map caching behaviour that differs from c8's default caching. Teams that rely on the standard Istanbul HTML report format for integration with tools like `jest-coverage-to-slack`, `coverage-badge-creator`, or SonarQube's Istanbul coverage import will find that monocart's output format requires custom integration work. Reserve this option for scenarios where Istanbul source-map remapping is demonstrably producing inaccurate reports and standard remapping fixes (e.g., `--exclude-after-remap`) have not resolved the issue.

---

### Pattern 217 — Jest `coverageReporters` with per-reporter options: `text` `skipFull`, `html` `subdir`, and `json` `file`  [official]

Jest's `coverageReporters` accepts both string shorthand (`'text'`, `'html'`) and two-element tuple form (`['text', { skipFull: true }]`, `['html', { subdir: 'html-report' }]`) to pass reporter-specific options. The most practically useful options are: `{ skipFull: true }` on the `text` reporter (hides 100%-covered files from console output, matching Vitest's `coverage.skipFull` behaviour); `{ subdir: 'html-report' }` on the `html` reporter (places HTML output in a named subdirectory of `coverageDirectory` rather than directly in it, useful when multiple reporters all write to the same base directory and their output files would collide); and `{ file: 'coverage-summary.json' }` on `json-summary` (controls the output filename, important for CI scripts that look for a specific filename). Jest uses Istanbul's reporter option system, so any Istanbul reporter option is valid in the tuple.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — per-reporter options for clean multi-format output
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',

  // Each reporter is a two-element tuple: [reporterName, reporterOptions].
  coverageReporters: [
    // Console output: hide fully-covered files for concise CI logs.
    ['text', { skipFull: true }],

    // HTML report: place in a named subdirectory to avoid filename collisions.
    ['html', { subdir: 'html-report' }],

    // JSON summary: use a predictable filename for CI badge scripts.
    ['json-summary', { file: 'coverage-summary.json' }],

    // LCOV: standard format for Codecov / Coveralls upload.
    'lcov',
  ],

  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
  },

  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.spec.ts',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
  ],
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: Jest's tuple reporter syntax (the `['reporterName', options]` form) was introduced in Jest 27 — earlier versions only accept string reporter names and will throw a configuration error if tuples are present. When maintaining a project that must support Jest 26 and Jest 27+ simultaneously (e.g., a library with a wide peer dependency range), the tuple form must be guarded behind a version check. Additionally, the `subdir` option for the `html` reporter is an Istanbul reporter option, not a Jest option — if Jest ever changes the underlying Istanbul version to one that renames or removes this option, the configuration silently stops working (the subdir is ignored and HTML files land in the root `coverageDirectory`). Prefer `reportsDirectory` (Vitest) over `subdir` tricks (Jest) when you have the choice.

---

### Pattern 218 — Vitest `coverage.customProviderModule`: building a custom coverage provider  [official]

Vitest's `coverage.customProviderModule` option (Vitest 2.0+) allows teams to plug in a completely custom coverage provider — any module that exports a class implementing the `CoverageProvider` interface from `vitest/coverage`. This is the extension point for integrating commercial coverage tools (e.g., Squash, Bullseye), alternative V8 processing engines (monocart, c8-core), or specialised coverage strategies (differential coverage, AI-generated test coverage attribution). The custom provider module must export a default class with at minimum `name`, `initialize()`, `reportCoverage()`, and `clean()` methods. The module is resolved from the Vitest config's base directory and runs in the main Node process (not in worker threads), so it has access to the full filesystem and can spawn child processes.

```typescript
// coverage-provider/smart-diff-provider.ts — minimal custom provider skeleton
import type {
  CoverageProvider,
  ResolvedCoverageOptions,
  Vitest,
} from 'vitest/node';

export default class SmartDiffCoverageProvider implements CoverageProvider {
  name = 'smart-diff';

  private ctx!: Vitest;
  private options!: ResolvedCoverageOptions<'custom'>;

  initialize(ctx: Vitest): void {
    this.ctx = ctx;
    this.options = ctx.config.coverage as ResolvedCoverageOptions<'custom'>;
  }

  resolveOptions(): ResolvedCoverageOptions<'custom'> {
    return this.options;
  }

  async clean(cleanupDirectories?: boolean): Promise<void> {
    // Remove previous coverage artifacts.
  }

  async onAfterSuiteRun(coverage: unknown): Promise<void> {
    // Called after each worker completes; accumulate raw coverage data.
  }

  async reportCoverage({ allTestsRun }: { allTestsRun: boolean }): Promise<void> {
    // Post-process accumulated data and write reports.
    // Access this.options.reporter, this.options.reportsDirectory, etc.
  }

  async generateCoverage(): Promise<unknown> {
    // Return raw coverage data; called by Vitest before reportCoverage.
    return {};
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: The `CoverageProvider` interface is part of Vitest's internal API surface (`vitest/node`), which does not follow the same stability guarantees as the public test API (`vitest`). Vitest minor releases (e.g., 4.0 → 4.1) have historically introduced breaking changes to the provider interface without a semver major bump — the `onAfterSuiteRun` signature changed between Vitest 3.x and 4.x. Teams building a custom provider must pin Vitest to a specific minor version and run provider integration tests against each Vitest upgrade before adopting it. The cost of maintaining a custom provider against a rapidly-evolving internal API is high — use `customProviderModule` only when the built-in V8 and Istanbul providers genuinely cannot meet your requirements.

---

### Pattern 219 — Vitest `coverage.thresholds` with glob patterns: per-path threshold enforcement  [official]

Vitest supports per-file-pattern threshold overrides within the `coverage.thresholds` block by using glob-pattern keys alongside the standard `lines`, `branches`, `functions`, and `statements` keys. For example, `thresholds['src/critical/**': { lines: 95, branches: 90 }]` enforces stricter coverage for files matching `src/critical/**` while the global thresholds remain at lower values. This mirrors Jest's `coverageThreshold` object with per-path keys but with Vitest's glob semantics (powered by `micromatch`). Unlike Jest, where the `global` key applies only to files not matched by any specific path key, Vitest's global thresholds apply to *all* files (including pattern-matched ones) — the per-pattern threshold then applies as an *additional* stricter constraint on top of the global, not as a replacement.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — layered global + per-pattern thresholds
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.spec.ts', 'src/**/*.d.ts'],
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      thresholds: {
        // Global baseline: applies to ALL files.
        lines:      80,
        branches:   70,
        functions:  80,
        statements: 80,
        perFile:    false,

        // Per-pattern overrides: ADDITIONAL constraints on top of global.
        // Files in src/core/ must meet 90% lines AND the global 80% (90 wins).
        'src/core/**': { lines: 90, branches: 85, functions: 90 },
        // Payment processing: near-100% required for compliance.
        'src/payments/**': { lines: 98, branches: 95, functions: 100 },
        // Legacy adapter layer: lower threshold during phased migration.
        'src/legacy/**': { lines: 60, branches: 50, functions: 60 },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The key behavioural difference between Vitest and Jest for per-pattern thresholds is the "global applies to all" vs "global applies to unmatched" distinction. In Jest, a file matched by a specific path key is *only* subject to that key's thresholds — the global threshold does not apply to it. In Vitest, the global threshold *also* applies, so you cannot use a per-pattern key to *relax* thresholds below the global baseline (the `src/legacy/**` example above sets lines to 60%, but if the global is 80%, the global still wins and legacy files must meet 80%). To genuinely lower thresholds for a legacy area in Vitest, you must either reduce the global threshold or exclude the legacy files from the global threshold calculation using `coverage.exclude`. This is a common source of confusion for teams migrating from Jest.

---

### Pattern 220 — Vitest `coverage.instrumenter` (Istanbul provider): switching the underlying instrumentation engine  [official]

Vitest's Istanbul provider supports an `instrumenter` sub-option (added in Vitest 4.1.5) that allows switching the underlying Istanbul instrumentation engine from the default `babel` instrumenter to the `swc` instrumenter (via `@vitest/coverage-istanbul` with SWC support). The SWC instrumenter is significantly faster for large TypeScript codebases because SWC's Rust-based parser and code generator operate 10–20x faster than Babel's JavaScript-based pipeline for transformation throughput. This matters at scale: for a project with 1,000 TypeScript files, switching from Babel to SWC instrumentation can reduce the instrumentation phase from 8 seconds to under 1 second. The SWC instrumenter respects all standard Istanbul `/* istanbul ignore */` directives and produces semantically identical coverage maps.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — Istanbul provider with SWC instrumenter
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      // Requires: npm install -D @vitest/coverage-istanbul
      // SWC instrumenter: 10–20x faster instrumentation phase for large TS codebases.
      // Introduced in Vitest 4.1.5 as an experimental option.
      instrumenter: 'swc',

      include: ['src/**/*.ts', 'src/**/*.tsx'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        'src/**/*.test.ts',
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/__mocks__/**',
      ],
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      thresholds: {
        lines:      85,
        branches:   75,
        functions:  85,
        statements: 85,
        autoUpdate: (n: number) => Math.floor(n),
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The SWC instrumenter is experimental (added in 4.1.5) and may not handle all TypeScript syntax edge cases that the Babel instrumenter handles — specifically, some decorator metadata patterns and certain `satisfies` + `as const` combinations in TypeScript 5.x produce slightly different instrumentation footprints. In practice, the SWC and Babel instrumenters produce identical coverage maps for the vast majority of TypeScript code, but teams using experimental TypeScript features (Stage 2/3 decorators, `using`/`await using` declarations) should validate that coverage maps are consistent before fully switching. Also note that the SWC instrumenter requires the `@swc/core` package to be installed — it is not bundled with `@vitest/coverage-istanbul` — so it adds a native binary dependency that may require platform-specific builds in CI.

## Cycle 44 Community Gotchas

### G146 — Vitest `coverage.changed: true` produces empty coverage reports when run inside a git worktree with a detached HEAD  [community]

Vitest's `coverage.changed` resolves the "changed files" list by running `git diff --name-only` against the specified ref. In CI pipelines that checkout code into a git worktree (a common pattern in monorepo CI systems where each job checks out a worktree in a temporary directory) or that use `git checkout --detach` to pin a specific commit, the git context may be in detached HEAD state with no upstream branch. When `coverage.changed` is set to `true` (meaning "compare against staged/unstaged changes"), a detached HEAD with a clean working tree produces a completely empty diff — and therefore an empty set of "changed files". Vitest silently emits a coverage report for zero files, all thresholds pass trivially (no files = no threshold violations), and the CI job reports green. **WHY it matters**: the coverage gate becomes a no-op: every PR passes because the changed-file set is empty, not because coverage is actually good. The symptom is a CI job that reports "Coverage: 100% (0/0 files)" — suspiciously perfect. The fix: always use the explicit `coverage.changed: 'BASE_SHA'` form in CI (never `true`), validate that `BASE_SHA` is a non-empty, reachable commit hash before Vitest starts, and add a pre-flight check that fails the job if `git diff --name-only $BASE_SHA` returns an empty result on a branch that is known to have changes.

### G147 — Istanbul `ignoreClassMethods` silently skips *all* methods of that name, including overloaded constructors  [community]

Vitest's Istanbul provider (and nyc) accept an `ignoreClassMethods` array listing method names to exclude from coverage. A common use case is suppressing coverage for lifecycle methods like `toJSON`, `toString`, or framework-generated `__metadata` methods that are always called internally and add noise to the report. The gotcha is that `ignoreClassMethods` matches by *method name only* — it applies to every class in the codebase that has a method with that name, regardless of class or module. Listing `'constructor'` in `ignoreClassMethods` suppresses coverage for *every* constructor in *every* class in the entire project. **WHY it matters**: a team that adds `'constructor'` to `ignoreClassMethods` to suppress noise from a single base class's complex constructor will inadvertently suppress constructor coverage for all 200 classes in the project, potentially hiding genuine coverage gaps in constructor validation logic (argument null-checks, invariant assertions). The fix: never add `'constructor'` or other universally-present method names to `ignoreClassMethods`; instead, add `/* istanbul ignore next */` directly above the specific constructor that should be suppressed, limiting the scope to that one instance.

### G148 — c8 `--all` with `--src` pointing to a symlinked directory emits duplicate file entries  [community]

c8's `--all` flag with `--src` scans the specified source directories for all files matching `--include` patterns and inserts them into the coverage map with 0% coverage before any tests run. When `--src` is set to a directory that is itself a symlink (e.g., `--src ./src` where `./src` is a symlink to `../packages/main/src`), c8 may enumerate both the symlink path (`./src/utils.ts`) and the real path (`../packages/main/src/utils.ts`) as separate entries, producing duplicate rows in the coverage report — one entry shows the actual test-run coverage, the other shows 0% (because coverage was attributed to the real path, not the symlink path). **WHY it matters**: the duplicate 0% entry drags down the aggregate coverage percentage and may trigger `--check-coverage` failures even though the code is actually well-covered. The symptom is seeing the same filename appear twice in the c8 HTML report with identical content but different paths. The fix: pass the real (resolved) path to `--src` rather than a symlink path; use `realpath --canonicalize-missing $(pwd)/src` in CI scripts to resolve symlinks before passing to c8.

### G149 — Jest `--coverage` flag overrides `collectCoverage: false` in config, but only when tests pass  [community]

Jest's `--coverage` CLI flag forces coverage collection regardless of the `collectCoverage: false` setting in `jest.config.ts`. This is expected and documented. The subtler gotcha is the reverse: when `collectCoverage: true` is set in config and tests *fail*, Jest still runs coverage instrumentation and produces a coverage report — but the coverage report is based on an incomplete test run (some tests never executed). The threshold check then runs against this incomplete coverage map and may *pass* (because the failing test file, which had low coverage, was the one that didn't run — removing it from the denominator makes everything else look better-covered). **WHY it matters**: a CI pipeline where tests fail but the coverage threshold also fails correctly catches two problems; but if the coverage threshold passes despite test failures, the pipeline may be configured to "fail on coverage but not on tests" and the broken tests go unnoticed for longer. The fix: always configure CI to fail the pipeline on any individual Jest exit code, not just on the coverage threshold; use `coverageThreshold` combined with `bail: 1` to ensure that the first failing test aborts the run rather than allowing Jest to continue accumulating partial coverage data from the remaining tests.

### G150 — Vitest `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate` writes to disk during `--run --watch=false` but not during interactive watch mode  [community]

`coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate` modifies the Vitest configuration file on disk when coverage exceeds the configured thresholds. This write only occurs in non-interactive runs (i.e., when Vitest is invoked with `--run` or `vitest run`). When Vitest is running in watch mode (the default when no `--run` flag is passed), `autoUpdate` is silently disabled — the thresholds are not updated and no warning is emitted. This means a developer who runs `vitest` (entering watch mode) and sees their coverage improve will *not* see the config file updated, then runs `vitest run` in CI and is surprised to see the thresholds *are* updated and a new diff appears in the working tree. **WHY it matters**: the asymmetric behaviour between watch-mode and run-mode leads to inconsistent developer expectations — "I thought autoUpdate was working because I saw 90% coverage in watch mode, but my config still says 80% and now CI is updating it." The fix: document in your contribution guide that `autoUpdate` only activates in `vitest run` mode; add a CI step comment that explicitly notes "this step may update coverage thresholds in vitest.config.ts — commit the result"; and consider using `autoUpdate: false` and a dedicated `vitest run --coverage && git diff --exit-code vitest.config.ts` check to make threshold drift explicit rather than auto-corrected.
