### Community Gotchas

**G237** — Vitest `coverage.all: true` without a matching `coverage.include` silently instruments `node_modules` test fixtures
When `coverage.all` is enabled without an explicit `coverage.include`, Vitest instruments every file under the project root that is not excluded. If the project root contains a `node_modules/.cache` directory with compiled JavaScript fixture files (common in projects that vendor test fixtures via npm link or local `file:` dependencies), those fixture files are instrumented and appear in the coverage report. The fixture files typically have very low coverage because they are never directly exercised by tests, which drags down aggregate metrics.
Why this matters: A project at 82% line coverage can drop to 71% overnight after a `npm install` that unpacks a new local-linked package containing JavaScript fixtures under `node_modules/`. The CI threshold gate fails, no code was changed, and the root cause is not obvious from the coverage report because the new low-coverage files appear under paths like `node_modules/my-local-package/fixtures/` which developers assume are excluded. The default `coverage.exclude` list does exclude `node_modules/**`, but `coverage.all` re-includes files by scanning the include glob, and if `include` is absent, Vitest's own internal scanning can bypass the node_modules exclusion for symlinked packages.
Fix: Always pair `coverage.all: true` with an explicit `coverage.include` that names only `src/**` or the equivalent application source directory. Example: `include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}']`. This prevents any ambiguity about which files are instrumented and makes the instrument set independent of what `npm install` drops under `node_modules`.

**G238** — Jest `collectCoverageFrom` pattern order gotcha: negation patterns before positive patterns are overwritten and produce over-inclusive coverage
Jest uses micromatch for glob evaluation in `collectCoverageFrom`, and micromatch processes all patterns in array order. If a negation pattern (e.g., `!src/**/*.stories.ts`) appears before the positive pattern it is intended to restrict (e.g., `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`), micromatch first excludes the stories files, then the subsequent positive pattern re-includes them, resulting in stories files appearing in coverage data. This is a micromatch semantic that surprises developers accustomed to gitignore-style pattern evaluation, where negation always overrides positive patterns regardless of order.
Why this matters: Storybook story files are particularly harmful in coverage data because they are rarely unit-tested — they exist for visual documentation, not logic — but they import and reference every component variant. When story files appear in coverage, every component function called only from stories (e.g., decorators, args factories) shows up as uncovered, generating dozens of false-positive coverage gaps. Teams waste time writing tests for code that is adequately covered by Storybook's visual testing pipeline, not unit tests.
Fix: Place all positive inclusion patterns first, then all negation patterns last in `collectCoverageFrom`. Treat the array as "include everything matching group A, then subtract groups B, C, D" — the subtraction must always come after the addition. Validate with: `node -e "const mm = require('micromatch'); const g = require('glob').sync; console.log(mm(g('src/**/*.ts'), ['src/**/*.ts','!src/**/*.stories.ts']).slice(0,5))"`.

**G239** — Vitest `thresholds.perFile: true` causes CI to fail on test helper files that are included in `coverage.include` but never directly called
When `coverage.thresholds.perFile` is `true`, every file matched by `coverage.include` must individually satisfy the threshold. If `coverage.include` inadvertently captures test helper files (e.g., `src/test-utils/render-helpers.ts`) that are imported by tests but whose internal functions are called indirectly through re-exports, V8 may report those helper files as partially covered because some re-exported utility functions are never invoked in isolation. Each such file then fails the per-file threshold, producing CI failures that are unrelated to business logic coverage quality.
Why this matters: The failure messages from per-file threshold violations list file paths and metric values but do not distinguish between "production code with insufficient tests" and "test infrastructure code with unusual call patterns". Engineers triaging the failure spend time investigating test helper files before realizing the issue is an overly broad `coverage.include` pattern rather than a genuine gap. This burns developer time on a false positive and reduces trust in the coverage gate.
Fix: Exclude test helper directories from `coverage.include` explicitly: add `'!src/test-utils/**'` and `'!src/**/__helpers__/**'` to the exclude list. Alternatively, place all test infrastructure in a directory outside `src/` (e.g., `test/helpers/`) so that `src/**` globs never capture them.

**G240** — NYC `ignore-class-method` config key is singular ("method") but the equivalent Vitest config key is plural ("Methods") — copying between tools silently fails
NYC's configuration key for ignoring class methods is `"ignore-class-method"` (singular, kebab-case). Vitest's equivalent is `coverage.ignoreClassMethods` (plural, camelCase). When a team migrates from NYC to Vitest and copies their `.nycrc.json` contents into `vitest.config.ts`, the `"ignore-class-method": ["render"]` entry is not recognized by Vitest — it is silently ignored without a warning. Vitest does not validate unknown configuration keys in the `coverage` object, so `ignoreClassMethods` defaults to `[]` and all formerly-ignored methods reappear in function coverage.
Why this matters: Lifecycle methods like Angular's `ngOnDestroy` or React class component's `componentDidCatch` that were previously excluded from coverage now count as uncovered functions. On a project with many components, this can drop function coverage by 5-15 percentage points. The migration PR's CI run fails the coverage gate, and the reviewer sees a large function-coverage drop with no corresponding code changes, making it appear that the migration itself damaged coverage rather than exposing a configuration translation error.
Fix: When migrating from NYC to Vitest, translate config keys explicitly rather than copying raw JSON. Keep a migration mapping comment: `// NYC: "ignore-class-method" → Vitest: ignoreClassMethods (plural, camelCase)`. Run `vitest --coverage --reporter=text` after migration and verify that the function count for files containing lifecycle methods matches the pre-migration NYC report.

**G241** — Jest `coverageThreshold` with glob patterns fails silently when no file matches the pattern — the threshold is skipped rather than erroring
When a `coverageThreshold` entry uses a glob pattern (e.g., `'./src/critical/**'`) and no files in the coverage data match that pattern, Jest silently skips the threshold check for that entry rather than failing with an error. This means a threshold configured to enforce 100% coverage on `src/critical/` will pass even if the directory is renamed to `src/core/` and the critical business logic is now completely uncovered.
Why this matters: Critical-file thresholds are typically added after a security review or incident to ensure specific modules always have near-total test coverage. If a directory rename or refactor breaks the pattern match, the threshold silently becomes a no-op, and the module that motivated the threshold is no longer protected. The coverage gate continues to pass, providing false confidence. This gap is especially dangerous for security-critical modules where 100% coverage is a compliance requirement.
Fix: Add a CI step that validates coverage threshold glob patterns against the actual directory structure before running Jest. A simple check: for each glob key in `coverageThreshold`, run `glob.sync(key, { cwd: projectRoot })` and fail if the result is empty. Alternatively, use Jest's `--verbose` output to inspect which threshold entries were evaluated — Jest logs "Threshold check skipped: no files found for pattern" in verbose mode, which can be grepped in CI.

## Cycle 63 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern P220** — Vitest `coverage.provider: 'v8'` with `resolveSourcemaps: true` for accurate TypeScript line mapping
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/__fixtures__/**'],
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'html'],
      // resolveSourcemaps ensures V8's raw JS positions are remapped
      // back to original TypeScript source lines via .map files
      resolveSourcemaps: true,
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
    },
  },
  resolve: {
    // Required: Vite must emit source maps for V8 to remap positions
    sourcemaps: true,
  },
});
// Validate: vitest --coverage 2>&1 | grep -i "could not map" should produce no output
```
Tradeoff: Setting `resolveSourcemaps: true` incurs a remapping pass over all V8 raw coverage entries after each test run, adding roughly 2–5 seconds per 1,000 instrumented files; on large monorepos this overhead compounds, making Istanbul (which instruments pre-transformed source once at startup) faster for total wall-clock CI time even though V8 is faster per test file.

**Pattern P221** — Jest `coverageThreshold` with `global` and per-directory tiers for mixed-criticality codebases
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/*.stories.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/index.ts',
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    // Baseline for all code
    global: {
      lines: 70,
      functions: 70,
      branches: 60,
      statements: 70,
    },
    // Elevated threshold for business-critical payment module
    './src/payments/': {
      lines: 95,
      functions: 95,
      branches: 90,
      statements: 95,
    },
    // Elevated threshold for authentication module
    './src/auth/': {
      lines: 90,
      functions: 90,
      branches: 85,
      statements: 90,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Per-directory glob thresholds in Jest are evaluated after the full coverage run and fail the process with a non-zero exit code that references the glob key, not a file path — meaning CI failure messages show the pattern string (`./src/payments/`) rather than the specific uncovered file, forcing developers to open the HTML report to identify the exact gap; contrast with `thresholds.perFile: true` in Vitest which names the specific failing file in the error output.

**Pattern P222** — NYC `.nycrc.json` `all: true` combined with `include` scoping to surface zero-tested files
```typescript
// .nycrc.json (plain JSON — no TypeScript, but define the shape here for reference)
// {
//   "all": true,
//   "include": ["src/**/*.js"],
//   "exclude": ["src/**/*.test.js", "src/**/__mocks__/**"],
//   "check-coverage": true,
//   "branches": 80,
//   "lines": 80,
//   "functions": 80,
//   "statements": 80,
//   "reporter": ["text", "lcov"],
//   "temp-dir": ".nyc_output"
// }

// Companion Node.js script to verify zero-tested files are detected:
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';

const report = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync('./coverage/coverage-summary.json', 'utf8')
);
const zeroTestedFiles = Object.entries(report)
  .filter(([k]) => k !== 'total')
  .filter(([, v]: [string, any]) => v.lines.pct === 0);

if (zeroTestedFiles.length > 0) {
  console.error('Zero-tested files detected:', zeroTestedFiles.map(([k]) => k));
  process.exit(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: `all: true` forces NYC to spawn a glob scan of all `include`-matching files before the test run, which adds significant startup latency (up to 10 seconds on repositories with 5,000+ source files) because NYC instruments every matched file whether or not it is `require`d during tests; without `all: true`, zero-tested files are completely invisible in the coverage summary and threshold checks, making it possible to ship entirely untested modules while passing CI.

**Pattern P223** — Vitest `thresholds.perFile: true` with a `coveragePathIgnorePatterns`-style exclude for generated proto files
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        // Generated protobuf files are deterministic; testing them adds no value
        'src/**/*.pb.ts',
        'src/**/*.pb-server.ts',
        'src/**/__generated__/**',
        'src/**/generated/**',
        // Test infrastructure that is called indirectly
        'src/test-utils/**',
      ],
      thresholds: {
        perFile: true,
        lines: 80,
        functions: 80,
        branches: 70,
        statements: 80,
      },
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'json-summary'],
    },
  },
});
// Run: vitest --coverage --reporter=verbose to see per-file pass/fail
```
Tradeoff: Enabling `thresholds.perFile: true` without excluding generated files causes every `.pb.ts` protobuf output file to fail the per-file threshold — protobuf-generated TypeScript contains dozens of serialization and deserialization functions, none of which are directly exercised by unit tests since they are exercised only through integration tests with a live gRPC endpoint; the exclude list must be maintained in sync with any code-generation pipelines to avoid threshold false positives after proto schema changes.

**Pattern P224** — Jest `coverageProvider: 'babel'` with custom `transformIgnorePatterns` for ESM-only npm packages
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  // babel provider (default) handles CommonJS transformation via Babel
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.(ts|tsx)$': ['babel-jest', {
      presets: [
        ['@babel/preset-env', { targets: { node: 'current' }, modules: 'commonjs' }],
        '@babel/preset-typescript',
      ],
    }],
  },
  // ESM-only packages must be listed here to be transformed (not ignored)
  transformIgnorePatterns: [
    '/node_modules/(?!(my-esm-pkg|another-esm-lib)/)',
  ],
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, functions: 80, branches: 70, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Adding ESM packages to the `transformIgnorePatterns` allowlist forces Babel to parse and transform their source on every test run, which increases test startup time proportionally with the size of the ESM package — a large ESM utility library (e.g., `date-fns` v3) can add 3–8 seconds to test startup; the V8 provider avoids this overhead entirely because V8 measures coverage at the bytecode level without Babel transformation, but V8 requires Node.js 18+ and produces less reliable branch coverage for transpiled async/await chains.

**Pattern P225** — Vitest `coverage.watermarks` for traffic-light HTML report colour bands
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      reporter: ['html', 'text', 'json-summary'],
      // watermarks define [low, high] percentage boundaries.
      // Below low  -> red  (critical gap)
      // low..high  -> yellow (acceptable but improving)
      // Above high -> green (healthy)
      watermarks: {
        statements: [70, 90],
        branches:   [60, 85],
        functions:  [70, 90],
        lines:      [70, 90],
      },
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      htmlDir: './coverage/html',
    },
  },
});
// Open coverage/html/index.html and verify red/yellow/green bands align with
// your team's quality expectations before committing the config.
```
Tradeoff: Lowering the `watermarks` low boundary (e.g., `statements: [50, 90]`) makes the HTML report show green even for modules at 55% coverage, which creates a false visual signal that the codebase is healthier than it actually is; teams that anchor `coverageThreshold` enforcement in CI at 70% but set watermarks with a low boundary of 50% will see HTML green indicators even when CI is about to fail the threshold gate on that same directory, causing confusion during code review.

**Pattern P226** — NYC `exclude-after-remap: false` with TypeScript declaration maps for source-accurate line attribution
```typescript
// Companion TypeScript configuration that drives NYC behaviour
// tsconfig.json (excerpt)
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "declarationMap": true,
//     "sourceMap": true,
//     "outDir": "dist"
//   }
// }

// .nycrc.json (excerpt)
// {
//   "exclude-after-remap": false,
//   "extension": [".ts", ".tsx"],
//   "require": ["ts-node/register"],
//   "reporter": ["text", "lcov"],
//   "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
// }

// Test runner invocation:
// nyc --exclude-after-remap false ts-mocha 'src/**/*.spec.ts'

// Verification script:
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
const output = execSync('nyc report --reporter=text').toString();
// Lines should reference src/*.ts paths, not dist/*.js paths.
// If dist paths appear, exclude-after-remap is incorrectly set to true.
const distReferences = output.split('\n').filter(l => l.includes('/dist/'));
console.assert(distReferences.length === 0, 'Coverage report references dist/ paths — set exclude-after-remap: false');
```
Tradeoff: Setting `exclude-after-remap: false` in NYC means the post-remap exclusion step is skipped, so any source file that source-maps back to a path that would otherwise be excluded (e.g., a `dist/` path generated from a test helper) now appears in the coverage output; teams must therefore ensure their `include` and `exclude` patterns in `.nycrc.json` correctly scope to `src/` paths rather than relying on the remap step to filter `dist/` artifacts, otherwise generated files re-enter the report.

**Pattern P227** — Jest `forceCoverageMatch` to collect coverage from test files that also contain production logic
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
  ],
  // forceCoverageMatch makes Jest collect coverage from files matching
  // these globs even if they are also test files.
  // Use case: co-located integration test files that export production
  // helper functions used by other tests.
  forceCoverageMatch: [
    'src/**/*.integration.ts',
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 75, functions: 75, branches: 65, statements: 75 },
  },
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: `forceCoverageMatch` is a blunt instrument — it adds an entire file class to coverage instrumentation, including the test scaffolding code within those integration files (describe blocks, beforeEach hooks, assertion callbacks), which inflates line and statement counts and makes coverage numbers appear higher than they actually are for production logic; prefer extracting shared production helpers from integration files into a dedicated `src/test-utils/` directory with its own coverage include rule rather than using `forceCoverageMatch`.

**Pattern P228** — Vitest `coverage.reportOnFailure: true` for CI coverage artifact preservation on red builds
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/*.stories.tsx'],
      // reportOnFailure ensures the coverage HTML report is written even
      // when tests fail. Without this, a failing test suite produces no
      // coverage artifact, so CI cannot upload coverage data to Codecov/Coveralls.
      reportOnFailure: true,
      reporter: ['html', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        functions: 80,
        branches: 70,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
// GitHub Actions step to upload coverage even on failure:
// - uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
//   if: always()  # <-- critical: run even when tests fail
//   with:
//     files: ./coverage/lcov.info
```
Tradeoff: Enabling `reportOnFailure: true` means every failing build writes a potentially large coverage directory (HTML reports can be 50–200 MB for large codebases), which is then uploaded as a CI artifact even when the test failures mean the coverage data is incomplete or misleading; teams that automatically post coverage percentages to PR comments from CI artifacts must guard against displaying partial coverage numbers from failed runs, or the PR coverage comment will show anomalously low coverage that disappears once tests pass.

**Pattern P229** — c8 `/* c8 ignore next N */` for TypeScript exhaustiveness check default branches
```typescript
// src/utils/assertExhaustive.ts
// Exhaustiveness helper that should never be reached at runtime.
// V8/c8 will flag the unreachable throw as an uncovered branch
// without an explicit ignore directive.

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  | { kind: 'rectangle'; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number };

function computeArea(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case 'circle':
      return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case 'rectangle':
      return shape.width * shape.height;
    case 'triangle':
      return 0.5 * shape.base * shape.height;
    /* c8 ignore next 3 */
    default:
      // TypeScript exhaustiveness guard — unreachable at runtime if types are sound.
      const _exhaustive: never = shape;
      throw new Error(`Unhandled shape: ${JSON.stringify(_exhaustive)}`);
  }
}

export { computeArea };
```
Tradeoff: Using `/* c8 ignore next 3 */` silences the V8 branch-coverage warning for the exhaustiveness default case, but also silences any future regression where the `default` branch becomes reachable due to a TypeScript type assertion override (`as any`) or an untyped external API call — the coverage ignore annotation masks the symptom rather than proving exhaustiveness; prefer asserting exhaustiveness via TypeScript's type system with `@ts-expect-error` on the `never` assignment to catch compile-time gaps, and reserve the ignore comment for runtime-confirmed-unreachable paths only.

**Pattern P230** — Vitest `coverage.ignoreClassMethods` for framework lifecycle hooks that are structurally required but never unit-testable
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts'],
      // ignoreClassMethods excludes specific method names from function
      // coverage counts across all classes. Useful for framework lifecycle
      // hooks that are only invoked by the framework runtime (not unit tests).
      ignoreClassMethods: [
        'ngOnInit',
        'ngOnDestroy',
        'ngAfterViewInit',
        'ngOnChanges',
        'componentDidCatch',
        'getSnapshotBeforeUpdate',
      ],
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov'],
      thresholds: {
        functions: 85,
        lines: 85,
        branches: 75,
        statements: 85,
      },
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Blanket-ignoring lifecycle method names across all classes means that a non-lifecycle method that happens to share a name (e.g., a domain object that coincidentally has an `ngOnInit` method due to a naming collision in a migration) is also silently excluded from function coverage, creating a genuine coverage gap without any indication in the report; prefer using `/* istanbul ignore next */` inline comments on individual lifecycle methods in files where the framework mandate is clear, reserving `ignoreClassMethods` only for projects with hundreds of Angular or React class components where inline annotation is impractical.

**Pattern P231** — Jest `coverageReporters` with `['text', { skipFull: true }]` to suppress fully-covered file noise
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/*.stories.tsx',
  ],
  // The text reporter with skipFull: true omits files at 100% from
  // the console table, showing only files with coverage gaps.
  // This dramatically reduces terminal output on mature codebases where
  // most files are fully covered and the interesting signal is the exceptions.
  coverageReporters: [
    ['text', { skipFull: true }],
    'lcov',
    'json-summary',
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      lines: 85,
      functions: 85,
      branches: 75,
      statements: 85,
    },
  },
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
};

export default config;
// Expected output: only files below 100% appear in the console table.
// Full coverage report is still written to coverage/lcov.info for CI upload.
```
Tradeoff: `skipFull: true` in the text reporter means developers running `jest --coverage` locally see only the files needing attention, but they lose the ability to quickly verify that a specific fully-covered file remained at 100% after a change — they must open `coverage/lcov.info` or the HTML report to confirm; in PR reviews where a reviewer wants to confirm that a new file has 100% coverage, the `skipFull` output is the correct signal (absence from the list means 100%), but this interpretation is non-obvious and requires team documentation.

**Pattern P232** — NYC `per-file: true` combined with `check-coverage` and `.nycrc.json` for monorepo workspace package enforcement
```typescript
// Root .nycrc.json (applied per workspace package via npm workspaces)
// {
//   "all": true,
//   "check-coverage": true,
//   "per-file": true,
//   "branches": 70,
//   "lines": 80,
//   "functions": 80,
//   "statements": 80,
//   "include": ["src/**/*.js"],
//   "exclude": [
//     "src/**/*.test.js",
//     "src/**/__mocks__/**",
//     "src/**/__fixtures__/**"
//   ],
//   "reporter": ["text", "lcov", "json-summary"],
//   "report-dir": "./coverage"
// }

// package.json test script integration
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

function runCoverageForWorkspace(packagePath: string): void {
  const result = execSync(
    `cd ${packagePath} && nyc --nycrc-path ../../.nycrc.json mocha 'src/**/*.test.js'`,
    { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: 'pipe' }
  );
  console.log(`Coverage passed for ${packagePath}`);
}

// CI invocation: npm workspaces run test:coverage
// Each workspace runs nyc independently; results are per-package, not aggregated.
```
Tradeoff: Running NYC with `per-file: true` in a monorepo means CI fails as soon as the first per-file threshold violation is detected in any workspace package, making the failure message reference only that file rather than providing a holistic view of which packages need the most work; teams frequently prefer running NYC with `per-file: false` first to identify which packages have aggregate coverage below threshold, then enabling `per-file` selectively only for packages that meet the aggregate bar, using a two-stage approach rather than a single gating step.

**Pattern P233** — Vitest `coverage.provider: 'istanbul'` with `/* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */` for esbuild comment stripping
```typescript
// src/env/featureFlags.ts
// esbuild (used by Vite/Vitest) strips comments during transpilation by default.
// The @preserve annotation tells esbuild to retain the istanbul directive.

export function isFeatureEnabled(flag: string): boolean {
  /* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') {
    // Test environment override path — always returns true in tests
    return true;
  }

  const flags = (globalThis as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__ ?? {};
  return Boolean(flags[flag]);
}

export function getEnvironmentTier(): 'dev' | 'staging' | 'prod' {
  /* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */
  if (!process.env.APP_ENV) {
    throw new Error('APP_ENV environment variable is required');
  }
  return process.env.APP_ENV as 'dev' | 'staging' | 'prod';
}
// Verification: run vitest --coverage and confirm that the ignored branches
// do not appear as uncovered in the HTML report. Without @preserve, esbuild
// strips the comment and istanbul sees an un-annotated uncovered branch.
```
Tradeoff: Adding `-- @preserve` to every Istanbul ignore comment is a Vitest-specific requirement driven by esbuild's comment-stripping behaviour; the `@preserve` annotation is not needed (and is silently harmless) when using Jest with Babel, but a team sharing a `src/` directory between a Vitest-based frontend and a Jest-based backend test suite must use `-- @preserve` everywhere to ensure the annotation survives both transpilers — omitting it on a file that is only tested by Jest will not cause a failure, but it creates an inconsistency where the same annotation is honoured in one test suite and silently dropped in the other.

**Pattern P234** — Jest `--coverageProvider=v8` CLI flag override for a single file investigation without changing `jest.config.ts`
```typescript
// jest.config.ts baseline (Istanbul provider for CI consistency)
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'babel', // Istanbul (default) for all CI runs
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, functions: 80, branches: 70, statements: 80 },
  },
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov'],
};

export default config;

// Local investigation command (overrides provider without editing config):
// jest --coverage --coverageProvider=v8 --testPathPattern=src/payments
//
// This runs only the payments test suite with V8 provider, producing
// native V8 coverage that can be compared against Istanbul output
// to identify discrepancies caused by Babel instrumentation artefacts.
//
// Comparison script (run after both providers):
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
const istanbul = JSON.parse(readFileSync('coverage-istanbul/coverage-summary.json', 'utf8'));
const v8 = JSON.parse(readFileSync('coverage-v8/coverage-summary.json', 'utf8'));
const diff = istanbul.total.lines.pct - v8.total.lines.pct;
console.log(`Istanbul vs V8 line coverage delta: ${diff.toFixed(1)}%`);
```
Tradeoff: The CLI `--coverageProvider` flag overrides the config value but does not affect how Babel or ts-jest transforms the source before V8 instruments it — if the project uses Babel transforms that alter branch structure (e.g., decorators compiled to class property assignments), V8 and Istanbul will produce different branch counts for the same source file, and using V8 locally to "investigate" Istanbul CI failures may lead to misleading conclusions where V8 shows higher coverage than Istanbul due to fewer synthetic branches.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G242** — Vitest esbuild comment stripping silently removes `/* istanbul ignore */` directives without `@preserve`, causing unexpected coverage failures after migrating from Jest
When Vitest's default esbuild transform processes source files, it strips all JavaScript comments as part of minification and dead-code optimisation, including `/* istanbul ignore next */` annotations. Without the `-- @preserve` suffix, these annotations disappear before the Istanbul coverage provider sees them. Developers migrating from Jest (which uses Babel and preserves comments) to Vitest discover that branches they had previously suppressed via ignore annotations are now reported as uncovered, failing CI thresholds.
Why this matters: The failure is silent and non-obvious — Vitest does not warn that coverage annotations were stripped. A team migrating a large codebase may see coverage drop by 5–15 percentage points immediately after switching to Vitest, with no clear error message indicating why. Every affected file requires its ignore comments to be suffixed with `-- @preserve`, and the count of affected files may be in the hundreds for a mature codebase with extensive environment-guard branches.
Fix: Run a one-time search-and-replace across the codebase: `grep -rn "istanbul ignore" src/ | grep -v "@preserve"` to find all non-preserved annotations, then replace `/* istanbul ignore next */` with `/* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */`. Add a lint rule (e.g., a custom ESLint rule or a pre-commit grep hook) to prevent future annotations from being added without `@preserve`.

**G243** — Jest `coverageThreshold` with `global` silently passes when `collectCoverageFrom` matches zero files due to a misconfigured project root
When `collectCoverageFrom` patterns resolve to zero files — typically because the working directory from which Jest is invoked differs from `<rootDir>` (common in monorepos where Jest is run from a subdirectory), or because a path separator mismatch on Windows causes glob patterns with forward slashes to fail — Jest collects no coverage data and reports 100% coverage for every metric against an empty file set. The `coverageThreshold` global check then passes trivially because 100% is greater than or equal to any threshold value.
Why this matters: A CI pipeline that uses `jest --coverage` as a coverage gate provides false assurance: every threshold passes, no HTML report is generated, and the coverage badge shows 100% — but zero files were actually instrumented. This situation is particularly dangerous when the jest config is shared across multiple packages and an incorrect `rootDir` or `roots` configuration is introduced. The symptom (100% coverage, no HTML artifacts) is mistaken for a healthy codebase rather than a configuration error.
Fix: Add an explicit validation step before the threshold check: `const summary = require('./coverage/coverage-summary.json'); const fileCount = Object.keys(summary).filter(k => k !== 'total').length; if (fileCount === 0) throw new Error('Coverage collected zero files — check collectCoverageFrom patterns');`. Alternatively, assert that `coverage-summary.json` exists and contains more than one key before the Jest process exits.

**G244** — NYC `all: true` combined with `ts-node/register` causes double-instrumentation of TypeScript files that are both `require`d and `import`ed via interop
When NYC runs with `all: true` and `ts-node/register` is active, TypeScript files are instrumented by NYC during the `require`/`import` phase. If the project uses both CommonJS `require` (through `ts-node`) and ES module dynamic `import()` interop (through a Node.js ESM loader), the same TypeScript file can be loaded twice — once via the CJS require path (instrumented by NYC) and once via the ESM import path (not instrumented, or instrumented by a separate loader). NYC's coverage aggregation then attributes only the CJS execution to the file's coverage counters, making functions called exclusively through the ESM path appear uncovered.
Why this matters: Projects that are mid-migration from CommonJS to ESM are particularly vulnerable. A utility function that has been moved to an ESM export but is still re-exported from a CJS barrel file will show 0% coverage for the ESM invocation path, even if the function is called extensively through the ESM import in every test. The aggregate coverage for the file drops dramatically, and threshold failures appear in modules that are well-tested but accessed through the wrong module resolution path.
Fix: Standardise on a single module system for the test suite. If migrating to ESM, use NYC's `--experimental-vm-modules` flag with Jest or configure Vitest (which handles ESM natively) rather than mixing `ts-node` CJS and ESM dynamic imports in the same coverage run. If CJS is required, ensure all `import()` calls are transpiled to `require()` before NYC instruments them.

**G245** — Vitest `coverage.all: true` in watch mode re-instruments the entire file set on every file save, causing multi-second delays in hot-reload cycles
When Vitest runs in watch mode with `coverage.all: true`, every file save that triggers a re-run causes Vitest to re-instrument all files matched by `coverage.include` from scratch before running the changed test. For projects with 500+ source files, this re-instrumentation pass takes 3–8 seconds, making the watch mode feedback loop frustratingly slow. Developers frequently disable coverage in watch mode entirely, losing the ability to monitor coverage changes while iterating.
Why this matters: The implicit expectation when enabling `coverage.all` is that it applies to full CI runs, not interactive development. However, Vitest applies the same configuration to both modes unless explicitly guarded. Teams that commit a `vitest.config.ts` with `coverage.all: true` and no watch-mode guard force every developer to experience slow hot-reload, reducing the appeal of using coverage-guided development techniques locally.
Fix: Guard `coverage.all` behind an environment variable that is only set in CI: `all: process.env.CI === 'true'`. This ensures local watch mode runs use lazy instrumentation (only files actually imported during the test run are instrumented), while CI runs instrument the full file set to detect zero-tested modules. Document the pattern in the project's `CONTRIBUTING.md` so developers understand why `all` is conditional.

**G246** — Jest `--testPathPattern` with `--coverage` collects coverage only for files exercised by the filtered tests, not the full `collectCoverageFrom` set — thresholds check the filtered subset
When Jest is run with both `--testPathPattern=src/payments` and `--coverage`, coverage is collected only for the files that are imported (directly or transitively) during the filtered test execution. If `collectCoverageFrom` contains `src/**/*.ts` but the payments tests only import 40 files out of 400, the coverage threshold is checked against those 40 files alone. A global threshold of 80% lines may pass trivially on the filtered 40 files even if many of them have only 60% coverage — because the filtered file set has inflated average coverage compared to the full codebase.
Why this matters: Developers running targeted coverage checks (e.g., `jest --testPathPattern=src/payments --coverage` before a PR) receive a false signal that their changes are well-covered, and the global threshold passes against the filtered file set. The full CI run with all tests may then fail the threshold against the complete 400-file set, revealing coverage gaps that the developer's local targeted run did not surface. This discrepancy erodes trust in local coverage checks as a meaningful pre-commit gate.
Fix: Use `--collectCoverageFrom='src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'` as an explicit CLI override when running targeted pattern tests to force Jest to include the full file set in coverage output even for a filtered test run. Alternatively, run `jest --coverage` without `--testPathPattern` in CI and use `--testPathPattern` only for local iteration without the `--coverage` flag.

## Cycle 64 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern P235** — Vitest V8 provider with `reportsDirectory` isolation per workspace package
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts (root workspace config)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reportsDirectory: './coverage/root',
      include: ['packages/*/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'packages/*/src/**/*.d.ts',
        'packages/*/src/**/__mocks__/**',
        'packages/*/src/**/index.ts', // barrel re-exports only
      ],
      all: process.env.CI === 'true',
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'html'],
    },
  },
});
// Each workspace package overrides reportsDirectory to prevent
// cross-package coverage report collisions during parallel runs:
// vitest.config.ts (packages/auth):
//   coverage.reportsDirectory: '../../coverage/auth'
```
Tradeoff: Isolating `reportsDirectory` per package prevents parallel Vitest workspace runs from clobbering each other's `lcov.info` files, but requires a post-CI merge step (using `lcov --add-tracefile`) to produce a unified coverage badge — if the merge step is omitted, Codecov or Coveralls will only ingest the last package's report uploaded, silently under-reporting aggregate coverage.

**Pattern P236** — Jest `coverageThreshold` with negative-number absolute cap for critical modules
```typescript
// jest.config.ts — mixed positive-percent and negative-absolute thresholds
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: {
      lines: 75,
      branches: 65,
      functions: 75,
      statements: 75,
    },
    './src/payments/': {
      lines: 95,
      branches: 90,
      functions: 100,
      statements: -0, // zero uncovered statements allowed
    },
    './src/auth/session.ts': {
      branches: 100,
      functions: 100,
      lines: 100,
      statements: 100,
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Using `statements: -0` (the negative-number syntax for zero allowed uncovered statements) on a payment module enforces absolute coverage without requiring 100% line coverage, but if the module grows by even one untested statement, CI fails immediately — this creates a ratchet effect where new developers must write tests before merging any payment logic change, which improves quality but slows down emergency hotfixes where time pressure is high.

**Pattern P237** — NYC `.nycrc.json` with `per-file: true` and workspace glob scoping
```typescript
// .nycrc.json (project root)
{
  "all": true,
  "per-file": true,
  "include": ["packages/*/src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": [
    "packages/*/src/**/*.spec.ts",
    "packages/*/src/**/*.test.ts",
    "packages/*/src/**/fixtures/**",
    "packages/*/src/**/mocks/**"
  ],
  "branches": 70,
  "lines": 80,
  "functions": 80,
  "statements": 80,
  "reporter": ["text", "lcov", "json-summary"],
  "exclude-after-remap": false
}
// Usage in package.json scripts:
// "test:coverage": "nyc --cwd . mocha 'packages/*/test/**/*.spec.js'"
// "coverage:check": "nyc check-coverage --per-file"
```
Tradeoff: Setting `per-file: true` in `.nycrc.json` catches zero-coverage files that are masked by high aggregate coverage in other modules, but a monorepo with 300+ files will produce a verbose per-file threshold failure table that is difficult to parse in CI logs — teams should pair this with a `nyc report --reporter=json-summary` step and a small Node script that formats only the failing files to keep CI output actionable.

**Pattern P238** — Vitest `thresholds.perFile` auto-fail for leaf utility modules
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enforce per-file thresholds with Istanbul provider
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/types.ts'],
      thresholds: {
        perFile: true,
        autoUpdate: false,
        // Global floor applied to every individual file:
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Vitest's `thresholds.perFile` applies the same threshold values to every file matched by `coverage.include`, so pure utility files and large orchestration modules are held to identical standards — teams that want tiered thresholds (100% on utils, 70% on controllers) must split coverage configuration across multiple Vitest project entries or accept that a single complex orchestration file below the threshold will fail the entire suite.

**Pattern P239** — Istanbul `/* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */` with esbuild and Vitest
```typescript
// src/utils/platform-guard.ts
// Pattern for annotating untestable environment branches in Vitest+esbuild

export function getStorageBackend(): Storage {
  /* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */
  if (typeof window === 'undefined') {
    // Server-side execution path — never reached in jsdom test environment.
    // The @preserve suffix prevents esbuild from stripping this annotation
    // during Vitest's default esbuild transform step.
    return new Map() as unknown as Storage;
  }
  return window.localStorage;
}

export function isSecureContext(): boolean {
  /* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */
  if (typeof window?.isSecureContext === 'undefined') {
    return false; // Node.js / old browser fallback
  }
  return window.isSecureContext;
}
```
Tradeoff: Adding `-- @preserve` to every ignore annotation prevents esbuild from stripping them during Vitest's transform, but it also means these annotations survive into production bundle analysis tools (like Webpack Bundle Analyzer or `source-map-explorer`) which may surface the annotations as unexpected source content — teams should audit whether their bundler also strips comments or whether preserved annotations leak into shipped JavaScript.

**Pattern P240** — Jest `collectCoverageFrom` with negated globs to exclude generated protobuf files
```typescript
// jest.config.ts — exclude generated code from coverage instrumentation
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    // Exclude generated protobuf and GraphQL files
    '!src/**/*.pb.ts',
    '!src/**/*.pb.d.ts',
    '!src/**/__generated__/**',
    '!src/**/generated/**',
    // Exclude barrel/re-export files (no logic to test)
    '!src/**/index.ts',
    '!src/**/index.tsx',
    // Exclude type-only files
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/types.ts',
    '!src/**/types.tsx',
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, functions: 80, branches: 70, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Excluding generated protobuf and GraphQL files from `collectCoverageFrom` keeps coverage metrics meaningful and prevents inflated line counts from skewing thresholds, but if any hand-written logic is accidentally co-located in a `__generated__` directory (e.g., custom resolvers auto-placed there by a code generator), it is silently excluded from coverage enforcement and can accumulate untested code without triggering threshold failures.

**Pattern P241** — Vitest `coverage.all: true` guarded by `CI` env with lazy local mode
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — environment-aware coverage.all
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // Only instrument ALL files in CI; locally use lazy instrumentation
      // to keep watch-mode hot-reload under 500 ms
      all: isCI,
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/fixtures/**'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      reporter: isCI
        ? ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary']
        : ['text'], // minimal reporter for local runs
      thresholds: isCI
        ? { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 }
        : undefined, // no threshold enforcement locally
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Disabling `coverage.all` locally means developers only see coverage for files imported during their specific test run — a new file added to `src/` but not yet imported by any test will appear to have 100% coverage locally (because it is not in the coverage report at all) but will appear as 0% in CI once `all: true` picks it up, creating a false sense of completeness that is only revealed at PR time rather than during local development.

**Pattern P242** — NYC `exclude-after-remap: false` for TypeScript declaration map coverage
```typescript
// .nycrc.json — prevent source-map remapping from dropping coverage data
{
  "all": true,
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["src/**/*.spec.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"],
  "extension": [".ts"],
  "require": ["ts-node/register"],
  "sourceMap": true,
  "instrument": true,
  "exclude-after-remap": false,
  "reporter": ["text", "lcov", "html"],
  "branches": 75,
  "lines": 80,
  "functions": 80,
  "statements": 80
}
// The exclude-after-remap: false flag is critical when TypeScript
// declaration maps (.d.ts.map) remap coverage back to .d.ts files,
// which are typically in an exclude list. Without this flag, NYC
// silently drops coverage data for remapped files.
```
Tradeoff: Setting `exclude-after-remap: false` prevents NYC from dropping coverage data that source maps remap to excluded files (such as `.d.ts` files), preserving accurate coverage for TypeScript projects with declaration maps; however, this can cause NYC to report coverage for `.d.ts` files in the output table, cluttering the report with type-only files that have no executable statements and making the "uncovered files" list harder to scan for genuine coverage gaps.

**Pattern P243** — Jest `forceCoverageMatch` to include co-located CLI scripts in coverage
```typescript
// jest.config.ts — force instrumentation of files not imported by tests
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  // Include CLI entry points that are executed directly by Node, not imported
  // by any test suite, so they would otherwise appear as 0% covered:
  forceCoverageMatch: [
    'bin/**/*.ts',
    'scripts/**/*.ts',
    'src/**/cli.ts',
    'src/**/migrate.ts',
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 75, functions: 75, branches: 65, statements: 75 },
    './bin/': { lines: 60, functions: 60, branches: 50, statements: 60 },
  },
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Using `forceCoverageMatch` to include CLI scripts that are not imported by any test suite forces them into the coverage report with 0% coverage until tests are written for them, which causes threshold failures and makes the gap visible — this is the desired ratchet behaviour, but on projects with many legacy scripts the sudden appearance of dozens of 0% files after enabling `forceCoverageMatch` can cause a large threshold regression that blocks CI until addressed en masse.

**Pattern P244** — Vitest `coverage.watermarks` for HTML report colour-band calibration
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — calibrate coverage colour bands to project maturity
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      reporter: ['html', 'text', 'lcov'],
      // Watermarks control colour bands in the HTML report:
      // [low, medium] — below low is red, between is yellow, above is green
      watermarks: {
        statements: [70, 85],
        branches: [60, 80],
        functions: [70, 85],
        lines: [70, 85],
      },
      thresholds: {
        lines: 70,
        branches: 60,
        functions: 70,
        statements: 70,
      },
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Aligning the lower watermark value with the threshold value means the HTML report colour-codes files as red exactly when they would fail CI, giving developers an intuitive visual mapping between red-in-report and fail-in-CI; however, if the threshold is later raised without also raising the watermark, files can appear green in the HTML report while still failing the numeric threshold, causing confusion where the visual report and the CI pass/fail signal disagree.

**Pattern P245** — Jest `coverageReporters` with `skipFull: true` for noise reduction
```typescript
// jest.config.ts — suppress fully-covered files from text reporter output
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  coverageReporters: [
    // Text reporter with skipFull suppresses 100%-covered files,
    // making the console output focus on files with gaps:
    ['text', { skipFull: true }],
    // Always generate lcov for CI upload to Codecov/Coveralls:
    'lcov',
    // JSON summary for programmatic threshold validation scripts:
    'json-summary',
    // HTML for human review of uncovered lines:
    ['html', { skipFull: true, subdir: 'html' }],
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, functions: 80, branches: 70, statements: 80 },
  },
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: The `skipFull: true` option on the `text` reporter reduces console noise from fully-covered files so developers can immediately see the gaps, but it makes it impossible to visually verify that a specific module is at 100% coverage by scanning the console output — developers who want to confirm that a critical module was not accidentally regressed must open the HTML report rather than trusting the console summary.

**Pattern P246** — NYC `check-coverage` as a separate CI step from test execution
```typescript
// package.json scripts — decouple test execution from coverage enforcement
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "mocha 'src/**/*.spec.ts' --require ts-node/register",
    "test:coverage": "nyc npm run test",
    "coverage:report": "nyc report --reporter=text --reporter=lcov --reporter=json-summary",
    "coverage:check": "nyc check-coverage --branches 70 --lines 80 --functions 80 --statements 80",
    "coverage:check:perfile": "nyc check-coverage --per-file --branches 60 --lines 70 --functions 70 --statements 70"
  }
}
// .nycrc.json
{
  "all": true,
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["src/**/*.spec.ts"],
  "reporter": ["lcov", "json"],
  "exclude-after-remap": false,
  "produce-source-map": true
}
// CI pipeline runs: npm run test:coverage && npm run coverage:report && npm run coverage:check
```
Tradeoff: Separating `nyc <test-runner>` (which collects data) from `nyc check-coverage` (which enforces thresholds) allows the CI pipeline to upload the lcov report to Codecov before failing on thresholds, ensuring coverage history is recorded even when a PR reduces coverage; the tradeoff is that the `nyc` temporary data directory (`.nyc_output/`) must be preserved between CI steps, which requires explicit artifact caching or sequential steps within the same job — if the `.nyc_output/` directory is not available when `coverage:check` runs, it silently reports 0% and check-coverage passes trivially.

**Pattern P247** — Vitest `coverage.ignoreClassMethods` for framework lifecycle exclusion
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — exclude React and Angular lifecycle methods from coverage
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'istanbul',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts'],
      // Exclude framework lifecycle methods that are called by the framework
      // itself, not by test code — testing these requires shallow rendering
      // which is often not worth the maintenance cost:
      ignoreClassMethods: [
        'ngOnInit',
        'ngOnDestroy',
        'ngOnChanges',
        'ngAfterViewInit',
        'ngAfterContentInit',
        'componentDidMount',
        'componentWillUnmount',
        'componentDidUpdate',
        'shouldComponentUpdate',
        'render', // class component render — use RTL, not coverage
      ],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Excluding lifecycle methods from coverage enforcement via `ignoreClassMethods` prevents spurious failures when framework-controlled methods are not directly tested, but it also means that a lifecycle method containing a critical bug (e.g., a `ngOnDestroy` that fails to unsubscribe from an Observable) can have zero test coverage and zero visibility in the coverage report — teams should compensate by adding at least one integration test per component that exercises the full mount/unmount cycle.

**Pattern P248** — Jest threshold ratcheting via external JSON config file
```typescript
// jest.config.ts — incremental coverage adoption in brownfield codebase
import type { Config } from 'jest';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { resolve } from 'path';

// Read current thresholds from a tracked JSON file so they can be
// ratcheted up incrementally via automated PR commits:
const thresholdsPath = resolve(__dirname, './coverage-thresholds.json');
const thresholds = JSON.parse(readFileSync(thresholdsPath, 'utf8'));

const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'babel',
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    'src/**/*.{ts,tsx}',
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/legacy/**', // legacy code excluded until refactored
  ],
  coverageThreshold: thresholds,
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
};

export default config;
// coverage-thresholds.json (tracked in git, bumped by CI bot):
// { "global": { "lines": 78, "branches": 68, "functions": 78, "statements": 78 } }
```
Tradeoff: Storing coverage thresholds in a separate `coverage-thresholds.json` file and importing them into `jest.config.ts` enables automated ratcheting (a bot can bump the values when coverage improves) without touching the Jest config directly, but it introduces a runtime `readFileSync` call during Jest configuration loading — if the file is missing or malformed (e.g., due to a merge conflict), Jest fails to parse its configuration entirely, blocking all test execution rather than just failing the coverage check.

**Pattern P249** — V8 `/* c8 ignore next N */` for switch exhaustiveness defaults
```typescript
// src/utils/status-formatter.ts
// c8 ignore comments for exhaustiveness-checked switch statements

type OrderStatus = 'pending' | 'processing' | 'shipped' | 'delivered';

export function formatOrderStatus(status: OrderStatus): string {
  switch (status) {
    case 'pending':
      return 'Awaiting confirmation';
    case 'processing':
      return 'Being prepared';
    case 'shipped':
      return 'On its way';
    case 'delivered':
      return 'Delivered successfully';
    /* c8 ignore next 3 */
    default:
      // TypeScript's exhaustiveness check prevents this branch at compile time,
      // but the runtime default is required for JavaScript callers and
      // deserialized data that bypasses TypeScript type checking.
      throw new Error(`Unhandled status: ${status as string}`);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `/* c8 ignore next N */` on exhaustiveness-guard default cases prevents the branch from appearing as uncovered in V8 coverage reports, accurately reflecting that the branch is unreachable through TypeScript-typed callers; however, if the `OrderStatus` union is later extended with a new member and the switch statement is not updated, the TypeScript compiler will catch the missing case at compile time — but if the ignore comment suppresses a genuinely reachable branch added by a JavaScript caller, the coverage gap is silently hidden and the runtime throw will never be tested.

### Community Gotchas

**G247** — Vitest V8 provider reports different branch counts than Istanbul for optional chaining expressions compiled by esbuild
When Vitest uses the V8 provider and esbuild transforms optional chaining (`a?.b?.c`) into conditional expressions, V8 counts the implicit null-checks as branches but associates them with the transpiled output lines rather than the original TypeScript source lines. Istanbul, which instruments before transpilation (or uses Babel), counts the same optional chain as a single branch in the original source. On a large codebase, switching from Istanbul to V8 can cause branch coverage to drop by 8–20 percentage points for the same test suite, even though the same logical paths are being executed.
Why this matters: A team that migrates from Vitest Istanbul to Vitest V8 for performance gains will observe a significant branch coverage drop in CI metrics, triggering threshold failures. The root cause is not reduced test quality — it is a difference in how the two providers count branches for syntactic sugar that desugars to conditional expressions. If thresholds are calibrated against Istanbul output, they must be recalibrated before switching to V8, or the migration will appear to cause a coverage regression.
Fix: Before migrating providers, run both providers against the full test suite and compare `coverage-summary.json` branch percentages. Recalibrate thresholds to the V8 baseline, not the Istanbul baseline. Add a comment in `vitest.config.ts` documenting the provider choice and the threshold values that correspond to it, so a future provider switch prompts a threshold review.

**G248** — NYC `all: true` with `--require ts-node/register` resolves `include` globs relative to process working directory, not the config file location
When NYC is run from a monorepo root with `--cwd packages/auth` and `.nycrc.json` specifies `"include": ["src/**/*.ts"]`, NYC resolves the glob relative to the current working directory of the Node.js process, not relative to the directory containing `.nycrc.json`. If the test runner changes `process.cwd()` (e.g., via Jest's `rootDir` or Mocha's `--file` option), the `include` patterns silently match no files, and `all: true` instruments the entire `node_modules` tree instead — causing orders-of-magnitude increases in coverage instrumentation time and producing a coverage report that mixes application code with dependency code.
Why this matters: The failure mode is non-obvious: NYC does not warn that `include` matched zero application files. Coverage run time increases from seconds to minutes, and the output report contains hundreds of `node_modules` files with near-zero coverage that drown out the application coverage data. The aggregate coverage percentage drops to near-zero because the entire `node_modules` tree is now in the denominator.
Fix: Always pass `--cwd <directory>` explicitly to NYC to pin the working directory, and validate that `include` patterns match at least one application file before running tests. Add a CI pre-check step that counts matched files and fails if the count is zero.

**G249** — Jest `coverageThreshold` glob path keys silently pass with 100% when the glob matches zero files, unlike literal paths which throw
Jest's `coverageThreshold` implementation distinguishes between literal file paths and glob patterns: a literal path (e.g., `'./src/auth/session.ts'`) throws an error if the file is not found, but a glob pattern (e.g., `'./src/auth/**/*.ts'`) silently passes with 100% coverage if the glob matches zero files. This asymmetry means that a glob-based threshold for a directory that was renamed or deleted stops enforcing coverage without any CI failure.
Why this matters: A team that relies on `'./src/payments/**/*.ts': { branches: 100 }` to enforce complete coverage of payment logic will silently lose that enforcement if the `src/payments/` directory is renamed to `src/billing/` during a refactor — the threshold glob no longer matches any files, Jest reports 100% (vacuous truth), and the renamed `src/billing/` directory has no corresponding threshold entry. Payment logic can accumulate coverage gaps without any CI signal.
Fix: Audit `coverageThreshold` glob keys after every directory rename or restructure. Add a post-coverage validation script that reads `coverage-summary.json` and asserts that every expected module path is present in the report — if a key path is absent, throw an error before the threshold check runs.

**G250** — Vitest `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate: true` silently lowers thresholds when coverage drops, treating regressions as new baselines
When `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate` is set to `true` in `vitest.config.ts`, Vitest automatically rewrites the threshold values in the config file to match the current coverage percentages whenever coverage drops below the configured thresholds — instead of failing CI, it updates the config to make the lower coverage pass. This means that a PR that reduces branch coverage from 82% to 71% will trigger an automatic config update that sets `branches: 71`, and the PR merges with no threshold failure and a silently degraded coverage floor.
Why this matters: The feature is intended for initial setup (bootstrapping thresholds from a greenfield codebase), but teams that enable it globally or forget to disable it in CI unknowingly convert their threshold config into a "current coverage is always the target" system. Over time, thresholds drift downward with every coverage regression, providing false assurance. The config file's threshold values become a historical record of the lowest coverage ever reached rather than a quality floor.
Fix: Never set `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate: true` in `vitest.config.ts` files committed to version control. If using it locally for bootstrapping, add it to `.gitignore`-excluded local config overrides, or add a `git diff --exit-code vitest.config.ts` step in CI that fails if the config was modified by the coverage run.

**G251** — Jest `collectCoverageFrom` negated globs are order-dependent and a positive glob after a negation re-includes previously excluded files
Jest processes `collectCoverageFrom` array entries in order, and a positive glob appearing after a negating `!` glob will re-include files that were previously excluded. For example, `['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/__mocks__/**', 'src/**/__mocks__/index.ts']` re-includes `src/**/__mocks__/index.ts` even though the preceding negation excluded the entire `__mocks__` directory. Developers who add new patterns to the array without understanding the ordering rules can accidentally re-include generated, mock, or test-helper files that inflate the total instrumented file count and reduce aggregate coverage percentages.
Why this matters: A developer adding a one-off include for a specific index file (`'src/**/index.ts'`) after a broad exclusion (`'!src/**/index.ts'`) accidentally re-enables coverage instrumentation for all barrel files, adding hundreds of files with near-zero coverage to the report and dropping aggregate coverage below thresholds. The failure is confusing because the glob patterns appear correct in isolation — the ordering dependency is not obvious from the Jest documentation.
Fix: Enforce a strict ordering convention in code review: all positive globs first, all negating `!` globs last. Validate the final resolved file list in CI by asserting that the count of instrumented files falls within an expected range between PRs to catch unexpected inclusions early.
